- **Impact number**, also **population impact number**, **NEPP**, **Population impact number of eliminating a risk factor**: measures expressing effect as counts in a population, the named members being the population impact number, case impact number, exposure impact number, exposed cases impact number, disease impact number, number of events prevented in your population, and PIN-ER-t.

- **Exposure misclassification**, also **Non-differential misclassification**, **Differential misclassification**, **Independent misclassification**, **Dependent misclassification**, **classical error structure**, **Berkson error structure**: wrong assignment of exposure status, sorted into non-differential and differential, independent and dependent forms, and modelled by the classical measurement error model or the Berkson measurement error model, which is an error structure rather than a bias named for Berkson.

- **Age-period-cohort analysis**, also **APC analysis**, **Age effect**, **calendar-time effect**, **Cohort effect**, **birth-cohort effect**, **Birth cohort analysis**, **cohort table**, **age-cohort format**, **Cross-sectional age gradient**, **cross-sectional age curve**, **Longitudinal age gradient**, **within-cohort age curve**, **Lexis triangle**, **Trend surface method**, **Cohort membership**, **birth-year grouping**: separation of age, period or calendar-time and cohort or generation effects in rate tables, displayed on the Lexis diagram, Lexis surface, age-by-period table and period-cohort format. - **Prediction model study**, also **prognostic model study**, **clinical prediction model study**, **Model development study**, **leave-one-centre-out validation**, **External validation**, **independent validation**, **Temporal validation**, **Geographic validation**, **Domain validation**, **model revision**, **recalibration**, **model impact study**, **clinical impact study**: development or evaluation of a model giving individual risk, staged as the model development or derivation study, internal validation, internal-external cross-validation, external, temporal, geographic and domain or transportability validation, model updating, and the impact study. - **Prognosis research strategy framework**, also **PROGRESS framework**, **Prognostic research**, **Prognostic factor study**, **prognostic marker study**, **type 1 prognosis research**, **type 4 prognosis research**, **predictors of treatment effect research**, **treatment effect modifier marker**: the four-theme typology of prognosis research, namely overall prognosis research, prognostic factor research, prognostic model research and stratified medicine research, with the prognostic factor and the predictive factor as its objects. ### Diagnostic accuracy and screening evaluation

- **Diagnostic accuracy study**, also **test accuracy study**, **test under evaluation**, **criterion standard**, **Imperfect reference standard**, **flawed reference standard**, **Composite reference standard**, **latent class analysis of test accuracy**, **discrepant resolution**: comparison of an index test against a reference standard, with the imperfect, composite and latent class reference standards, and discrepant analysis or delayed verification as a criticised repair. - **Single-gate design**, also **one-gate design**, **cohort-type accuracy study**, **Two-gate design**, **two-gate sampling**: one consecutive series of patients suspected of the condition, all receiving index test and reference standard, set against the two-gate or case-control accuracy design that samples known cases and known non-cases separately. - **Positive predictive value**, also **PPV**, **precision**, **NPV**, **Positive likelihood ratio**, **diagnostic likelihood ratio positive**, **diagnostic likelihood ratio negative**: the proportion of positives that are true, paired with the negative predictive value, and computed with the positive and negative likelihood ratios. - **Phases of biomarker development**, also **Pepe phases**, **five-phase biomarker framework**, **analytic validity clinical validity clinical utility framework**: the staged programme running from preclinical exploratory studies to cancer control, paired with the ACCE framework of analytic validity, clinical validity, clinical utility and associated implications. - **Prevalence screen**, also **prevalent screen**, **first screen**, **Incidence screen**, **referral rate for further assessment**, **uptake rate**, **attendance rate**, **coverage of the target population**, **rescreening rate**, **diagnostic yield**, **Screen-detected case**: the first screening round, followed by the incidence or subsequent screen at each interscreening interval, and described by the screening participation rate, screening coverage, reattendance rate, recall rate, yield of screening and detection rate. - **Interval case**, also **interval cancer**: a case arising between scheduled screens or after a negative screen, whose interval cancer rate is set against programme sensitivity, episode sensitivity and programme specificity, with lead time and sojourn time governing what screening could have caught.

- **Cluster sampling**, also **Single-stage cluster sampling**, **one-stage cluster sampling**, **Two-stage sampling**, **Multistage sampling**, **multi-stage cluster sampling**, **Primary sampling unit**, **PSU**, **Secondary sampling unit**, **ultimate cluster method**, **listing segment**, **area probability sampling**, **Two-per-stratum design**: groups selected and their members enumerated, in single-stage, two-stage and multistage forms, with the primary and secondary sampling unit, the segment or listing chunk, the ultimate cluster, area sampling and the two-per-stratum or paired selection design. - **Probability proportional to size sampling**, also **PPS sampling**, **unequal probability sampling**, **PPS with replacement**, **PPSWR**, **PPS without replacement**, **PPSWOR**, **Systematic PPS sampling**, **PPS systematic selection**, **PPES**, **Lahiri's method**, **Lahiri selection**, **Brewer's method**, **Durbin's method**, **Midzuno-Sen sampling**, **Midzuno scheme**, **Midzuno-Sen scheme**, **Rao-Hartley-Cochran scheme**, **RHC scheme**, **Sampford sampling**, **measure of size**, **MOS**: selection with probability set by a size measure, with PPS with and without replacement, systematic PPS, probability proportional to estimated size, the cumulative total method, Lahiri's, Brewer's, Durbin's, Midzuno-Sen, Rao-Hartley-Cochran and Sampford's methods. - **Poisson sampling**: independent Bernoulli selection of each unit, with Bernoulli sampling at a common rate, conditional Poisson or maximum entropy sampling, sequential Poisson sampling, order sampling and Pareto sampling. - **Balanced sampling**, also **cube method**, **generalized random tessellation stratified sampling**, **Deville-Tille splitting**: selection constrained so sample totals of auxiliary variables match known population totals, with doubly balanced sampling, the local pivotal method, spatially balanced sampling or GRTS, the splitting method and Tille's elimination procedure. - **Two-phase sampling**, also **double sampling**, **two-phase stratification**, **double sampling for nonresponse**: a large first-phase sample measured cheaply and a subsample measured fully, used for double sampling for stratification, two-phase sampling for nonresponse and multiphase sampling. - **Adaptive cluster sampling**, also **Line-intercept sampling**, **line intersect sampling**, **Line transect sampling**, **distance sampling**, **Point transect sampling**, **point count sampling**, **plot sampling**, **RSS**: neighbourhoods added whenever a sampled unit meets a condition, alongside adaptive sampling, sequential sampling to a stopping rule, inverse sampling, ranked set sampling, and line-intercept, line transect or distance, point transect and quadrat sampling. - **Network sampling**, also **multiplicity sampling**, **GWSM**: units reached through links to other units so each has several selection routes, with indirect sampling and the generalized weight share method assigning weights when the sampled and target populations differ. - **Sampling frame**, also **frame**, **Multiple frame sampling**, **multiframe sampling**, **Dual-frame design**, **dual-frame sampling**, **Screening dual-frame design**, **screening design**, **overlap domain weighting**, **Address-based sampling**: the list or procedure from which units are selected, in list frame, master sample or master frame, area, address-based, multiple frame, dual-frame and screening dual-frame forms, with the dual-frame overlap adjustment or compositing factor. - **Taylor series linearization**, also **linearization variance estimation**, **delta method**, **FPC**, **finite population factor**, **With-replacement approximation**: the variance of a nonlinear survey estimator approximated by a first-order expansion, applied with the finite population correction and the with-replacement or ultimate cluster approximation. - **Generalized variance function**, also **GVF**, **collapsed strata method**, **coefficient of variation of an estimate**: a fitted relation predicting an estimate's variance from its magnitude, published as a relative standard error so users need no replicate weights, with the collapsed stratum variance estimator handling single-unit strata. - **Total Survey Error**, also **TSE**, **total survey error framework**, **representation error**, **observation error**, **nonobservation error**, **Mean squared error of a survey estimate**, **survey MSE**, **Trade-off between error and cost**: every error in a survey estimate accounted together, split into errors of representation and errors of measurement or observation, covering sampling error, nonsampling error and errors of nonobservation, summarised as a survey mean squared error. - **Coverage error**, also **frame error**, **frame imperfection**, **duplication in the frame**, **ineligible units on the frame**, **frame maintenance error**: the mismatch between the frame and the target population, comprising undercoverage or noncoverage, overcoverage, frame multiplicity or duplicate listings, foreign elements or ineligible frame units, and frame births and deaths, producing frame bias and noncoverage bias.
- **Nonresponse error**, also **Unit nonresponse**, **item missingness**, **Wave nonresponse**, **sample mortality**, **dropout**, **weighting error**, **temporary dropout**, **wave gap**: failure to obtain data from a selected unit, in the forms of unit or total nonresponse, item nonresponse, wave or occasion nonresponse, intermittent nonresponse and panel attrition, yielding nonresponse bias and attrition bias, with adjustment error the residue weighting leaves.
- **Response variance**, also **simple response variance**, **SRV**, **correlated response variance**, **CRV**, **variable error**, **US Census Bureau survey model**: the variable part of measurement error across repeated trials under fixed essential survey conditions, measured by the index of inconsistency or gross difference rate, against response bias and measurement bias as its systematic counterpart, with the Hansen-Hurwitz-Bershad model's response deviation.

## F6. Measurement

Two cultures of measurement sit here, and their vocabularies look like
translations of each other without being translations. Psychometrics measures a
latent attribute that has no value independent of the instrument. Metrology
measures a physical quantity that has one, and anchors an instrument to a
realised standard. Reliability is not repeatability, validity is not trueness,
classical measurement error is not measurement uncertainty, and calibration
means relating a score to a criterion in one culture and an instrument to a
standard in the other. The groups below keep the two apart, and entries on
genuinely analogous concepts name the counterpart in the other culture.

### Validity and the argument for a score interpretation

- **Validity**: the degree to which evidence supports an intended interpretation of scores for a proposed use, a property of the interpretation rather than of the instrument. Metrology's nearest counterpart is trueness, which presumes a true value a latent attribute lacks.
- **Construct**, also **latent construct**, **latent variable**, **latent factor**, **latent trait**: the unobservable attribute a measure targets, reached only through manifest variables, also called observed variables or indicators, whose covariation is the only evidence of it.
- **Unitary conception of validity**, also **unified validity**: the position that all validity is construct validity. It displaced the trinitarian view, or holy trinity of validity, and absorbed Messick's progressive matrix with its evidential basis, consequential basis and the term consequential validity.
- **Sources of validity evidence**: the five headings of the Standards, evidence based on test content, on response processes, on internal structure, on relations to other variables, and on consequences of testing. No single heading suffices, and assembling all five outlasts most projects.
- **Argument-based approach to validation**, also **Kane's approach**, **interpretive argument**, **interpretation and use argument**, **IUA**: validation as stating the inferences from performance to decision, named scoring, generalization, extrapolation and implication, each resting on a warrant with its backing. Demands the argument be written before evidence is gathered.
- **Content validity**, also **content relevance**, **content representativeness**, **content coverage**: the match of items to a defined domain, quantified by the content validity index as I-CVI and S-CVI, the content validity ratio or Lawshe CVR, and the item-objective congruence or Rovinelli-Hambleton index. Every figure depends on the panel chosen.
- **Test blueprint**, also **table of specifications**, **test specification**, **domain definition**, **universe of content**: the table fixing how many items each content and process cell receives. An alignment study, usually against the Webb criteria of categorical concurrence and depth-of-knowledge consistency, audits it. Publishing one constrains later domain change.
- **Criterion-related validity**, also **criterion validity**, **concurrent validity**, **predictive validity**, **postdictive validity**, **incremental validity**: score relations to an external standard measured at the same time, later or earlier, summarised by a validity coefficient, with incremental validity the gain over predictors already held.
- **Criterion problem**: the difficulty that the standard of comparison is itself a measurement, described through ultimate criterion, criterion relevance, criterion deficiency, criterion contamination and criterion distortion, each a way the criterion misrepresents the outcome actually of interest.
- **Multitrait-multimethod matrix**, also **MTMM matrix**: Campbell and Fiske's layout of trait-method units, read through the reliability diagonal, the validity diagonal, the heterotrait-monomethod block and the heterotrait-heteromethod block for convergent and discriminant, or divergent, validity. Needs several traits by several methods in one sample.
- **Method-variance modelling**, also **common method variance**, **common method bias**, **CMV**, **method effect**: separating collection-related variance from trait variance, by the correlated trait correlated method, correlated trait correlated uniqueness and correlated trait correlated method minus one models, with Harman's single-factor test and marker variable technique as screens. These models often fail to converge.
- **Construct-irrelevant variance**, also **construct-irrelevant difficulty**, **construct-irrelevant easiness**: score variance from something other than the target attribute, the twin of construct underrepresentation, in which the measure omits part of the domain it claims to cover.
- **Jingle fallacy**, also **jangle fallacy**, **jingle-jangle problem**, **construct identity fallacy**: treating differently named constructs as one because their labels agree, or one construct as two because its labels differ, the mechanism behind construct proliferation and construct redundancy.
- **Nomological network**, also **nomological net**: Cronbach and Meehl's web of lawful relations that gives a construct its meaning, carrying surplus meaning, the bootstrapped construct and the open concept. Loevinger's substantive, structural and external components and Embretson's construct representation and nomothetic span are later decompositions.
- **Face validity**, also **faith validity**: whether a measure looks appropriate to those who take it, which bears on cooperation and acceptance but is not evidence for an interpretation, faith validity naming validity simply assumed.
- **Realist account of validity**, also **Borsboom's definition of validity**: the position that a test is valid when the attribute exists and variation in it causes variation in test outcomes, which makes validity a claim about the world rather than about accumulated evidence.
- **Validity generalization**, also **VG**, **synthetic validity**, **job component validity**, **transportability of validity**: importing validity evidence from other settings by meta-analysis, by composing job components, or by matching situations. Range restriction and validity shrinkage bound how far it travels, and local evidence is given up.
- **Bandwidth-fidelity dilemma**, also **bandwidth-fidelity tradeoff**: the constraint that fixed testing time cannot both cover many narrow attributes and measure any of them precisely, so breadth and precision trade against each other in every blueprint.
- **Multi-informant assessment**, also **multi-source measurement**, **Achenbach cross-informant comparison**: gathering ratings of one person from several reporters and comparing them systematically. Informant discrepancy is the usual result rather than an anomaly, so a rule for combining reporters has to be fixed in advance.

### Reliability and error in classical test theory

- **Classical test theory**, also **CTT**, **classical true score theory**: the model decomposing an observed score, also called a fallible score, into a true score plus an error score, with errors uncorrelated with true scores over replications. Everything downstream, reliability included, follows from that decomposition.
- **True score**: the expected observed score over independent replications, a statistical definition rather than a real quantity, with the platonic true score and strong and weak true score theory as its variants. Metrology's true quantity value is a different notion entirely.
- **Error of measurement**, also **error score**, **random error of measurement**, **unsystematic error**, **systematic error of measurement**, **constant error**: the departure of an observed score from its true score, random across replications or constant. This is not metrological measurement uncertainty, which is an interval attributed to a result rather than a realised deviation.
- **Reliability**, also **precision of measurement**, **reliability coefficient**, **reliability index**: the share of observed score variance that is true score variance, the reliability index being the correlation of observed with true scores. Metrology's counterpart is repeatability under stated repeatability conditions, which fixes conditions instead of partitioning variance.
- **Parallel tests**, also **parallel forms**, **randomly parallel tests**, **tau-equivalent tests**, **essentially tau-equivalent tests**, **congeneric tests**: the ladder of assumptions about equal true scores, equal loadings and equal error variances, with the domain sampling model treating items as drawn from a universe. Which rung holds decides which coefficient is defensible.
- **Coefficient alpha**, also **Cronbach's alpha**, **standardized alpha**, **Kuder-Richardson formula 20**, **KR-20**, **Kuder-Richardson formula 21**, **KR-21**, **stratified alpha**: internal consistency from item covariances in one administration, a lower bound under essential tau-equivalence, stratified alpha covering composites of known strata. A high value is not evidence of unidimensionality, and it rises with test length whatever the items measure.
- **Split-half reliability**, also **Spearman-Brown prophecy formula**, **Rulon's formula**, **Flanagan's formula**, **Angoff-Feldt coefficient**, **Raju's coefficient**, **Feldt-Raju coefficient**, **maximum split-half reliability**: reliability from two halves stepped up to full length, with named corrections for unequal halves and congeneric parts. The estimate depends on which split is taken, so an arbitrary halving buys an arbitrary number.
- **Guttman lambda coefficients**, also **lambda 1 to lambda 6**, **Guttman lambda 2**, **Guttman lambda 4**, **Guttman lambda 6**, **coefficient beta**, **greatest lower bound**, **Ten Berge and Zegers mu coefficients**: the family of lower bounds on reliability, lambda 4 the best split and Revelle's beta the worst, the greatest lower bound the highest attainable. That bound is badly upward biased in small samples.
- **McDonald's omega**, also **omega total**, **omega hierarchical**, **omega subscale**, **coefficient H**, **maximal reliability**, **composite reliability**: factor-analytic reliability, omega hierarchical giving the variance share due to a general factor and coefficient H the reliability of an optimally weighted composite. Each requires a fitted factor model that itself has to be defended.
- **Test-retest reliability**, also **coefficient of stability**, **retest reliability**, **alternate-form reliability**, **coefficient of equivalence**, **coefficient of stability and equivalence**: reliability from repeated or alternate administrations across a chosen retest interval. Short intervals import carryover and practice effects, long ones confound real change in the attribute with unreliability.
- **Standard error of measurement**, also **SEM**, **conditional standard error of measurement**, **CSEM**, **score band**, **Kelley's regression estimate**: the standard deviation of errors in the score metric, reported conditionally where precision varies by score level, with Kelley's estimate shrinking a true score toward the mean. Reporting bands complicates pass-fail communication.
- **Correction for attenuation**, also **disattenuation**, **Spearman correction**: dividing an observed correlation by the square root of the product of the two reliabilities to estimate the correlation between true scores. Overcorrection returns coefficients above one, and no correction repairs a badly measured construct.
- **Correction for range restriction**, also **Thorndike corrections**, **direct range restriction**, **explicit selection**, **indirect range restriction**, **incidental selection**: adjustments returning a validity coefficient from a selected sample to the applicant population. They require an unrestricted variance the selected data cannot supply, so the correction rests on an assumed value.
- **Attenuation paradox**, also **reliability-validity paradox**: the point beyond which raising internal consistency lowers validity, because the heterogeneous items discarded to raise it carried construct variance the surviving homogeneous items do not.
- **Reliable change index**, also **RCI**, **Jacobson-Truax index**, **clinically significant change criterion**: a rule for calling one person's change larger than measurement error, resting on the reliability of difference scores, which is lower than that of either component. Needs a defended reliability estimate and a normative reference point.
- **Item-total correlation**, also **corrected item-total correlation**, **item-remainder correlation**, **average interitem correlation**, **alpha if item deleted**, **item reliability index**, **item validity index**: item indices used to purify a scale, the corrected form removing the item from its own criterion. Purifying on one sample capitalises on chance and overstates the reliability then reported.
- **Reliability induction**: reporting a coefficient from another sample as though it described the present data, when reliability is a property of scores in a population. Reliability generalization pools such coefficients, and Feldt-Woodruff, Bonett or bootstrap intervals show how little one estimate settles.
- **Minimum acceptable reliability convention**, also **reliability required for a decision**: the practice of requiring a coefficient above a stated value before scores are used, set higher for individual than for group decisions. The familiar cutoffs are conventions with no theoretical derivation.
- **Speededness**, also **speed contamination of reliability**: the degree to which scores reflect how far examinees reached rather than what they could do, which inflates internal consistency and adds a time demand irrelevant to the construct.

### Generalizability theory

- **Generalizability theory**, also **G theory**: Cronbach's replacement of a single reliability coefficient with variance components, estimating a universe score over a universe of admissible observations and a universe of generalization. It costs a designed measurement study before any coefficient can be quoted.
- **Facet**, also **measurement facet**, **facet of differentiation**, **object of measurement**, **facet of generalization**, **random facet**, **fixed facet**, **hidden facet**, **confounded facets**: any condition of measurement that can vary, split into what is being differentiated and what is generalized over. Cardinet's principle of symmetry and instrumentation face let those roles swap.
- **G study**, also **generalizability study**, **D study**, **decision study**, **variance component**: the first estimates variance components under a crossed, nested or partially nested design, the second projects dependability for a design not yet run. Unbalanced data forces analogous ANOVA or bootstrap estimation, and negative components must still be reported.
- **Generalizability coefficient**, also **E rho squared**, **G coefficient**, **dependability coefficient**, **index of dependability**, **phi coefficient**, **phi lambda coefficient**, **signal-to-noise ratio in generalizability**: relative decisions use relative error variance, absolute decisions use absolute error variance, and phi lambda serves a fixed cut score, so the coefficient must match the decision. Gauge repeatability and reproducibility studies partition variance the same way.
- **Multivariate generalizability theory**, also **multivariate G theory**, **composite universe score**: the extension to profiles of scores, estimating covariance components and the dependability of a weighted composite. It multiplies design demands, since every facet must be crossed with every dimension of the profile.

### Agreement between raters and observers

- **Percent agreement**, also **observed agreement**, **raw agreement**, **weighted percent agreement**, **exact agreement rate**, **adjacent agreement rate**: the share of cases two raters classify identically, or within one category. It counts the agreement expected from chance alone, which is the whole reason chance-corrected coefficients exist.
- **Cohen's kappa**, also **kappa**, **weighted kappa**, **Cohen weighted kappa**, **intraclass kappa**: agreement corrected for chance under the assumption of independent rater marginals, weighted for ordinal categories by linear Cicchetti-Allison or quadratic Fleiss-Cohen weights. The chance model makes it sensitive to prevalence and to marginal imbalance.
- **Chance-corrected agreement coefficients**, also **Fleiss' kappa**, **Conger's kappa**, **Light's kappa**, **free-marginal kappa**, **Brennan-Prediger coefficient**, **Bennett's S coefficient**, **Scott's pi**, **Krippendorff's alpha**, **Gwet's AC1**, **Gwet's AC2**, **prevalence-adjusted bias-adjusted kappa**, **PABAK**, **Aickin's alpha**, **Maxwell's RE coefficient**: the family differing only in how chance agreement is modelled, Krippendorff's alpha carrying nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio metrics. Coefficients disagree most where prevalence is extreme, and conditional against unconditional inference changes the interval.
- **Kappa paradoxes**, also **first kappa paradox**, **second kappa paradox**: high observed agreement with a low coefficient when one category dominates, and an inflated coefficient under unbalanced marginals, diagnosed through the prevalence index, the bias index and marginal homogeneity.
- **Agreement benchmark scales**, also **Landis and Koch benchmarks**, **Altman's benchmark scale**, **Fleiss benchmark scale**: the verbal grades attached to coefficient ranges, with membership-probability benchmarking replacing a point estimate by the probability of reaching a grade. The grades are arbitrary conventions, and precision falls sharply with few raters or subjects.
- **Intraclass correlation coefficient**, also **ICC**, **one-way random-effects ICC**, **two-way random-effects ICC**, **two-way mixed-effects ICC**, **single-measurement ICC**, **average-measurement ICC**, **absolute agreement ICC**, **consistency ICC**: variance-ratio agreement for continuous ratings, named ICC(1,1), ICC(2,1) and ICC(3,1) by Shrout and Fleiss and by design in McGraw and Wong. Reporting one without naming the form is uninterpretable.
- **Concordance correlation coefficient**, also **Lin's CCC**, **total deviation index**, **coverage probability of agreement**, **coefficient of individual agreement**, **Barnhart CIA**, **Kendall's coefficient of concordance**, **Kendall's W**, **Finn coefficient**: agreement indices for continuous or ranked data combining precision with accuracy, displayed by the Bangdiwala agreement chart and its B statistic. A stated agreement target must name its index.
- **Limits of agreement**, also **LoA**, **Bland-Altman plot**, **difference plot**, **repeatability coefficient**, **within-subject standard deviation**, **standard error of measurement agreement**, **smallest detectable change**, **smallest real difference**: the interval within which two measurements of one subject fall, plotted against their mean. Requires replicates on each subject. Analytical metrology uses the identical plot for method comparison.
- **Rater severity**, also **rater harshness**, **rater leniency**, **rater drift**, **scorer drift**: the systematic tendency of an individual scorer to mark high or low, and to move over a scoring window, which enters scores as bias rather than as disagreement noise.
- **Rater calibration**, also **rater training and qualification**, **backreading**, **read-behind**, **score resolution procedure**, **consensus scoring**, **third-rater arbitration**: qualifying scorers against anchor papers and monitoring them live, with discrepant scores adjudicated. It consumes scorer time continuously. This is not metrological calibration, since anchor papers are agreed exemplars rather than traceable standards.

### Factor analysis and internal structure

- **Exploratory factor analysis**, also **EFA**, **common factor model**, **communality**, **uniqueness**: modelling observed covariances as arising from fewer common factors plus variable-specific uniqueness, with sampling adequacy screened by the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure and Bartlett's test of sphericity. Solutions are unstable in small samples and rotation-dependent.
- **Principal component analysis**, also **PCA**: reduction of variables to weighted composites maximising explained variance, with no error term and no latent common cause. It is not factor analysis, so it cannot support a claim about a latent construct.
- **Factor extraction methods**, also **principal axis factoring**, **PAF**, **minimum residual extraction**, **MINRES**, **maximum likelihood factor extraction**, **unweighted least squares extraction**, **weighted least squares extraction**, **alpha factoring**, **image factoring**, **Rao's canonical factor analysis**, **centroid method**, **nonlinear factor analysis**: the estimators fitting a common factor model, differing in fit criterion and in whether they yield a likelihood. Maximum likelihood buys a test statistic and demands normality.
- **Factor loading**, also **pattern matrix**, **pattern coefficients**, **structure matrix**, **structure coefficients**, **cross-loading**: the regression weight of a variable on a factor, distinct from its correlation with the factor once factors are oblique. Thurstone's simple structure is the target, and rotational indeterminacy is why one is chosen rather than found.
- **Rotation**, also **orthogonal rotation**, **oblique rotation**, **varimax rotation**, **quartimax rotation**, **equamax rotation**, **orthomax family**, **promax rotation**, **oblimin rotation**, **quartimin rotation**, **geomin rotation**, **oblimax rotation**, **bi-quartimin rotation**, **simplimax rotation**, **infomax rotation**, **parsimax rotation**, **Crawford-Ferguson rotation family**, **tandem criteria rotation**, **Harris-Kaiser independent cluster rotation**, **target rotation**, **Procrustes rotation**, **bifactor rotation**, **Kaiser normalization**: transformations of a factor solution toward simple structure, orthogonal ones forcing uncorrelated factors. Choosing one fixes the interpretation without changing the fit.
- **Factor retention rules**, also **Kaiser criterion**, **eigenvalue-greater-than-one rule**, **scree test**, **parallel analysis**, **Horn's parallel analysis**, **minimum average partial test**, **Velicer MAP test**, **Hull method**, **comparison data method**, **Ruscio-Roche method**, **very simple structure criterion**, **empirical Kaiser criterion**, **bootstrap eigenvalue test**, **acceleration factor**, **optimal coordinates**, **broken stick criterion**, **objective scree test**, **Cattell-Nelson-Gorsuch scree test**, **standard error scree**, **next eigenvalue sufficiency test**, **sequential chi-square difference test for factor retention**, **exploratory graph analysis**: the rules deciding how many factors to keep, prone to overextraction or underextraction. They disagree routinely, so the rule must be named in advance.
- **Factor score**, also **regression factor score**, **Thurstone factor score**, **Bartlett factor score**, **Anderson-Rubin factor score**, **coarse factor score**, **sum-score proxy**: estimates of a person's position on a factor, non-unique because of factor score indeterminacy and gauged by the factor determinacy coefficient. Croon's correction and two-stage path analysis repair the bias they carry into later regressions.
- **Heywood case**, also **improper solution**, **nonpositive definite matrix**: a fitted solution carrying a negative uniqueness or a communality above one, which signals overextraction, too small a sample or a misspecified model rather than a computational accident.
- **Confirmatory factor analysis**, also **CFA**, **measurement model**: fitting a factor structure fixed in advance, with loadings, residuals and factor covariances specified rather than rotated. It cannot discover structure, and a model that fits is one of many that would.
- **Categorical confirmatory factor analysis**, also **ordinal CFA**, **polychoric correlation**, **tetrachoric correlation**, **robust weighted least squares**, **WLSMV**, **diagonally weighted least squares**, **ordinal alpha**, **full information maximum likelihood**: treating ordered item responses as thresholded continuous variables rather than as interval scores. Threshold estimation needs cases in every category, so sparse categories must be collapsed.
- **Bifactor model**, also **nested factor model**, **general-specific model**, **bifactor item response model**, **bifactor S-1 model**, **higher-order factor model**, **second-order factor model**, **Schmid-Leiman transformation**: a general factor with orthogonal specific factors, summarised by explained common variance, the percentage of uncontaminated correlations and item explained common variance or I-ECV. It almost always fits better, which makes fit uninformative here.
- **Exploratory structural equation modeling**, also **ESEM**: a rotated measurement model inside a structural equation model, allowing cross-loadings that confirmatory analysis fixes at zero, alongside multilevel confirmatory factor analysis, the random intercept factor model and item parceling. It reintroduces rotational choice into a confirmatory setting.
- **Reflective measurement**, also **effect indicator model**, **formative measurement**, **causal indicator model**, **composite indicator**: whether indicators are caused by the construct or compose it, which decides whether interchangeability of indicators applies. MIMIC models, partial least squares path modelling, confirmatory composite analysis and the vanishing tetrad test belong to this dispute.
- **Average variance extracted**, also **AVE**, **Fornell-Larcker criterion**, **heterotrait-monotrait ratio**, **HTMT**: convergent and discriminant validity indices computed from a fitted measurement model, the ratio comparing across-construct with within-construct correlations. Their thresholds are conventions, and results shift with which items enter each block.
- **Unidimensionality**, also **item homogeneity**, **local independence given the factor**: the property that one factor accounts for the item covariances, so that responses are conditionally independent given the factor. It is a testable claim about structure and is not established by a high internal consistency coefficient.

### Structural equation models, identification and fit

- **Structural equation modeling**, also **SEM**, **covariance structure analysis**, **structural model**, **latent path model**, **latent variable path model**, **path analysis**: simultaneous estimation of a measurement model and of relations among latent variables, path analysis being the observed-variable special case. Causal reading of the paths comes from the design, never from the fit.
- **Model identification**, also **under-identified model**, **just-identified model**, **saturated model**, **over-identified model**, **empirical underidentification**, **counting rule**, **t-rule**, **two-indicator rule**, **three-indicator rule**, **recursive rule**, **null beta rule**, **two-step identification rule**, **phantom variable**: whether the data determine unique parameter estimates, checked against degrees of freedom and the named sufficient rules. Underidentification surfaces as nonconvergence or an improper solution rather than as a warning.
- **Latent variable scaling**, also **marker variable scaling**, **reference indicator method**, **effects-coding identification**, **fixed-factor scaling**, **latent variable standardization**: the choice giving a latent variable a metric, by fixing one loading, by constraining loadings to average one, or by fixing the factor variance. Fit is unchanged, but parameter values and their tests are not.
- **Model chi-square**, also **likelihood ratio chi-square**, **T statistic**, **normed chi-square**, **chi-square to degrees of freedom ratio**, **Hoelter's critical N**: the test that a model reproduces the covariance matrix exactly, extended to nested comparison by the chi-square difference test, the Satorra-Bentler scaled difference test, robust maximum likelihood and the Bollen-Stine bootstrap. It rejects any model in a large sample.
- **Root mean square error of approximation**, also **RMSEA**, **test of close fit**, **test of not-close fit**, **RMSEA confidence interval**, **equivalence testing approach to model fit**: a fit index penalising complexity and reported with an interval, supporting tests of close and not-close fit. It is upward biased with few degrees of freedom and small samples.
- **Incremental fit indices**, also **comparative fit index**, **CFI**, **Tucker-Lewis index**, **TLI**, **non-normed fit index**, **normed fit index**, **Bentler-Bonett index**, **incremental fit index**, **relative fit index**, **relative noncentrality index**, **goodness-of-fit index**, **adjusted goodness-of-fit index**, **parsimony normed fit index**, **parsimony goodness-of-fit index**, **parsimony ratio**, **gamma hat**, **McDonald's centrality index**, **expected cross-validation index**, **Browne-Cudeck criterion**: indices comparing a model against a null or predicting cross-sample fit. All rest on a baseline model few authors inspect.
- **Standardized root mean square residual**, also **SRMR**, **weighted root mean square residual**, **root mean square residual**, **residual correlation matrix**, **standardized residuals**: fit read from what the model failed to reproduce, element by element, rather than from one global index. Inspecting residuals shows where misfit sits and costs the convenience of a single number.
- **Fit index cutoffs**, also **Hu and Bentler cutoffs**, **conventional fit thresholds**, **golden rules critique**, **dynamic fit index cutoffs**, **sample size to parameter ratio**, **N to q rule**: the conventional thresholds separating acceptable from unacceptable fit, criticised as golden rules derived under conditions unlike most applications and replaced by simulation-derived model-specific cutoffs. Dynamic cutoffs cost a simulation per model.
- **Local fit**, also **global fit**, **local misfit**, **modification index**, **Lagrange multiplier test**, **expected parameter change**, **Wald test of parameter dropping**, **model respecification**, **specification search**, **correlated residuals**, **method factor**: misfit located in particular parameters rather than summarised globally, with data-driven respecification the standard response. Every respecification on the same data turns confirmation into exploration.
- **Equivalent models**, also **model equivalence problem**, **model fit against model utility**: distinct models reproducing the same covariance matrix, so fit cannot choose between them, and a well-fitting model may still be useless for the decision the work was run to inform.
- **Longitudinal latent models**, also **longitudinal factor model**, **latent state model**, **latent trait-state model**, **trait-state-occasion model**, **latent growth curve model**, **latent change score model**, **latent difference score model**, **errors-in-variables regression**, **multilevel structural equation modelling**, **Bayesian structural equation modelling**: models separating stable from occasion-specific variance and modelling change in a latent variable. Each needs at least three waves and invariant measurement across them.

### Item response theory, item fit and person fit

- **Item response theory**, also **IRT**, **latent trait theory**, **item characteristic curve**, **item response function**, **trace line**, **test characteristic curve**: modelling the probability of a response as a function of a latent trait, placing persons and items on one metric called the theta scale in logit units. Estimation needs large calibration samples.
- **Item difficulty parameter**, also **b parameter**, **location parameter**, **item discrimination parameter**, **a parameter**, **slope**, **pseudo-guessing parameter**, **c parameter**, **lower asymptote**, **upper asymptote parameter**, **d parameter**, **carelessness parameter**: the parameters of a trace line, giving where an item sits on the trait, how sharply it separates, and the floor and ceiling of its response probability.
- **Logistic item response models**, also **one-parameter logistic model**, **1PL**, **two-parameter logistic model**, **2PL**, **three-parameter logistic model**, **3PL**, **four-parameter logistic model**, **4PL**, **normal ogive model**, **three-parameter normal ogive model**: the dichotomous family, adding discrimination, guessing and a ceiling in turn. Each added parameter needs far more data, and the 3PL guessing parameter is weakly identified.
- **Polytomous item response models**, also **graded response model**, **Samejima GRM**, **partial credit model**, **generalized partial credit model**, **rating scale model**, **Andrich rating scale model**, **nominal response model**, **Bock nominal model**, **sequential response model**, **continuation ratio model**, **continuous response model**, **item response tree**, **IRTree**: models for ordered or unordered multi-category responses, differing in whether thresholds are shared and whether categories are ordered. Sparse categories break threshold estimation.
- **Multidimensional item response theory**, also **MIRT**, **compensatory MIRT model**, **noncompensatory MIRT model**, **conjunctive MIRT model**, **testlet response model**, **bundle model**, **item response surface**: models with more than one latent dimension, compensatory ones letting a high standing offset a low one and conjunctive ones not. Dimensions are rotationally indeterminate and demand very large samples.
- **Explanatory item response models**, also **linear logistic test model**, **LLTM**, **mixture item response model**, **mixed Rasch model**, **ideal point model**, **unfolding IRT model**, **generalized graded unfolding model**, **GGUM**: models putting item properties or unobserved classes into the trace line, or replacing monotone response with proximity to a person's ideal point. Each buys interpretation with stronger assumptions.
- **Test information function**, also **TIF**, **item information function**, **standard error of theta**, **marginal reliability**, **IRT-based reliability**, **empirical reliability**, **test information targeting**: precision as a function of trait level, the reciprocal square root of information giving the conditional standard error. Targeting information where decisions fall leaves other regions of the scale poorly measured.
- **Ability estimation**, also **maximum likelihood ability estimation**, **maximum a posteriori estimation of theta**, **Bayes modal estimate**, **expected a posteriori estimation of theta**, **EAP**, **expected a posteriori summed score conversion**, **weighted likelihood estimation**, **Warm's WLE**, **plausible values**, **pattern scoring**, **number-correct scoring**: estimators of a person's trait level, Bayesian ones shrinking toward the prior and maximum likelihood failing for perfect scores. Plausible values serve population estimates, not individual reporting.
- **Item calibration**, also **marginal maximum likelihood**, **conditional maximum likelihood**, **pairwise conditional estimation**, **expectation-maximization calibration**, **Bock-Aitkin EM**, **Bayesian item response estimation**, **Metropolis-Hastings Robbins-Monro algorithm**, **MH-RM**, **empirical histogram method**, **kernel smoothing of item response functions**: estimating item parameters from a calibration sample, with the latent density either assumed normal or estimated. The calibration sample must resemble the operational population.
- **Local independence**, also **conditional independence assumption**, **local dependence**, **Yen's Q3 statistic**, **LD X2 statistic**, **Chen-Thissen local dependence index**, **monotonicity assumption**, **unidimensionality assumption in IRT**, **parameter invariance**: the assumptions a trace line rests on, that responses are independent given the trait and that item parameters do not depend on the sample. Violations inflate information and overstate precision.
- **Item fit statistics**, also **infit mean square**, **outfit mean square**, **standardized fit statistic**, **ZSTD**, **S-X2 item fit statistic**, **Orlando-Thissen fit**, **Yen's Q1 statistic**, **likelihood ratio item fit statistic**, **M2 statistic**, **C2 statistic**, **RMSEA2**: tests of whether observed responses match a fitted trace line, from item-level residual means to limited-information global statistics. All are sample-size sensitive, so a flagging rule needs a stated sample.
- **Person fit**, also **appropriateness measurement**, **lz person-fit statistic**, **lz star statistic**, **U3 statistic**, **caution index**, **modified caution index**, **extended caution index**, **Tatsuoka extended caution indices**: statistics flagging a response pattern the model cannot account for, with Guttman errors counting reversals and aberrant response pattern as the general label. A flag names no cause.

### Rasch measurement and the scaling traditions

- **Rasch model**, also **simple logistic model**, **dichotomous Rasch model**, **logit unit**: the one-parameter model whose measures are additive in logits, giving specific objectivity, invariant measurement and sufficiency of the raw score. It requires data to fit the model rather than the reverse, so misfitting items are removed rather than accommodated.
- **Rasch fit and invariance checks**, also **Andersen's likelihood ratio test**, **Martin-Lof test**, **item-trait interaction chi-square**, **principal component analysis of Rasch residuals**, **point-measure correlation**, **item misfit flagging**, **anchoring of item measures**, **common-item Rasch linking**: the standard battery testing invariance across score groups, unidimensionality of residuals and item-level fit. Mean-square flagging rules are conventions, and residual components are easy to overread.
- **Person-item map**, also **Wright map**, **item-person map**, **construct map**, **item hierarchy**, **item-person targeting**, **person separation index**, **item separation index**, **strata index**: the display putting person measures and item difficulties on one vertical scale, with separation indices reporting how many distinguishable levels the instrument supports. Poor targeting wastes items where no persons sit.
- **Category threshold**, also **step difficulty**, **tau parameter**, **Thurstone threshold**, **category probability curve**, **category response curve**, **disordered thresholds**, **threshold reversal**, **category collapsing**, **rating scale functioning analysis**: the points on the trait where adjacent response categories become equally likely. Disordered thresholds signal categories respondents do not distinguish, and collapsing them discards information deliberately.
- **Many-facet Rasch measurement**, also **MFRM**, **many-facet Rasch model**, **rater severity measure**, **rater facet estimate**, **bias interaction analysis**, **facet interaction analysis**, **Rasch Poisson counts model**: the extension placing raters, tasks and other conditions on the same logit scale as persons, so scores can be adjusted for measured severity. Adjustment requires enough connectivity between raters and performances.
- **Guttman scaling**, also **scalogram analysis**, **coefficient of reproducibility**, **coefficient of scalability**: deterministic ordering in which endorsing an item implies endorsing every easier one, reproducibility measuring how few responses violate the pattern. Real data almost never meet it, which is why probabilistic descendants exist.
- **Mokken scale analysis**, also **nonparametric IRT scaling**, **monotone homogeneity model**, **MHM**, **double monotonicity model**, **DMM**, **Loevinger H coefficient**, **scalability coefficient H**, **HT coefficient**, **Sijtsma HT**: scaling requiring only monotone trace lines and, for item ordering, non-intersecting ones, with H grading scalability and HT grading person scalability. Ordinal measurement is all it delivers.
- **Thurstone scaling**, also **method of equal-appearing intervals**, **method of paired comparisons**, **law of comparative judgment**, **successive intervals method**, **Bradley-Terry-Luce scaling**: deriving interval-scale values from judgments of order or apparent distance, with multidimensional scaling and unidimensional unfolding as later geometric descendants. Paired comparisons grow quadratically with the number of objects.
- **Likert scaling**, also **summated rating scale method**, **semantic differential**, **Osgood semantic differential**, **Q-sort technique**, **best-worst scaling**, **MaxDiff**, **forced-choice response format**, **normative measurement**: summing or ranking judgments across items to place respondents, forced-choice and best-worst formats producing ipsative measurement. Ipsative scores are relative within a person and cannot be compared across people without a model.
- **Levels of measurement**, also **Stevens' scales of measurement**, **nominal scale**, **ordinal scale**, **interval scale**, **ratio scale**: Stevens' four classes, ordered by the transformations that leave a scale meaningful, with the ordinal-to-interval fallacy naming the routine treatment of ranked scores as though their distances were equal.
- **Representational theory of measurement**, also **axiomatic measurement theory**, **fundamental measurement**, **derived measurement**, **additive conjoint measurement**, **concatenation**, **double cancellation**: the account requiring an empirical structure to be shown homomorphic to a numerical one before numbers are assigned, double cancellation being the testable axiom and concatenation the physical operation psychology lacks. Michell's quantitative imperative names the assumption usually skipped.

### Adaptive testing, item banking and diagnostic classification

- **Computerized adaptive testing**, also **CAT**, **tailored testing**, **multistage testing**, **MST**, **linear on-the-fly testing**, **LOFT**: delivery choosing each item or module from a provisional ability estimate and stopping on a fixed-precision or fixed-length rule. It buys precision per minute and costs a calibrated bank, secure delivery and any examinee review of earlier items.
- **Adaptive item selection**, also **maximum information item selection**, **a-stratified item selection**, **Kullback-Leibler information item selection**, **maximum posterior weighted information**, **Owen's Bayesian sequential procedure**, **randomesque item selection**, **Kingsbury-Zara randomesque procedure**, **shadow test approach**: the rules picking the next item, trading measurement efficiency against pool usage and constraint satisfaction. Pure maximum information overuses the most discriminating items.
- **Item exposure control**, also **Sympson-Hetter exposure control**, **Stocking-Lewis conditional multinomial method**, **Davey-Parshall method**, **progressive-restricted exposure control**, **test overlap rate**, **conditional item exposure rate**: probabilistic limits on how often an item is administered, monitored through overlap and exposure rates. Every constraint costs measurement precision and needs simulation to set its parameters.
- **Automated test assembly**, also **optimal test design**, **weighted deviations model**, **Swanson-Stocking heuristic**, **normalized weighted absolute deviation heuristic**, **NWADH**, **maximin test assembly model**, **content balancing constraint**: building forms by optimisation against content, statistical and exposure constraints rather than by hand. Infeasible constraint sets fail silently as poor forms unless feasibility is checked first.
- **Item bank**, also **item pool for adaptive delivery**, **anchor item**, **common item**, **link item**: the calibrated store of items carrying parameters on a common scale, kept usable by replenishment and by watching item parameter drift, the slow change in an item's statistics across administrations. Maintaining one is a permanent programme cost.
- **Diagnostic classification model**, also **DCM**, **cognitive diagnostic model**, **DINA model**, **deterministic input noisy and gate**, **DINO model**, **deterministic input noisy or gate**, **Q-matrix**, **attribute hierarchy method**, **attribute mastery profile**: models reporting mastery of discrete attributes rather than one trait, the Q-matrix mapping items to attributes. Results are only as good as an expert-specified Q-matrix nobody can validate cheaply.

### Latent classes, mixtures and psychometric networks

- **Latent class analysis**, also **LCA**, **latent profile analysis**, **LPA**, **latent transition analysis**, **latent Markov model**, **factor mixture model**, **mixture Rasch model**, **grade of membership model**, **located latent class model**: models treating heterogeneity as unobserved groups rather than as a continuum, transition models adding movement between classes over time. Classes remain model artefacts until validated against something external.
- **Class enumeration**, also **bootstrap likelihood ratio test**, **BLRT**, **Lo-Mendell-Rubin test**, **sample-size adjusted BIC**, **approximate weight of evidence criterion**, **consistent Akaike information criterion**, **entropy of classification**, **average posterior probability**, **odds of correct classification ratio**: deciding how many classes to keep from information criteria, likelihood tests and classification diagnostics. Nonnormality produces spurious classes, and label switching, local maxima and boundary solutions make solutions unreplicable.
- **Class assignment**, also **modal class assignment**, **proportional class assignment**, **pseudo-class draws**, **BCH approach**, **Bolck-Croon-Hagenaars method**, **class-membership covariate model**, **three-step latent class regression**: how membership enters later analysis, from assigning each case to its most likely class to methods carrying classification uncertainty forward. Modal assignment understates standard errors.
- **Taxometric analysis**, also **taxometrics**, **MAXCOV**, **MAMBAC**, **MAXEIG**, **L-Mode**, **comparison curve fit index**, **base rate estimation in taxometrics**: procedures asking whether a latent structure is categorical or dimensional, judged by comparing observed curves against simulated categorical and dimensional data. They need a large sample, a high base rate and strongly valid indicators.
- **Network psychometrics**, also **psychometric network model**, **centrality stability coefficient**, **CS-coefficient**, **network comparison test**, **node redundancy analysis**: treating items as interacting nodes rather than as indicators of a latent cause, with stability and comparison procedures checking whether an estimated network survives resampling. Dense networks need large samples before centrality claims mean anything.
- **Idiographic measurement**, also **P-technique factor analysis**, **dynamic factor analysis**, **idiographic filter**, **measurement burst design**: modelling one person's repeated measurements to recover within-person structure, since the ergodicity assumption that between-person structure describes within-person process usually fails. It demands many occasions per person.

### Measurement invariance and differential item functioning

- **Measurement invariance**, also **factorial invariance**, **measurement equivalence**, **configural invariance**, **metric invariance**, **weak invariance**, **scalar invariance**, **strong invariance**, **strict invariance**, **residual invariance**, **partial invariance**, **dimensional invariance**, **longitudinal measurement invariance**, **multilevel measurement invariance**: the nested sequence testing equal factor structure, loadings, intercepts and residuals across groups or occasions. Without scalar invariance, observed mean differences are uninterpretable.
- **Invariance decision rules**, also **delta CFI criterion**, **delta RMSEA criterion**, **alignment optimization**, **approximate measurement invariance**, **permutation test of alignment invariance**, **latent mean comparison**: the thresholds and approximate methods used when exact invariance fails, alignment estimating group-specific parameters under minimal noninvariance. Change-in-fit thresholds are simulation conventions, and alignment gives up an exactly common metric.
- **Measurement bias**, also **Mellenbergh's definition of bias**: dependence of the expected observed score on group membership once the latent variable is held constant, distinguished from item impact, a real group difference in the attribute that no fair test can remove.
- **Differential item functioning**, also **DIF**, **item bias**, **uniform DIF**, **non-uniform DIF**, **crossing DIF**, **differential test functioning**, **DTF**, **differential bundle functioning**, **DBF**, **differential distractor functioning**, **DDF**, **differential step functioning**, **differential speededness**: unequal response probabilities across groups at equal trait level, uniform where the gap is constant and crossing where it reverses. Aggregation to test level can cancel item-level effects.
- **Observed-score DIF procedures**, also **Mantel-Haenszel DIF procedure**, **standardized p-difference**, **SIBTEST**, **crossing SIBTEST**, **Poly-SIBTEST**, **logistic regression DIF procedure**, **Swaminathan-Rogers procedure**, **ordinal logistic regression DIF**, **Mantel test for polytomous DIF**, **Liu-Agresti common odds ratio**, **Breslow-Day test for differential item functioning**, **delta plot method**, **transformed item difficulty method**: methods matching examinees on total score before comparing item performance. Matching on a contaminated total score confounds impact with bias.
- **Model-based DIF procedures**, also **IRT likelihood ratio DIF**, **Thissen IRT-LR DIF**, **Lord's chi-square test**, **Raju's area measures**, **Wald DIF test**, **DFIT framework**, **compensatory differential item functioning index**, **noncompensatory differential item functioning index**, **MIMIC differential item functioning detection**, **DIF variance component method**: methods comparing fitted item parameters across groups after placing them on a common scale. They need large per-group samples and a defensible linking step.
- **DIF purification**, also **iterative anchor purification**, **anchor item selection for DIF**, **constant anchor**, **all-other anchor**: iteratively removing flagged items from the matching or linking set so the anchor is itself unbiased. The anchoring problem remains, since a contaminated anchor produces flags that purification then treats as data.
- **ETS DIF classification**, also **A-B-C DIF categories**: the operational rule sorting items into negligible, intermediate and large differential functioning from effect size and significance together, deciding which items remain usable. The boundaries are programme conventions rather than derived thresholds.
- **Test bias**, also **predictive bias**, **differential prediction**, **Cleary model of test bias**, **intercept bias**, **slope bias**, **differential validity**: systematic error in prediction for a subgroup, tested by comparing regression intercepts and slopes of criterion on test across groups. Distinct from adverse impact, a difference in selection rates screened by the four-fifths rule.

### Fairness, accessibility and cross-cultural adaptation

- **Fairness in testing**, also **sensitivity review**, **bias and sensitivity review panel**: the Standards' four views, fairness as lack of measurement bias, as access to the construct, as equitable treatment during testing, and as validity of individual score interpretation. Sensitivity review panels catch offence and stereotyping, not construct-irrelevant difficulty.
- **Universal design of assessment**, also **universal test design**, **accessibility of a test**: designing items and delivery so the widest range of examinees can show what they know without an accommodation, by removing demands unrelated to the construct. It constrains item formats and stimulus choices from the outset.
- **Testing accommodation**, also **accommodation**, **test modification**, **nonstandard alteration**, **alternate assessment**, **linguistic complexity reduction**, **construct-irrelevant language demand**, **flagging of scores from nonstandard administration**: a change in conditions meant to remove a barrier without altering the construct, against a modification which alters it. The differential boost hypothesis is the justification, and comparability of accommodated scores the standing doubt.
- **Opportunity to learn**: whether examinees have been taught the content a test samples, which bears on whether a low score reflects the attribute or the instruction received, and which no property of the instrument can settle.
- **Test translation and adaptation**, also **cross-cultural test adaptation**, **ITC Guidelines for Translating and Adapting Tests**, **forward translation**, **back translation**, **committee translation approach**, **decentering**, **linguistic validation**, **cognitive debriefing**, **simultaneous development of language versions**, **successive development of a language version**: producing a version for another language and culture rather than a literal translation. Back translation checks wording only, so cognitive debriefing with target respondents is the real evidence.
- **Equivalence in cross-cultural measurement**, also **conceptual equivalence**, **linguistic equivalence**, **semantic equivalence**, **functional equivalence**, **metric equivalence**, **cross-cultural validity**: the levels at which two language versions may match, from shared concept to a common numerical scale, with construct bias, method bias and item bias the corresponding failures. Emic and etic approaches mark the two starting points.
- **Cross-lingual linking designs**, also **separate monolingual groups design**, **matched monolingual groups design**, **bilingual group design**, **dual-language test booklet**, **score comparability across languages**: the designs putting scores from two language versions on one scale, differing in who takes which version. Bilingual examinees are unrepresentative of either monolingual population, the price of the cleanest design.

### Scale construction, item writing and scoring

- **Construct explication**, also **construct definition**, **conceptual framework of a measure**, **measurement framework**, **domain specification**, **construct map specification**: writing down what the attribute is, what it excludes and how it is expected to vary before any item exists. Skipping it leaves item content as the only definition of the construct.
- **Item generation**, also **item writing**, **deductive item generation**, **inductive item generation**, **item pool**, **item-writing guidelines**: producing candidate items from theory or from respondents' own language, assembled into an initial pool. Items are built from a stem, response options including distractors, and a keyed response. Overgenerating costs review time and buys room for deletion.
- **Selected-response item formats**, also **multiple-choice item**, **true-false item**, **multiple true-false item**, **alternate-choice item**, **complex multiple-choice item**, **Type K item**, **matching item**, **extended matching item**, **ordered multiple-choice item**, **context-dependent item set**, **cloze procedure**, **technology-enhanced item**: formats scored against a key, cheap to score and wide in coverage. Each carries a format effect, and complex formats measure test-wiseness alongside the construct.
- **Constructed-response item formats**, also **open-ended item**, **free-response item**, **performance task**, **portfolio assessment**, **situational judgment item format**, **key feature item**, **script concordance test**, **objective structured clinical examination**, **OSCE**, **mini-clinical evaluation exercise**, **standardized patient assessment**, **progress test**: formats requiring the examinee to produce a response, reaching skills a key cannot. They cost trained scorers, rubric development and far more testing time per score point.
- **Reverse-scored item**, also **reverse-keyed item**, **balanced keying**: an item worded against the construct's direction and rescored, used to break acquiescence. The negatively worded item effect appears as a method factor, so balanced keying trades one artefact for another.
- **Cognitive pretesting**, also **cognitive interviewing of items**, **item tryout**, **field test**, **pretest item embedding**, **seeded pretest items**, **pilot administration**: trying items on target respondents before operational use, by think-aloud interview or by embedding unscored items in a live form. Seeding costs testing time and requires examinees not to know which items count.
- **Item analysis**, also **item difficulty index**, **p-value of an item**, **item discrimination index**, **D index**, **upper-lower index**, **point-biserial correlation**, **biserial correlation**, **distractor analysis**, **distractor efficiency**, **non-functioning distractor**, **endorsement rate**, **item variance**: the classical statistics screening items after a tryout, including how often each distractor is chosen. All are sample-dependent, so decisions from a small tryout will not hold.
- **Item reduction**, also **scale purification**, **item selection**, **item retention decision**, **short-form development**, **scale shortening**, **ant colony optimization for item selection**, **genetic algorithm item selection**, **item retirement**: cutting a pool to a working form by judgement or by combinatorial search against several objectives at once. A short form inherits the long form's validity evidence only if the reduction is cross-validated.
- **Automatic item generation**, also **AIG**, **item model**, **item template**, **item clone family**, **item cloning**, **isomorph generation**, **faceted item design**: generating families of items from a template whose slots are systematically varied. Isomorphs are not statistically identical, so a family needs calibration evidence that its members are interchangeable.
- **Response format selection**, also **Likert-type response scale**, **visual analogue scale**, **numeric rating scale**, **verbal rating scale**, **graphic rating scale**, **behaviourally anchored rating scale**, **behavioural observation scale**, **ranking response format**, **number of response categories**, **midpoint option**, **anchoring vignette**: choosing how a respondent answers, including how many categories and whether a neutral midpoint exists. Few categories lose information, many exceed what respondents discriminate.
- **Scoring rubric**, also **holistic rubric**, **analytic rubric**, **trait scoring**, **anchor paper**, **benchmark exemplar**, **range finder**: the scale and criteria a human scorer applies, holistic giving one judgement and analytic one per dimension, trained against anchor papers. Automated essay scoring replaces the scorer and is defended by human-machine score agreement, which rewards surface features.
- **Sum score**, also **total raw score**, **summated score**, **unit weighting**, **differential item weighting**, **weighted scoring**, **prorated scoring**, **person mean imputation**: adding item responses, with equal or differential weights and rules for missing items. Guessing correction and omitted response treatment decide how blanks and chance are handled, and unit weighting usually predicts as well as optimal weights.

### Response styles and protocol validity

- **Response style**, also **response set**, **responding bias**, **acquiescence bias**, **yea-saying**, **disacquiescence**, **nay-saying**, **extreme response style**, **midpoint response style**: a respondent's habitual way of using a scale irrespective of item content, which shifts scores and can create factors reflecting style rather than trait.
- **Socially desirable responding**, also **social desirability bias**, **impression management**, **other-deception**, **self-deceptive enhancement**, **faking good**, **faking bad**, **negative impression management**, **malingering**: answering to present a favourable or an impaired picture, split into deliberate management of the audience and honest self-enhancement the respondent believes.
- **Careless responding**, also **insufficient effort responding**, **IER**, **straight-lining**, **non-differentiation**, **invariant responding**, **random responding**: answering without engaging the items, by repeating one option, by responding at random or by pattern filling, which adds noise and can manufacture spurious relations.
- **Screens for invalid responding**, also **long-string index**, **instructed response item**, **instructional manipulation check**, **bogus item**, **infrequency item**, **attention check**, **even-odd consistency index**, **psychometric synonyms index**, **Mahalanobis distance for multivariate outlying response**, **response time as validity screen**, **overclaiming technique**, **warning against faking**, **validity scale**: indices and planted items detecting inattentive or dishonest protocols. Each costs survey space or run time, and cutoffs discard honest respondents along with careless ones.
- **Test compromise**, also **item exposure breach**, **item harvesting**, **answer copying detection**, **K-index**, **omega index**, **erasure analysis**, **aberrance detection**, **test collusion detection**, **test security protocol**: loss of item security and the statistical detection of copying, answer changing and collusion, governed by a written security plan. Detection statistics support an investigation and never prove misconduct on their own.
- **Score pollution**, also **coaching effect**, **test-wiseness**, **teaching to the test**: score gains from preparation that does not raise the attribute, whether through coaching, format familiarity or instruction narrowed to the tested sample. Score cancellation and a retesting policy are the administrative responses.

### Norms, cut scores and score linking

- **Norming**, also **norm development**, **norm group**, **normative sample**, **reference sample**, **standardization sample**, **local norms**, **user norms**, **subgroup norms**, **continuous norming**, **inferential norming**, **co-norming**, **interpolated norms**, **seasonal norms**, **quartermonth norms**, **school norms**, **item norms**, **norm obsolescence**, **empirical norms date**: building the reference distribution against which a score is read, national or local, smoothed across age or grade. Norms go stale, so a dated sample quietly biases every interpretation.
- **Norm-referenced interpretation**, also **norm-referenced score**, **criterion-referenced interpretation**, **criterion-referenced score**, **domain-referenced interpretation**, **mastery test**, **mastery level**: reading a score against other people, against a defined performance standard, or against a content domain. The three answer different questions, and one scale cannot serve all three well.
- **Derived score**, also **percentile rank**, **standard score**, **z score**, **T-score**, **stanine**, **sten score**, **normal curve equivalent**, **normalized standard score**, **deviation quotient**, **scaled score**, **raw-to-scale transformation**, **score reporting scale**, **truncated scale**: transformations placing a raw score on a reporting metric, some linear and some area transformations that normalise the distribution. Coarse metrics discard real differences, and a truncated scale hides floor and ceiling cases.
- **Developmental score**, also **grade equivalent score**, **age equivalent score**, **test age**, **mental age score**, **growth score**, **student growth percentile**, **curriculum-based measurement**, **out-of-level testing**, **ability-achievement discrepancy model**, **predicted achievement score**: scores expressing performance as the level at which it would be typical, or as growth relative to peers with similar histories. Grade and age equivalents invite overreading of small differences.
- **Standard setting**, also **cut-score setting**, **cut score**, **passing score**, **performance standard**, **performance level descriptor**, **achievement level descriptor**, **standard setting panel**, **borderline examinee conceptualization**, **minimally competent candidate**, **impact data feedback**, **normative feedback in standard setting**, **panelist consistency**, **standard error of a cut score**, **cut-score validation**: the judgemental process fixing where a score scale is divided, panellists trained on a described borderline examinee and shown consequences data. The result is a policy decision defended by procedural, internal and external evidence, not a discovery.
- **Test-centred standard setting methods**, also **Angoff method**, **modified Angoff method**, **Yes-No Angoff method**, **extended Angoff method**, **Nedelsky method**, **Ebel method**, **Jaeger method**, **bookmark method**, **ordered item booklet**, **response probability criterion**, **item-descriptor matching method**, **mapmark method**, **construct mapping standard-setting method**: methods asking panellists to judge items, either as the expected performance of a borderline examinee or as a bookmark in an ordered booklet. Judgements about items are hard to make and drift across rounds.
- **Examinee-centred standard setting methods**, also **contrasting groups method**, **borderline group method**, **body of work method**, **analytic judgment method**, **booklet classification method**, **whole booklet method**, **performance profile method**, **dominant profile method**, **judgmental policy capturing**, **cluster analysis method for standard setting**, **integrated judgment procedure**, **reasoned judgment method**, **briefing book method**, **objective standard setting**: methods asking panellists to classify people or whole performances rather than items. They need real work samples across the score range, which a new programme does not have.
- **Compromise standard setting methods**, also **Hofstee method**, **Beuk method**, **direct consensus method**, **vertically moderated standard setting**: methods reconciling a content-based standard with an acceptable failure rate, or aligning cut scores across grades so that growth looks coherent. They admit the pass rate into the standard, which content-based methods try to exclude.
- **Decision consistency**, also **classification consistency**, **decision accuracy**, **classification accuracy**, **Livingston-Lewis method**, **Subkoviak method**, **Huynh's decision consistency procedure**, **Hanson-Brennan procedure**, **Breyer-Lewis procedure**: how often a pass-fail decision would repeat on a parallel form and how often it matches true status, with false positive and false negative classifications as the two errors. Estimates come from one administration and depend on the model chosen.
- **Equating**, also **score equating**, **mean equating**, **linear equating**, **equipercentile equating**, **kernel equating**, **chained equipercentile equating**, **frequency estimation equating**, **poststratification equating**, **Tucker method**, **Levine observed score method**, **Levine true score method**, **Braun-Holland method**, **identity equating**, **circle-arc equating**, **IRT true-score equating**, **IRT observed-score equating**: making scores on alternate forms interchangeable by matching moments, whole distributions or fitted item parameters. Only forms built to one blueprint can be equated, and the weakest link is the anchor.
- **Equating designs**, also **single group design**, **random groups design**, **equivalent groups design**, **counterbalanced design for equating**, **nonequivalent groups with anchor test design**, **NEAT design**, **anchor test**, **common-item set**, **internal anchor**, **external anchor**, **miniature test anchor**, **miditest anchor**, **common-person equating**, **scaling test design**, **pre-equating**: the data collection plans supporting an equating, differing in who takes what. The anchor must be a miniature of the total test, and short anchors make every method unstable.
