- **Standard error of equating**, also **SEE**, **presmoothing**, **log-linear presmoothing**, **postsmoothing**, **cubic spline postsmoothing**, **difference that matters**, **population invariance of equating**, **percent relative error**, **kernel equating bandwidth selection**, **synthetic population**: the apparatus judging whether an equating function is good enough, from sampling error to whether it holds across subpopulations. Smoothing reduces random error by accepting bias.
- **Linking taxonomy**, also **score linking**, **calibration linking**, **projection linking**, **statistical moderation**, **social moderation**, **moderated judgment linking**, **concordance**, **battery scaling**, **anchor scaling**: the published sorting of relations weaker than equating, from concordance tables between different tests to moderation by judgement. A concordance is not interchangeability, and reporting one as though it were misleads users.
- **Vertical scaling**, also **vertical linking**, **developmental scaling**, **concurrent calibration**, **separate calibration**, **fixed-parameter calibration**, **Stocking-Lord method**, **Haebara method**, **mean-mean linking**, **mean-sigma linking**, **equating chain**, **scale maintenance**: placing adjacent grades or successive administrations on one continuous scale by transforming item parameters. Long chains accumulate scale drift, which only periodic rebasing removes.

### Test design, administration and documentation

- **Test design**, also **assessment design**, **test development cycle**, **statement of intended use**, **construct-centred design**, **test specification document**, **test framework**, **parallel form construction**, **spiraling**: the staged process from a written statement of intended use to assembled forms distributed across examinees. Design decisions taken early cannot be revisited once norms and scales exist.
- **Evidence-centred design**, also **ECD**, **domain analysis**, **domain modelling**, **student model**, **evidence model**, **task model**, **assembly model**, **assessment triangle**: designing an assessment backwards from the claims to be supported, through models of the proficiency, the observable evidence and the tasks eliciting it. Its documentation burden is heavy, which is why it is more cited than used.
- **Standardized administration**, also **standardization of conditions**, **administration script**, **standardized instructions**, **test administration manual**, **proctoring**, **remote proctoring**, **time limit**, **basal rule**, **ceiling rule**, **ancillary examiner**: holding conditions constant so that scores mean the same thing, with entry and stopping rules on individually administered tests. Standardization costs flexibility, and any third-party observer changes the conditions it documents.
- **Mode of administration**, also **delivery mode**, **mode effect**, **computer-based testing**, **CBT**, **paper-and-pencil equivalence study**, **unproctored internet testing**, **UIT**, **verification test**, **score comparability**: how a test reaches the examinee, mode effects threatening comparability across modes and forms. Unproctored delivery buys reach and requires a supervised verification test before a score is trusted.
- **Score report**, also **individual score report**, **interpretive report**, **narrative report**, **score interpretation guidance**, **technical manual**, **test manual**, **supporting documentation for a test**, **scoring process control**: what a programme publishes, from a person's results to the technical documentation supporting every claimed interpretation. Documentation not written at the time is rarely reconstructed later.
- **Test taker rights and responsibilities**, also **informed consent for testing**, **confidentiality of test results**, **right to explanation of scores**, **test disclosure**, **item release**, **test user qualification**, **obsolete test version**: the obligations owed to the person tested, including consent, confidentiality and an explanation of results, against the security interest in withholding items. Releasing items retires them permanently.

### Kinds of instrument and uses of a testing programme

- **Instrument purpose types**, also **achievement test**, **attainment test**, **aptitude test**, **ability test**, **diagnostic assessment**, **screening test**, **placement test**, **formative assessment**, **assessment for learning**, **summative assessment**, **assessment of learning**: the labels naming what a measure is for rather than how it is built, since the same items can serve several purposes. The purpose, not the format, decides what validity evidence is needed.
- **Maximal performance measure**, also **maximum performance test**, **typical performance measure**, **typical behaviour test**, **speed test**, **power test**, **objective test**, **subjective test**, **projective technique**: the split between measures asking for the best a person can do and measures asking what they usually do, which decides whether faking, effort or speed is the main threat.
- **Measurement modes**, also **performance-based measure**, **behavioural observation measure**, **momentary sampling measure**, **ecological momentary assessment**, **diary measure**, **structured interview measure**, **semi-structured measurement interview**, **assessment centre method**, **work sample measure**, **situational judgment test**, **biodata measure**, **implicit measure**, **conditional reasoning measure**, **adaptive behaviour rating**, **checklist instrument**, **inventory**, **single-item measure**, **multi-item scale**: the ways data about a person are collected, differing in who reports and when. Intensive modes buy ecological detail at high participant burden.
- **Composite score**, also **composite measure**, **subscale score**, **domain score**, **profile score interpretation**, **subscore added value**, **proportional reduction in mean squared error**, **Haberman subscore criterion**, **augmented subscore**, **test battery**, **test battery composite**, **index against scale distinction**: scores formed by combining parts, and the question whether a reported subscore adds information beyond the total. Most subscores fail that test, and reporting them anyway invites unsupported profile interpretation.
- **Testing programme use**, also **high-stakes testing**, **accountability testing**, **credentialing examination**, **job analysis for test development**, **practice analysis**, **role delineation study**, **content validation for credentialing**, **subject matter expert linkage ratings**, **selection procedure validation**, **test use for program evaluation**, **single-score overinterpretation**: the settings where scores carry consequences, licensure and selection resting on a documented analysis of the work sampled. Raising the stakes raises coaching, compromise and the cost of every error.
- **Selection decision rules**, also **top-down selection**, **test score banding**, **sliding band method**, **multiple-hurdle decision rule**, **compensatory decision rule**, **Pareto-optimal predictor weighting**, **actuarial prediction**, **mechanical prediction**, **clinical judgment against actuarial prediction**: how scores become decisions, from strict rank order to bands treating small differences as equivalent. Banding trades expected performance for other objectives, the diversity-validity dilemma made operational.
- **Utility analysis**, also **incremental utility of testing**, **Brogden-Cronbach-Gleser utility model**, **Taylor-Russell table**, **Naylor-Shine table**, **expectancy table**, **expectancy chart**, **selection ratio**, **success ratio**, **diagnostic efficiency statistics for a test**: models converting validity, selection ratio and base rate into expected gain or hit rates. Each needs a criterion in usable units, and base rate neglect wrecks the interpretation of any cut score.

### Health outcome measurement and thresholds for change

- **COSMIN taxonomy**, also **COSMIN measurement property taxonomy**, **COSMIN Risk of Bias checklist**, **COSMIN methodology for systematic reviews of outcome measures**, **criteria for good measurement properties**, **worst score counts**, **measurement property**, **psychometric property**, **PROM development study**: the consensus scheme naming which measurement properties exist and how well each was studied, scoring methodological quality by the worst item in a box. That rule lets one weak detail sink an otherwise sound study.
- **Patient-reported outcome measure**, also **PROM**, **clinician-reported outcome measure**, **ClinRO**, **observer-reported outcome measure**, **ObsRO**, **performance outcome measure**, **PerfO**, **outcome measurement instrument**, **proxy report**, **recall period**, **core outcome set**, **core outcome measurement instrument selection**: instruments classified by who supplies the observation, with a stated recall period and, in a trial programme, an agreed core set. Proxy and self-report are not interchangeable.
- **Content validity in COSMIN**, also **relevance of items**, **comprehensiveness of a measure**, **comprehensibility of items**, **structural validity in COSMIN**, **hypotheses testing for construct validity**, **interpretability**, **feasibility of an instrument**: the property set a review grades, content validity splitting into relevance, comprehensiveness and comprehensibility, with interpretability and feasibility as characteristics rather than properties. Grading demands patient and expert input most developers never gathered.
- **Responsiveness**, also **sensitivity to change**, **standardized response mean**, **Guyatt's responsiveness statistic**, **effect size for change**, **floor effect**, **ceiling effect**: the ability of an instrument to detect change that has occurred, quantified against a construct or an external indicator. Floor and ceiling effects cap it, and responsiveness in one population does not carry to another.
- **Minimal important change**, also **MIC**, **minimal important difference**, **minimal clinically important difference**, **MCID**, **minimal detectable change**, **MDC**, **global rating of change anchor**, **measurement error as a property**: the smallest change patients regard as meaningful, estimated by anchor-based methods, by distribution-based rules such as the half standard deviation criterion, by Terluin's predictive modelling or by a receiver operating characteristic cut point. Anchor and distribution methods disagree routinely.
- **Response shift**, also **recalibration response shift**, **reprioritization response shift**, **reconceptualization response shift**: change in what a respondent means by the scale rather than in the attribute, through changed internal standards, changed priorities or a changed concept. The then-test and the ideal-scale test attempt to detect it.
- **Preference-based scoring**, also **utility measure scoring**, **standard gamble**, **time trade-off**, **TTO**, **discrete choice experiment for valuation**, **person-centred scoring**, **patient-specific measure**: scoring health states by how much people value them rather than by summing items, so that scores enter economic evaluation. Valuation studies are expensive and the resulting weights are population-specific.

### Psychophysical and detection measurement

- **Psychometric function**, also **absolute threshold**, **detection threshold**, **difference threshold**, **just noticeable difference**, **point of subjective equality**, **interval of uncertainty**, **lapse rate**, **guess rate**: the curve relating stimulus intensity to the probability of a response, thresholds being conventional points read off it and lapse and guess rates fixing its asymptotes. Metrology's limit of detection answers a related question about an instrument.
- **Classical psychophysical methods**, also **method of limits**, **method of serial exploration**, **method of constant stimuli**, **method of adjustment**, **magnitude estimation**, **ratio estimation**, **magnitude production**, **cross-modality matching**, **anchor stimulus**: the fixed procedures for locating a threshold or scaling sensation directly, presenting ordered, random or observer-controlled intensities. Ordered presentation invites the time error, and direct scaling shows response compression.
- **Adaptive threshold procedures**, also **staircase method**, **transformed up-down method**, **weighted up-down method**, **Kaernbach weighted up-down**, **PEST procedure**, **Best PEST**, **QUEST procedure**, **ZEST procedure**, **psi method**: procedures placing each trial near the current threshold estimate, converging in far fewer trials than constant stimuli. Bayesian variants assume a functional form, and a wrongly assumed slope biases the estimate.
- **Forced-choice tasks**, also **two-alternative forced choice**, **2AFC**, **three-alternative forced choice**, **yes-no detection task**, **ABX discrimination task**, **same-different task**, **oddity task**, **catch trial**: tasks requiring a choice among presented intervals rather than a report of detection, which removes the observer's criterion from the measurement. They cost more trials per threshold and longer sessions.
- **Signal detection theory**, also **SDT**, **d prime**, **sensitivity index**, **response criterion**, **likelihood ratio bias measure**, **isosensitivity curve**, **A prime**, **confidence rating procedure**, **unequal-variance signal detection model**, **high-threshold model**, **meta-d prime**, **ideal observer analysis**: separating sensitivity from decision bias in a detection or recognition task, the rating procedure tracing a full receiver operating characteristic. Equal-variance assumptions are routinely violated, which biases d prime.

### Aggregation and multilevel measurement

- **Composition model**, also **composition theory of aggregation**, **direct consensus composition model**, **referent-shift consensus model**, **additive composition model**, **dispersion composition model**, **process composition model**, **global unit property**, **shared unit property**, **configural unit property**: the stated rule by which individual responses become a group-level construct, including whether an item refers to the person or to the unit. Without one, isomorphism across levels is assumed rather than argued.
- **Within-group agreement index rwg**, also **rwg**, **multi-item within-group agreement index**, **rwg(j)**, **awg agreement index**, **average deviation index**: indices comparing observed dispersion within a group against the dispersion expected from random responding, used to justify aggregating. The result depends entirely on the null distribution chosen, and a uniform null is generous.
- **ICC1 for aggregation**, also **ICC2 for aggregation**, **multilevel reliability**, **within-and-between analysis**, **random group resampling**, **aggregation justification**, **agreement against reliability distinction**, **level of measurement against level of theory**: the share of variance lying between groups and the reliability of the group mean, the two statistics behind any aggregation claim. Agreement and reliability answer different questions, and the ecological measurement fallacy follows from confusing levels.

### Usability and workload instruments

- **Standardized usability questionnaire**, also **System Usability Scale**, **SUS**, **Usability Metric for User Experience**, **UMUX**, **UMUX-LITE**, **Single Ease Question**, **After-Scenario Questionnaire**, **Post-Study System Usability Questionnaire**, **Computer System Usability Questionnaire**, **Questionnaire for User Interface Satisfaction**, **Software Usability Measurement Inventory**, **Website Analysis and Measurement Inventory**, **SUPR-Q**, **User Experience Questionnaire**, **AttrakDiff**, **Net Promoter Score**, **Single Usability Metric**: published instruments scoring perceived usability, made comparable across studies by normative benchmarks such as the curved grading scale. Perceived usability tracks measured performance only loosely.
- **Usability metrics**, also **task success rate**, **completion rate**, **time on task**, **error rate as a usability metric**, **efficiency metric**, **learnability metric**, **usability benchmark**, **severity rating of a usability problem**, **formative usability test**, **summative usability test**: the behavioural measures taken during a test, compared against a stated benchmark target and prioritised by problem severity. A summative test needs enough participants for interval estimates, unlike a formative one.
- **Usability inspection method**, also **heuristic evaluation**, **cognitive walkthrough**, **pluralistic walkthrough**, **retrospective think-aloud**, **constructive interaction**, **Wizard of Oz method**, **critical incident technique**, **Keystroke-Level Model**, **GOMS analysis**: expert and protocol methods finding problems without a full user test, with the problem discovery rate model and its Good-Turing adjustment estimating what remains unfound. The magic number five understates that need, and the evaluator effect is large.
- **Subjective workload measures**, also **NASA Task Load Index**, **NASA-TLX**, **Raw Task Load Index**, **RTLX**, **Subjective Workload Assessment Technique**, **Workload Profile**, **Rating Scale Mental Effort**, **Subjective Mental Effort Question**, **Bedford Workload Scale**, **Cooper-Harper Rating Scale**, **Instantaneous Self-Assessment**: rating instruments asking operators how hard a task felt, some multidimensional and some a single probe during the task. Retrospective ratings are recency weighted, and in-task probes intrude on the task.
- **Performance-based workload measures**, also **secondary-task method**, **Detection Response Task**, **embedded secondary task**, **Situation Awareness Global Assessment Technique**, **Situation Present Assessment Method**, **fixation-based workload measure**, **area of interest analysis**, **scanpath analysis**, **pupillometric workload index**: workload inferred from spare capacity, from probed situation awareness or from eye and pupil behaviour. Every one trades sensitivity against intrusiveness, and diagnosticity against a single global number.

### Named testing standards, codes and appraisal tools

- **Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing**, also **the Standards**, **AERA-APA-NCME Standards**: the joint document stating what test developers and users owe, organised into foundations, operations and applications, and the reference against which most testing disputes are argued. It states obligations without enforcement, and compliance is self-declared.
- **Code of Fair Testing Practices in Education**, also **Rights and Responsibilities of Test Takers**: two short companion documents, one stating the obligations of developers and users to those tested, the other what a test taker may expect and must do. Both are advisory codes carrying no sanction.
- **ITC guideline series**, also **ITC Guidelines on Test Use**, **ITC Guidelines on Computer-Based and Internet-Delivered Testing**, **ITC Guidelines on Quality Control in Scoring, Test Analysis, and Reporting of Test Scores**, **ITC Guidelines on the Security of Tests, Examinations, and Other Assessments**, **ITC Guidelines for Practitioner Use of Test Revisions, Obsolete Tests, and Test Disposal**, **ITC Guidelines on the Use of Tests and Other Assessment Instruments for Research Purposes**, **ITC Statement on the Use of Tests for Research**, **ITC and ATP Guidelines for Technology-Based Assessment**: the International Test Commission's guideline set covering use, delivery, scoring, security, retirement and research. Guidelines describe good practice and bind nobody.
- **Principles for the Validation and Use of Personnel Selection Procedures**, also **SIOP Principles**, **Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures**, **UGESP**, **ISO 10667**, **EFPA Test Review Model**: the documents governing employment testing, the Principles stating professional practice, the Uniform Guidelines carrying legal force in the United States, ISO 10667 covering assessment service delivery and the EFPA model specifying test appraisal. The Uniform Guidelines predate current validity theory.
- **Outcome-measure appraisal standards**, also **ISOQOL minimum standards for patient-reported outcome measures**, **FDA Patient-Reported Outcome Guidance**, **ISPOR good research practices for electronic patient-reported outcomes**, **OMERACT filter**, **EMPRO**, **Terwee quality criteria for measurement properties**, **mode equivalence of electronic administration**: the published criteria for judging whether an outcome instrument is fit for a trial or a labelling claim, the OMERACT filter asking for truth, discrimination and feasibility. Each sets thresholds few existing instruments meet.

### Questionable measurement practice and measurement critique

- **Questionable measurement practices**, also **QMPs**, **measurement flexibility**, **measurement degrees of freedom**, **undisclosed item modification**, **undisclosed scale shortening**, **ad hoc measure creation**, **measure without validity evidence**, **post hoc subscale creation**, **selective reporting of measures**, **scale reuse without revalidation**, **sum score by fiat**, **invariance untested across compared groups**: undisclosed choices about how a construct was measured, each changing the result while leaving the report unchanged. Failure to report reliability and uncritical alpha reporting belong to the same list.
- **Measurement transparency**, also **reporting of measurement decisions**, **measurement reporting checklist**, **measurement disclosure statement**: reporting the origin of every measure, its exact items, any alterations made and the reliability estimated in the present sample. It lengthens a manuscript and exposes decisions authors would rather leave unstated.
- **Construct validity crisis**, also **measurement crisis**, **reification**, **operationism**, **validity treated as a property of the test**, **reliability treated as validity**, **construct label as evidence**, **measurement heterogeneity across studies**, **construct proliferation through new scales**, **validity evidence decay**: the charge that whole literatures rest on instruments never validated, on constructs treated as things because they have names, and on validity claims inherited from an ageing citation rather than re-examined.

### Quantities, units and their realisation

- **Quantity**, also **kind of quantity**, **base quantity**, **derived quantity**, **quantity dimension**, **quantity of dimension one**, **dimensionless quantity**, **system of quantities**, **International System of Quantities**, **ISQ**: a property with a magnitude expressible as a number and a reference, sorted into base and derived quantities inside a system whose dimensional relations are fixed.
- **Unit of measurement**, also **measurement unit**, **base unit**, **derived unit**, **coherent derived unit**, **system of units**, **coherent system of units**, **off-system measurement unit**, **multiple of a unit**, **submultiple of a unit**, **International System of Units**, **SI**: a particular quantity taken by convention as the reference for others of its kind, a system being coherent when derived units carry no numerical factor beyond one.
- **Quantity value**, also **value of a quantity**, **numerical quantity value**, **quantity calculus**, **quantity equation**, **unit equation**, **numerical value equation**, **conversion factor between units**: a number and a unit taken together, manipulated algebraically so that equations between quantities, between units and between numerical values stay distinct.
- **Ordinal quantity**, also **ordinal quantity-value scale**, **quantity-value scale**, **conventional reference scale**, **nominal property**: a quantity ordered by magnitude but with no meaningful differences or ratios, placed on a conventional reference scale, against a nominal property which has no magnitude at all.
- **Unit realization**, also **realization of a unit**, **primary realization**, **mise en pratique**, **dissemination of a unit**: producing a physical embodiment of a unit's definition, published as a mise en pratique and passed down to working instruments. Realising a unit is expensive and belongs to a few laboratories, which is what makes dissemination necessary.

### Measurement, the measurand and the measurement result

- **Measurement**, also **metrology**: the process of experimentally obtaining values that can reasonably be attributed to a quantity, metrology being the science of it. It presupposes a described procedure, a calibrated system and a quantity specified closely enough to be measured at all.
- **Measurand**, also **specification of the measurand**, **measurand definition**, **well-defined measurand requirement**, **definitional uncertainty**, **intrinsic uncertainty**: the quantity intended to be measured, stated with every condition that affects its value. Incomplete specification leaves definitional uncertainty, a floor no better instrument can get below.
- **Measurement procedure**, also **measurement principle**, **measurement method**, **method of measurement**, **standard operating procedure for measurement**, **reference measurement procedure**, **primary reference measurement procedure**: the written detail sufficient for an operator to obtain a result, resting on a stated physical principle and a generic method. A reference procedure buys traceability and costs a full uncertainty evaluation.
- **Measurement result**, also **result of a measurement**, **measured quantity value**, **measured value**: a set of values attributed to a measurand together with their uncertainty, distinct from the true quantity value it estimates, from a conventional quantity value agreed by convention and from a reference quantity value used for comparison.
- **Measurement model**, also **model of measurement**, **measurement function**, **input quantity in a measurement model**, **output quantity in a measurement model**, **influence quantity**: the mathematical relation between the quantities entering a measurement and the measurand, including influence quantities that affect the result without being measured. Writing one down is what makes an uncertainty budget possible.

### Accuracy, trueness, precision and measurement error

- **Measurement accuracy**, also **accuracy of measurement**: closeness of agreement between a measured value and the true value of the measurand, a qualitative notion combining trueness with precision and never given a number. Psychometrics has no single counterpart, since validity and reliability answer different questions.
- **Measurement trueness**, also **trueness**: closeness of agreement between the average of many replicate measured values and a reference value, expressed numerically as bias. It is the nearest thing metrology has to validity, but it presumes a reference value a latent attribute never has.
- **Measurement precision**, also **precision**: closeness of agreement between measured values obtained by replicate measurement under specified conditions, reported as a standard deviation. Psychometric reliability is a variance ratio in a population, so a precise procedure and a reliable test are not the same claim.
- **Measurement error**, also **error of measurement**, **systematic measurement error**, **measurement bias**, **random measurement error**, **systematic effect**, **random effect**, **uncorrected bias**: the difference between a measured value and a reference value, split into a systematic part that repeats and a random part that does not. A known systematic effect left uncorrected must still be carried in the uncertainty.
- **Measurement repeatability**, also **repeatability**, **repeatability condition of measurement**, **intermediate measurement precision**, **intermediate precision condition of measurement**, **measurement reproducibility**, **reproducibility condition of measurement**: precision under conditions held constant, partly varied, or varied across laboratories, the stated condition being what the number means. This reproducibility is a condition of measurement, not computational reproducibility of an analysis.
- **Correction**, also **bias correction**, **correction factor**: a value added to or a factor multiplying an uncorrected result to compensate for a known systematic effect, as when a recovery-corrected result is reported. The correction itself carries uncertainty, which must enter the budget rather than vanish.
- **Metrological comparability of measurement results**, also **metrological comparability**, **metrological compatibility of measurement results**, **metrological compatibility**: comparability holds when results are traceable to the same reference, compatibility when the difference between two results is small against the uncertainty of that difference. Psychometrics pursues the same goal through measurement invariance.

### Measurement uncertainty and its evaluation

- **Measurement uncertainty**, also **uncertainty of measurement**, **instrumental measurement uncertainty**, **null measurement uncertainty**, **target measurement uncertainty**, **relative uncertainty**, **fractional uncertainty**: a non-negative parameter characterising the dispersion of values reasonably attributed to the measurand. It is a stated property of a result rather than a realised error, and unlike classical test theory's error it presumes no replication population.
- **Standard uncertainty**, also **standard measurement uncertainty**, **combined standard measurement uncertainty**, **relative standard measurement uncertainty**, **expanded measurement uncertainty**, **coverage factor**, **coverage interval**, **coverage probability**, **level of confidence**, **reporting of expanded uncertainty with a stated coverage factor**: uncertainty expressed as a standard deviation, combined across components and multiplied by a coverage factor to give an interval. A reported interval means nothing without its coverage factor stated.
- **Type A evaluation of measurement uncertainty**, also **Type B evaluation of measurement uncertainty**, **experimental standard deviation**, **standard uncertainty of an arithmetic mean**, **prior information in a Type B evaluation**, **uncertainty from a manufacturer tolerance statement**, **rectangular distribution assignment**, **triangular distribution assignment**, **U-shaped distribution assignment**, **normal distribution assignment**: evaluation from statistical analysis of repeated observations, against evaluation from any other information, the latter assigning a distribution to a stated limit. Type B assignments are judgements that must be recorded.
- **Law of propagation of uncertainty**, also **propagation of uncertainty**, **GUM uncertainty framework**, **sensitivity coefficient**, **effective degrees of freedom**, **Welch-Satterthwaite formula**, **pooled standard deviation**, **correlated input quantities**, **covariance term in an uncertainty budget**, **Kragten spreadsheet method**, **numerical differentiation of a measurement model**: combining component uncertainties through the first-order partial derivatives of the measurement model. It assumes near-linearity, so higher-order terms or a numerical method are needed when the model curves.
- **Monte Carlo method for uncertainty evaluation**, also **MCM**, **propagation of distributions**, **adaptive Monte Carlo procedure**, **numerical tolerance in Monte Carlo evaluation**, **shortest coverage interval**, **probabilistically symmetric coverage interval**, **discrete representation of a distribution function**: propagating whole distributions by simulation rather than propagating standard deviations, giving asymmetric coverage intervals where the model is nonlinear. It costs computation and a stated numerical tolerance for the trial count.
- **Uncertainty budget**, also **error budget**, **uncertainty budget table**, **budget table**, **dominant uncertainty component**, **cause and effect diagram for uncertainty**, **fishbone diagram**, **Ishikawa diagram**, **double counting of uncertainty contributions**, **reconciliation of uncertainty sources**: the tabulated contributions with their distributions, sensitivity coefficients and combined effect, usually built from a cause and effect diagram. Sources listed twice inflate the result, so the list must be reconciled before combination.
- **Bottom-up uncertainty evaluation**, also **component-by-component approach**, **modelling approach**, **top-down uncertainty evaluation**, **empirical approach to uncertainty**, **precision-based uncertainty estimation**, **validation-data approach to uncertainty**, **proficiency-test-based uncertainty estimation**, **quality-control-data approach to uncertainty**: building an estimate from a modelled list of components, or deriving it from reproducibility, validation, proficiency or control data already held. The empirical route is cheaper and hides which component dominates.
- **Uncertainty from sampling**, also **sampling uncertainty**, **Measurement Uncertainty Arising from Sampling**, **duplicate method for sampling uncertainty**, **balanced nested design for sampling uncertainty**, **unbalanced nested design for sampling uncertainty**, **variance component estimation for sampling and analysis**, **optimized uncertainty approach**, **sampling target**, **sampling theory approach to uncertainty**, **uncertainty factor approach**: the contribution from taking the sample rather than from analysing it, estimated by duplicated sampling and nested designs. It usually exceeds the analytical contribution and is usually omitted.
- **Uncertainty of results near zero**, also **uncertainty at low concentration**, **uncertainty on a ratio of two measured quantities**, **uncertainty due to finite resolution**, **quantization uncertainty**, **uncertainty due to rounding**: the cases where the standard treatment misleads, at concentrations where a coverage interval crosses zero, on ratios where relative uncertainties combine, and where display resolution or rounding sets a floor.

### Calibration, traceability and measurement standards

- **Calibration**, also **calibration hierarchy**, **traceability hierarchy**, **calibration curve**, **calibration function**, **calibration diagram**: establishing the relation between instrument indications and values provided by standards, with their uncertainties. It does not adjust the instrument, and it holds only under the stated conditions. Psychometric calibration means something else, estimating item parameters.
- **Metrological traceability**, also **traceability**, **metrological traceability chain**, **traceability chain**, **metrological traceability to a measurement unit**, **unbroken chain of calibrations**: the property of a result of being related to a reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing to the uncertainty. It costs a maintained chain, and a break anywhere voids the claim below it.
- **Measurement standard**, also **etalon**, **international measurement standard**, **national measurement standard**, **primary measurement standard**, **secondary measurement standard**, **reference measurement standard**, **working measurement standard**, **travelling measurement standard**, **transfer measurement device**, **intrinsic measurement standard**, **conservation of a measurement standard**: a realisation of a quantity with stated value and uncertainty, ranked by where it sits in the chain. Higher-ranked standards cost more to hold and must be conserved rather than used routinely.
- **Key comparison**, also **supplementary comparison**, **degree of equivalence**, **calibration and measurement capability**, **CMC**: the organised comparisons through which national measurement institutes demonstrate equivalence of their standards, publishing each degree of equivalence and the capabilities claimed. Participation is slow and demanding, which is why such comparisons are infrequent.
- **Verification**, also **metrological verification**, **validation**, **metrological confirmation**: confirmation that specified requirements are met, validation being verification against requirements for an intended use, and metrological confirmation the operations making equipment fit for that use. Verification is a check against a specification and produces no calibration.
- **Adjustment of a measuring system**, also **adjustment**, **zero adjustment of a measuring system**, **zeroing**, **two-point calibration**, **zero and span calibration**, **zero-drift correction**: setting an instrument to give indications corresponding to given values, at zero alone or at zero and span. Adjustment invalidates the preceding calibration, so calibration must follow it rather than precede it.
- **Calibration interval**, also **recalibration interval**, **recalibration**, **intermediate check of equipment**, **metrological confirmation interval review**, **equipment out-of-tolerance condition**, **reverse traceability of affected results**, **reference standard usage log**: how often equipment returns for calibration, shortened or lengthened on its recorded history and supported by intermediate checks. An out-of-tolerance finding forces review of every result since the previous calibration.
- **Uncertainty statement for a calibration certificate**, also **reported uncertainty with coverage factor**, **traceability of a workshop measurement**, **traceable calibration of shop-floor equipment**: what a certificate must carry, the measured values, their expanded uncertainty and the coverage factor, so a shop-floor instrument inherits a defensible chain. Certificates without a stated coverage factor cannot be used in a budget.

### Measuring instruments and their metrological properties

- **Measuring instrument**, also **measuring system**, **measuring transducer**, **sensor**, **detector**, **indicating measuring instrument**, **displaying device**, **scale of a displaying device**, **material measure**, **measuring chain**, **measuring device under test**, **unit under test**: the device or assembled chain producing a measurement, from the sensing element through the elements transforming a signal to the display or the embodied measure.
- **Indication**, also **instrument reading**, **blank indication**, **background indication**, **indication interval**, **nominal indication interval**, **range of a nominal indication interval**, **nominal quantity value**, **measuring interval**, **working interval**, **span**: the value an instrument provides, the set of values it can display, the interval over which it meets stated accuracy, and the difference between that interval's limits.
- **Sensitivity of a measuring system**, also **sensitivity**, **selectivity of a measuring system**, **resolution**, **resolution of a displaying device**, **discrimination threshold**, **dead band**, **dead zone**, **detection limit**, **step response time**, **response characteristic**: how much the indication changes per change in the measurand, the smallest change detectable, the interval producing no change at all, and the smallest value distinguishable from a blank.
- **Instrumental drift**, also **drift**, **stability of a measuring instrument**, **sensitivity drift**, **span drift**, **hysteresis**, **repeatability of an instrument**, **linearity of an instrument**, **variation due to an influence quantity**, **warm-up requirement**, **overload of a measuring instrument**: the ways an instrument's behaviour changes over time, with load history, with ambient conditions or after overload, all distinct from its error at a single moment.
- **Accuracy class**, also **instrument class**, **maximum permissible measurement error**, **limit of error**, **MPE**, **intrinsic measurement error**, **datum measurement error**, **zero error**, **instrumental bias**: the declared class placing an instrument within stated limits of permissible error, intrinsic error being measured under reference conditions and zero error at a zero indication. Buying a class buys guaranteed limits, not a known error.
- **Rated operating condition**, also **rated condition**, **limiting operating condition**, **reference operating condition**, **reference condition**, **steady-state condition**: the conditions under which an instrument's stated metrological properties hold, the conditions it can endure without damage, and the conditions prescribed for evaluating or comparing performance.

### Reference materials and their certification

- **Reference material**, also **RM**, **certified reference material**, **CRM**, **certified value**, **non-certified property value**, **indicative value**, **matrix reference material**, **pure substance reference material**, **calibrator**, **spiked matrix material**, **in-house reference material**, **reference data**, **standard reference data**: material homogeneous and stable enough for a stated property, certified ones carrying a traceable value with its uncertainty. Certified materials are costly and finite, so routine control runs on in-house material.
- **Characterization of a reference material**, also **value assignment study**, **interlaboratory characterization exercise**, **producer traceability statement**, **uncertainty of characterization**: assigning the property value by one reference procedure, by several methods in one laboratory, or by a network of laboratories, with the assigned uncertainty stated. - **Between-unit homogeneity**, also **between-bottle homogeneity**, **within-unit homogeneity**, **minimum sample intake**, **short-term stability**, **long-term stability**, **isochronous stability study**, **classical stability study design**, **uncertainty due to inhomogeneity**, **uncertainty due to instability**, **shelf life of a reference material**, **reference material period of validity monitoring**, **trend analysis in a stability study**, **sample preparation for homogeneity assessment**, **batch-to-batch consistency of reference materials**: the properties a producer must demonstrate and convert into uncertainty components, an isochronous design removing analytical drift from a stability study. Below the minimum sample intake the certified value does not apply.
- **Commutability of a reference material**, also **commutability**, **commutability assessment**, **commutable external quality assessment material**, **control material matrix effect**: whether a processed material behaves like a real patient or field sample across measurement procedures. A non-commutable material creates an apparent bias belonging to the material rather than to the procedure.

### Interlaboratory precision studies

- **Collaborative study**, also **interlaboratory study**, **collaborative trial**, **ring trial**, **precision experiment**, **trueness experiment**, **uniform-level experiment**, **split-level experiment**, **Youden pair**, **staggered nested design**, **nested design for a precision experiment**, **cell in a precision experiment**, **level of a collaborative study**, **minimum number of laboratories**, **alternative design for a precision experiment with heterogeneous material**: a designed trial in which many laboratories analyse identical materials to estimate a method's precision and bias. - **Repeatability standard deviation**, also **within-laboratory standard deviation**, **reproducibility standard deviation**, **between-laboratory standard deviation**, **repeatability variance**, **between-laboratory variance**, **repeatability limit**, **reproducibility limit**, **critical difference**, **critical range**, **critical range factor**, **repeatability relative standard deviation**, **RSDr**, **reproducibility relative standard deviation**, **RSDR**: the two precision measures a collaborative study yields, and the limits below which two results may be treated as consistent.
- **Intermediate measures of precision**, also **intermediate precision measures**, **time-different intermediate precision condition**, **operator-different intermediate precision condition**, **equipment-different intermediate precision condition**, **calibration-different intermediate precision condition**: precision within one laboratory when one named factor is deliberately varied, sitting between repeatability and reproducibility. Which factor was varied must be reported, since the number means nothing without it.
- **Cochran test**, also **Cochran's test for variance outliers**, **Grubbs test**, **Grubbs' test for outlying means**, **Mandel h statistic**, **Mandel k statistic**, **straggler**, **statistical outlier in a collaborative study**, **outlier retention decision**, **robust analysis of collaborative study data**, **Youden plot**: the consistency checks applied to collaborative data, separating stragglers from outliers and displaying laboratory bias graphically. Discarding laboratories flatters the precision estimate, so robust estimation is often preferred to exclusion.
- **Laboratory bias**, also **laboratory component of bias**, **method bias**, **bias of the measurement method**, **expectation of a measurement method**, **assessment of trueness against an accepted reference value**, **practical applications of accuracy values**: the fixed offset of one laboratory from the method's expectation, and of the method itself from an accepted reference value. Separating the two needs a reference value the study cannot produce for itself.
- **Horwitz function**, also **Horwitz curve**, **Horwitz trumpet**, **HorRat ratio**, **Horwitz ratio**, **Thompson modification of the Horwitz function**, **predicted relative standard deviation from the Horwitz model**, **functional relationship of precision to level**: the empirical relation making reproducibility relative standard deviation a function of concentration alone, HorRat comparing an observed value against it. Thompson's correction exists because the curve fails at low concentration.

### Proficiency testing and external quality assessment

- **Proficiency testing**, also **PT**, **external quality assessment**, **EQA**, **proficiency test item**, **proficiency test round**, **sequential proficiency testing scheme**, **measurement comparison scheme**, **sample distribution design**, **anonymity of participants**, **educational proficiency testing**, **accuracy-based proficiency testing**, **interpretive proficiency testing**, **qualitative proficiency test scoring**, **split-level design in proficiency testing**: periodic distribution of identical items to laboratories whose results are scored against an assigned value. It samples one occasion under best behaviour and cannot describe routine performance.
- **Assigned value**, also **assigned quantity value**, **consensus value**, **formulation-based assigned value**, **certified reference value as assigned value**, **expert laboratory consensus**, **uncertainty of the assigned value**, **number of participants requirement**: the value taken as correct for a round, from formulation, from a certified material, from expert laboratories or from the participants themselves. A participant consensus inherits any bias shared across the field.
- **Robust mean**, also **robust average**, **Algorithm A**, **Algorithm S**, **Q and Hampel estimators**, **normalized interquartile range**, **nIQR**, **median absolute deviation**, **standard deviation for proficiency assessment**, **fitness-for-purpose standard deviation**: estimators of location and spread that resist outlying participants, together with the dispersion actually used for scoring. A fitness-for-purpose value scores against what the measurement needs rather than what the field achieves.
- **z-score**, also **z-prime score**, **zeta-score**, **En number**, **percentage difference score**, **difference score**, **combined performance score**, **rescaled sum of scores**, **warning signal**, **action signal**, **satisfactory performance**, **questionable performance**, **unsatisfactory performance**: the performance scores of a round, differing in whether the assigned value's uncertainty and the participant's own uncertainty enter the denominator. A zeta or En score therefore tests an uncertainty claim, not only a result.
- **Homogeneity testing of a proficiency test item**, also **homogeneity check**, **stability testing of a proficiency test item**, **stability check**, **sufficiently homogeneous criterion**, **between-sample standard deviation**: checks that every participant received effectively the same material and that it survived transport, residual heterogeneity being added to the uncertainty of the assigned value. Skipping them turns item variation into participant blame.
- **Graphical review of performance over time**, also **kernel density plot of participant results**, **bar plot of standardized performance scores**, **Shewhart chart of participant scores**, **Youden plot for paired proficiency data**, **performance trend review**: the displays showing a participant's history and the shape of a whole round, a Youden plot separating systematic from random components across paired items. A single satisfactory score says nothing about trend.
- **Standard deviation index**, also **SDI**, **coefficient of variation ratio**, **CVR**, **peer group**, **method principle group**, **all-method mean**, **matrix-related bias in proficiency testing**, **uncertainty claim evaluation in proficiency testing**, **retrospective bias estimation from proficiency data**: peer-group metrics comparing one laboratory's bias and imprecision against others running the same method and instrument. A peer group hides a bias shared by the whole method group.

### Method validation and analytical performance characteristics

- **Method validation**, also **analytical method validation**, **method verification**, **confirmation of performance in the user laboratory**, **verification of a standard method**, **nonstandard method validation**, **validation plan**, **validation protocol**, **performance characteristic**, **method performance parameter**, **single-laboratory validation**, **in-house validation**, **full collaborative study validation**, **method-performance study**, **laboratory-performance study**, **material-certification study**, **acceptance criteria table for validation**, **validation report**, **revalidation trigger**, **applicability statement of a method**, **scope of a method**, **reportable range verification**, **reference interval verification**, **The Fitness for Purpose of Analytical Methods**, **ICH Q2(R2)**, **USP General Chapter 1225**, **USP General Chapter 1226**, **IUPAC harmonised guidelines for single-laboratory validation**, **AOAC Official Methods of Analysis**, **AOAC Standard Method Performance Requirements**, **SMPR**: establishing by experiment that a procedure meets stated performance requirements, verification confirming only that a laboratory achieves published performance for a standard procedure. - **Selectivity check**, also **interference study**, **interference testing**, **chromatographic interference check**, **orthogonal analytical procedure**, **contamination control**, **blank monitoring for contamination**, **sample carryover check between runs**, **carryover verification**, **haemolysed matrix selectivity**, **hyperlipidaemic matrix selectivity**, **anticoagulant counter-ion effect**: the experiments that spike candidate interferents at defined concentrations and observe the change in result, an orthogonal procedure serving as independent evidence. - **Working range**, also **analytical range**, **linear range**, **linear dynamic range**, **linearity**, **response**, **analytical response**, **response function**, **reportable range**, **reportable interval**, **working sample concentration range**, **limit of detection**, **LOD**, **limit of blank**, **LoB**, **limit of quantification**, **quantitation limit**, **LOQ**, **lower limit of quantification**, **LLOQ**, **upper limit of quantification**, **ULOQ**, **critical value of the measurand**, **decision limit**, **minimum detectable value**, **detection capability**, **false positive rate at the detection limit**, **false negative rate at the detection limit**, **practical detection limit for a routine method**, **signal-to-noise approach to the detection limit**, **standard deviation of the response approach**, **visual evaluation approach to the detection limit**, **analytical sensitivity**, **slope of the calibration function**: the concentration interval over which a procedure performs, bounded below by blank, detection and quantification limits fixed by chosen error rates and a named determination route, linear or modelled inside. - **Calibration standard**, also **calibrant**, **calibration solution**, **single-point calibration**, **bracketing calibration**, **matrix-matched calibration**, **matrix-matched standards**, **standard addition**, **spiking calibration**, **internal standard**, **surrogate standard**, **isotope dilution**, **isotope dilution mass spectrometry**, **IDMS**, **weighted least-squares calibration**, **nonlinear calibration model**, **lack-of-fit test for a calibration**, **residual plot for a calibration**, **back-calculated calibrator concentration**, **anchor point calibrator**, **reference standard characterisation**, **certificate of analysis**, **CoA**: the prepared materials and fitted function relating instrument response to concentration, weighting and matrix matching correcting for unequal variance and matrix effects. Every added calibrator costs run time, and a fit accepted without residual inspection hides curvature.
- **Recovery**, also **analytical recovery**, **apparent recovery**, **observed recovery**, **extraction recovery**, **process efficiency**, **matrix factor**, **MF**, **internal standard normalized matrix factor**, **ion suppression**, **signal suppression**, **ion enhancement**, **signal enhancement**: the proportion of analyte carried through a procedure and detected, resolved in mass spectrometry into extraction recovery, the matrix factor and their product, matrix suppressing or enhancing ionisation without altering the amount present.
- **Spike recovery experiment**, also **fortification experiment**, **trueness assessment against a certified reference material**, **CRM-based trueness check**, **trueness assessment by method comparison**, **comparison against a reference procedure**, **recovery acceptance window by concentration**, **Harmonised guidelines for the use of recovery information**, **endogenous analyte quantification**, **standard-addition approach for endogenous analytes**, **background-subtraction approach**: the three routes to a bias estimate, adding a known amount to a sample, measuring a certified material, or comparing against a reference procedure. Spiked analyte need not behave like native analyte, so a certified material outranks a spike.
- **Robustness testing**, also **robustness test**, **robustness factor screening**, **deliberate variation of method conditions**, **ruggedness testing**, **ruggedness test**, **ruggedness trial**, **Youden ruggedness trial**, **Youden and Steiner ruggedness design**, **design of experiments for robustness screening**, **DoE robustness study**: varying method conditions on purpose to find which ones matter and how far each may drift, a saturated Youden design testing seven factors in eight runs. Screening designs confound main effects with interactions, so a robust verdict can hide one.
- **Analyte stability testing**, also **sample stability study**, **freeze-thaw stability**, **freeze-thaw cycle testing**, **bench-top stability**, **short-term sample stability**, **processed sample stability**, **autosampler stability**, **extract stability**, **on-instrument stability**, **solution stability**, **stock solution stability**, **working solution stability**, **whole blood stability**, **long-term matrix stability**, **frozen matrix stability**, **incurred sample stability**, **ISS**, **forced degradation study**, **stress testing of a sample**, **peak purity assessment**, **mass balance in a degradation study**: the studies fixing how long a sample, extract or solution may be held at each stage, forced degradation deliberately stressing material to prove a method sees its degradants. Each condition demands its own timed replicate set.
- **Dilution integrity**, also **dilution validation**, **parallelism assessment**, **dilutional linearity**, **minimum required dilution**, **MRD**, **dilution quality control**, **DQC**, **specimen dilution and spiking**, **surrogate matrix**, **substitute matrix**, **surrogate analyte**, **blank sample**, **matrix blank**, **zero sample**, **challenge sample**: the checks that a diluted sample reads back to its undiluted value and that a sample above the measuring interval may be reported after dilution. Extending an interval by dilution requires its own validation at each factor used.

### Bioanalytical method validation

- **Full validation**, also **complete bioanalytical validation**, **partial validation**, **cross validation**, **cross-validation of bioanalytical methods**, **ICH M10**, **FDA Bioanalytical Method Validation Guidance**, **BMV guidance**: the three tiers of bioanalytical qualification, full for a new method, partial after a defined change, cross validation between methods, sites or matrices supporting one study. Tiering saves work and leaves the burden of arguing a change was minor.
- **Quality control sample levels**, also **LQC**, **MQC**, **HQC**, **run acceptance criteria**, **batch acceptance criteria**, **4-6-15 rule**, **repeat analysis of study samples**, **repeat analysis rules**, **reinjection reproducibility**, **reinjection integrity**, **study sample analysis**, **sample analysis phase**: the low, middle and high controls placed through every analytical run, with the stated fraction of calibrators and controls that must pass before results are released. Tight acceptance rules force repeat runs on scarce study samples.
- **Incurred sample reanalysis**, also **ISR**: reanalysing a portion of real study samples on a later occasion and comparing the two values, which tests the method on material containing metabolites that spiked controls lack. It consumes limited sample volume and can invalidate a completed study.

### Analytical procedure lifecycle and transfer
