## F7. Interpretive and case-based inquiry

### Paradigms and interpretive stances

- **Inquiry paradigm**, also **research paradigm**, **worldview**: the belief system a study works from, answering ontology, epistemology, axiology and methodology together. Costs a commitment declared before evidence arrives, and can rule out designs a question actually needs.
- **Competing paradigms of inquiry**, also **Guba and Lincoln's paradigm table**, **positivist paradigm**, **post-positivism**: the tabulated alternatives a design chooses between, named positivism, postpositivism, critical theory, constructivism and the participatory paradigm, each with its own ontology, epistemology and methodology. Costs commensurability with work in the other columns.
- **Philosophical commitments of a qualitative design**, also **Dualist and objectivist epistemology**, **Modified dualist epistemology**, **modified objectivist epistemology**, **Transactional and subjectivist epistemology**: the declared positions on ontology, epistemology, axiology and methodology, the epistemologies named dualist and objectivist, modified dualist, and transactional and subjectivist, the methodologies hermeneutical and dialectical, and dialogic and dialectical. Costs an allegiance stated before fieldwork.
- **Ontological positions in qualitative inquiry**, also **relativist ontology**, **Historical relativism**: the graded answers to what exists apart from inquiry, named naive realism, critical realism, Hammersley's subtle realism, scientific realism, the historical realism of critical theory, and relativism. Choosing one bounds what a finding may claim.
- **Constructivism**, also **constructivist paradigm**, **Interpretivism**, **interpretive paradigm**: the paradigm holding realities to be locally constructed and co-created in the encounter, reached by hermeneutical and dialectical methodology, with social constructionism and radical constructivism as its named variants. Costs any claim that findings stand independent of the researcher.
- **Critical theory as an inquiry paradigm**, also **critical paradigm**, **critical inquiry**, **Dialogic and dialectical methodology**: research aiming at critique and transformation of unjust structures, its ontology historical realism and its methodology dialogic and dialectical. Costs neutrality, and commits a study to a political position it must defend.
- **Feminist standpoint epistemology**, also **standpoint theory**, **feminist empiricism**, **Feminist standpoint theory**, **Feminist research methodology**, **feminist methodology**, **view from nowhere**: the position that knowledge begins from marginalized experience, carrying Harding's strong objectivity, Haraway's situated knowledges, and the god trick as the name for the disembodied claim. Costs the appearance of detachment.
- **Transformative paradigm**, also **transformative framework**, **queer inquiry**, **critical disability research**, **Transformative-emancipatory paradigm**: the paradigm placing rights and social justice at the centre of design, kin to the participatory worldview, critical race methodology, queer methodology and emancipatory disability research. Costs a stated value commitment and community involvement the timetable must fund.
- **Paradigm incommensurability**, also **incommensurability thesis**: the claim that paradigms rest on beliefs with no common measure, the ground of the paradigm wars, opposed by the compatibility thesis holding that methods from different paradigms may be combined.
- **Naturalistic inquiry**, also **naturalistic paradigm**, **Axioms of naturalistic inquiry**, **Working hypothesis**, **working hypotheses instead of generalisations**, **Naturalistic inquiry axioms**, **the naturalist axioms**: the programme of studying settings without manipulation, resting on axioms of multiple constructed realities, inseparability of knower and known, working hypotheses, mutual simultaneous shaping and value-boundedness. Costs experimental control and statistical generalization alike.
- **Researcher as human instrument**, also **human instrument**, **researcher as instrument**: the position that a person rather than a schedule does the sensing in fieldwork, drawing on tacit knowledge. Costs a training and reflexivity burden, and makes the analyst's judgement part of the evidence.
- **Emergent design**, also **emergent research design**, **design flexibility**: a design permitted to change as fieldwork teaches what matters, its devices named progressive focusing, focus-determined boundaries and negotiated outcomes. Costs a fixed plan, and obliges the report to document decisions taken mid-study.
- **Emic and etic perspective**, also **insider perspective**, **outsider perspective**, **Emic perspective**, **emic account**, **emic research position**, **First-order and second-order construct**, **lay and researcher construct**, **emic stance**, **etic stance**: the contrast between members' own categories and the analyst's imported ones, extended by the insider stance, the outsider stance and the insider-outsider debate. Working emic buys fidelity and costs comparability across settings.
- **Idiographic inquiry**, also **idiographic interpretation**, **idiography**, **Idiographic commitment**, **idiographic focus**, **Idiographic study**: study aimed at the particular case in its own terms, set against nomothetic inquiry's search for general law and expressed in tentative application. Costs any statement of how far a finding travels.
- **Crises of representation, legitimation and praxis**, also **Crisis of representation**, **Crisis of praxis**, **seven moments**, **eight moments**: the reflexive turn's three named crises, over whether a text can capture lived experience, on what authority it claims validity, and whether it changes anything, periodized in the moments of qualitative research alongside blurred genres.
- **Post-qualitative inquiry**, also **postqualitative research**, **New materialist inquiry**, **diffractive reading**, **diffraction**: the refusal of method as procedure, carrying new materialist and posthumanist inquiry, rhizomatic inquiry, agential realism with intra-action, and diffractive methodology as the reading of one text through another. Costs the procedural warrant reviewers expect.
- **Critical realist research design**, also **retroductive inference**, **judgemental rationality**: inquiry moving from events to the mechanisms that produced them by retroduction, holding ontological realism, epistemic relativism and judgmental rationality together, with analytical dualism, the morphogenetic approach, demi-regularity and explanatory critique. Costs mechanisms nobody can observe.
- **Interactionist and ethnomethodological traditions**, also **dramaturgical analysis**, **Interpretive interactionism**: the schools reading social life as accomplished in interaction, named symbolic interactionism, dramaturgy, ethnomethodology and the documentary method of interpretation, with praxeography studying practices as enacted. Costs attention to structure and history beyond the encounter.
- **Bricolage**, also **bricoleur**: assembling a method from whatever traditions a problem needs rather than adopting one whole. Costs the defence a named tradition supplies, and puts the whole burden of coherence on the analyst.
- **Empathic neutrality**: the fieldwork stance of caring about people while withholding judgement on their accounts, positioned against both value neutrality and open advocacy. Costs the commitment advocacy offers and the distance detachment offers, satisfying neither fully.
- **Epistemic injustice**, also **testimonial injustice**, **hermeneutical injustice**: the wrong done when a speaker's credibility is discounted or when a community lacks the concepts to make its experience intelligible, a standing hazard in interview-based work.

### Indigenous, decolonizing and justice-centred traditions

- **Indigenous research paradigm**, also **indigenous paradigm**, **Relational ethics**: inquiry whose ontology and ethics are set by an Indigenous nation rather than by the academy, with relational accountability as the researcher's obligation to the relations a study touches. Costs authority over design and publication.
- **Decolonizing methodology**, also **decolonial methodology**, **Smith's indigenous projects**: research reframed as an Indigenous agenda rather than an outsider's project, enumerated as twenty-five indigenous projects including claiming, testimonies, storytelling, celebrating survival, remembering, reframing and naming. Costs the researcher's ownership of the questions.
- **Kaupapa Maori research**, also **pūrākau**: Maori-controlled inquiry conducted on Maori terms, carrying whakawhanaungatanga as the relationship-building protocol and purakau as its narrative form. Costs eligibility for researchers outside those relationships, and a timetable set by community rather than funder.
- **Indigenous dialogic methods**, also **talanoa research methodology**, **sharing circle**: culturally governed conversational forms of data generation, named yarning and the yarning circle, talanoa, dadirri as deep listening, the talking circle, fa'afaletui as the weaving of viewpoints, and the tivaevae model. Costs transcription-ready structure and outsider facilitation.
- **Indigenous storywork**, also **Storywork principles**, **seven principles of storywork**: Archibald's use of story as method and theory, governed by the named principles of respect, responsibility, reciprocity, reverence, holism, interrelatedness and synergy. Costs the analyst's freedom to fragment a story into codes.
- **Two-Eyed Seeing**, also **Etuaptmumk**: the practice of holding Indigenous and Western knowledge together without subordinating either, each seen with its own eye. Costs a single adjudicating standard when the two accounts of a phenomenon disagree.
- **Indigenous data governance**, also **OCAP principles**, **CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance**: two named doctrines over who holds research data, OCAP asserting ownership, control, access and possession, CARE asserting collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility and ethics. Costs open-data compliance.
- **Four Rs**, also **respect, relevance, reciprocity and responsibility**, **respect relevance reciprocity responsibility**: the four obligations a study owes an Indigenous community, offered as the test of whether education or research serves it. Costs extractive designs that return nothing to the setting.
- **Ubuntu research paradigm**, also **Afrocentric methodology**, **Africentric paradigm**: African-centred inquiry grounding knowledge in communal personhood and cultural location rather than individual observation. Costs the individualist unit of analysis most instruments assume.
- **Critical race methodology**, also **critical race theory in research**, **counter-narrative**, **counterstory**, **TribalCrit**: inquiry treating race as central and endemic rather than a covariate, with counter-storytelling, testimonio, Chicana feminist epistemology and tribal critical race theory as its named forms. Costs the posture of a neutral analyst.
- **Culturally responsive evaluation**, also **CRE**: evaluation whose questions, measures and interpretation are negotiated with the culture being evaluated. Costs comparability with standard instruments, and lengthens the design phase considerably.

### Grounded theory as a tradition

- **Grounded theory**, also **GT**: the methodology that builds theory from data through simultaneous collection and analysis rather than testing a hypothesis brought to the field. Costs a literature-led rationale at the proposal stage and a predictable endpoint.
- **Variants of grounded theory**, also **Glaserian grounded theory**, **classical grounded theory**, **Charmaz's grounded theory**, **Clarke's situational analysis**: the schools disputing what grounding means, named Glaserian or classic grounded theory, Straussian grounded theory, constructivist grounded theory, situational analysis, dimensional analysis, feminist grounded theory and second-generation grounded theory. Choosing one commits the analyst to its coding apparatus.
- **Theoretical sampling**, also **sampling of documents**: selecting the next participants, settings or documents according to what the developing analysis needs, not a frame fixed in advance. Costs an ethics application that can name its sample, and a defensible recruitment plan on paper.
- **Theoretical sensitivity**, also **theoretical agnosticism**: the analyst's trained capacity to see analytic possibility in data, held together with a studied refusal to privilege any existing theory. Costs the guidance an adopted framework gives a novice.
- **Theoretical saturation in grounded theory**, also **saturation in grounded theory**: the point at which further theoretical sampling yields no new properties of a category, grounded in the concept-indicator model and in the interchangeability of indices. Distinct from a sample-size claim made about interview counts.
- **Theoretical sufficiency**, also **theoretical completeness**: the alternative endpoints claimed for a grounded theory, sufficiency conceding that categories are adequately developed rather than exhausted, completeness asserting that the core category accounts for the variation, with conceptual density as the density of relations built.
- **Core category**, also **central category**, **core variable**, **BSP**, **BSPP**: the category that accounts for most variation in the data and around which the theory integrates, often stated as a basic social process or basic social psychological process answering the participants' main concern.
- **Substantive and formal theory**, also **formal grounded theory**, **FGT**: the two levels of grounded theory, substantive theory holding within one empirical area and formal theory holding across areas, formal grounded theory being the procedure that raises one to the other. Costs a second round of comparison.
- **All is data**, also **slice of data**, **slices of data**: the dictum admitting field notes, documents, talk and the analyst's own experience as material, each slice a different angle on the same category. Costs any claim that the corpus was defined before analysis.
- **Delayed literature review**, also **deferred literature review**: postponing the substantive literature until categories have emerged, so that existing concepts cannot be imposed. Costs early positioning, and risks rediscovering what a field already settled.
- **Forcing**, also **forcing the data**, **emergence against forcing**: imposing preconceived categories on data instead of letting them emerge, with emergent fit naming the disciplined alternative of testing an existing concept against the data before adopting it.
- **Analytic induction**, also **modified analytic induction**, **negative case sampling**, **deviant case analysis**: the procedure of revising a hypothesis or the definition of a phenomenon until no case in hand contradicts it, driven by negative case selection. Costs the closure a probabilistic claim allows, since a single deviant case reopens the analysis.
- **Sensitizing concept**, also **sensitising concept**: a concept offered as a direction to look rather than a definition to apply, giving an inquiry a starting orientation. Costs the precision a fully specified construct provides.

### Phenomenological traditions

- **Phenomenology**, also **phenomenological research**: inquiry into the structure of experience as it is lived, before explanation or causal account. Costs any claim about frequency, cause or effect, and demands participants who can articulate experience.
- **Descriptive phenomenology**, also **transcendental phenomenology**, **Husserlian phenomenology**: the strand seeking the invariant structure of a phenomenon through reduction and free imaginative variation, taught as Giorgi's descriptive phenomenological method and the empirical phenomenological psychological method of the Duquesne school. Costs interpretation beyond what appears.
- **Hermeneutic phenomenology**, also **interpretive phenomenology**, **Heideggerian phenomenology**, **Dutch school of phenomenology**: the strand holding that description is already interpretation, practised as van Manen's phenomenology of practice and in the Utrecht school. Costs the claim that the analyst's own historical position was set aside.
- **Interpretative phenomenological analysis**, also **IPA**: the approach committed to the particular case before any cross-case claim, working through a double hermeneutic in which the analyst interprets a participant interpreting experience. Costs sample size, since idiographic depth caps how many cases one study can carry.
- **Other named phenomenological approaches**, also **RLR**, **heuristic research**: the further schools a reader will meet, named post-intentional phenomenology, reflective lifeworld research, the Vancouver School of doing phenomenology, phenomenography as the study of variation in ways of understanding, and heuristic inquiry. Each brings its own steps and warrant.
- **Epoche**, also **epoché**, **bracketing**, **phenomenological bracketing**, **Analytic bracketing**, **Bracketing as a rigour device**, **methodological bracketing**, **reflexive bracketing interview**: the setting aside of prior belief about a phenomenon so it can show itself, operationalized as the bracketing interview and, in Dahlberg's version, as bridling. Costs the analyst's declared expertise as a resource.
- **Phenomenological reduction**, also **eidetic reduction**, **transcendental reduction**, **Heuristic reduction**, **Hermeneutic reduction**, **Experiential reduction**: the disciplined moves from the natural attitude toward what is essential in an experience, extended by van Manen's heuristic, hermeneutic, experiential and methodological reductions. Costs everything about the phenomenon that is merely factual.
- **Free imaginative variation**, also **imaginative variation**, **eidetic variation**: varying a phenomenon in imagination to find which features cannot be removed without destroying it. Costs empirical grounding, since the test runs in the analyst's imagination rather than in the data.
- **Essence**, also **eidos**, **essential structure**, **general structure of experience**, **eidetic structure**: the invariant constituents without which a phenomenon would not be that phenomenon, the stated object of descriptive phenomenological analysis.
- **Lifeworld**, also **Lebenswelt**, **Lifeworld existentials**, **van Manen's existentials**, **Erlebnis**, **corporeality**, **relationality**, **Lifeworld fractions**, **Ashworth's fractions of the lifeworld**, **lived materiality**, **Van Manen's lifeworld existentials**, **the four lifeworld existentials**: the pre-reflective world of everyday experience, described through the existentials of lived body, lived space, lived time, lived relation and lived things, and through Ashworth's fractions of selfhood, sociality, embodiment, temporality, spatiality, project, discourse and mood.
- **Natural attitude**, also **phenomenological attitude**: the everyday unquestioned acceptance of the world's existence, contrasted with the deliberately wondering stance an analyst adopts, with intentionality naming consciousness always being of something, noema the object as experienced and noesis the act of experiencing.
- **Fusion of horizons**, also **Horizontverschmelzung**, **horizon of experience**, **Dasein**, **fore-conception**, **pre-understanding**: the meeting of the interpreter's horizon with the text's, presupposing a fore-structure of understanding and a being-in-the-world that no reader can step outside of.
- **Phenomenological writing**, also **vocative writing**, **reader resonance**: writing that makes a reader feel the phenomenon rather than summarize it, using the phenomenological anecdote as its device, wonder as its attitude and the phenomenological nod as its sign of resonance. Costs the conventions of a results section.
- **First-person experience methods**, also **Microphenomenology**, **micro-phenomenological interview**, **phenomenological introspection**: procedures generating fine-grained accounts of momentary experience, named the microphenomenological or explicitation interview, descriptive experience sampling, systematic self-observation and neurophenomenology. Costs participant training time and any pretence that the prompt did not shape the experience reported.

### Ethnography and fieldwork

- **Ethnography**, also **ethnographic research**, **field research**, **Naturalistic observation**: sustained study of a group's culture in its own setting, written up as an account of how members see and do things, with deep hanging out naming its least formal mode. Costs months of access and a portable design.
- **Participant observation**, also **unobtrusive observation**: taking part in a setting while recording it, along the named roles of complete participant, participant as observer, observer as participant and complete observer, with non-participant observation and observant participation at the edges. Costs the boundary between researcher and member.
- **Degrees of participation and phases of observation**, also **grand tour observation**, **selected observation**, **Passive participation**, **Moderate participation**: two staged scales for fieldwork, involvement running nonparticipation, passive, moderate and active participation, and attention running descriptive observation, focused observation and selective observation. Moving up either scale buys depth and costs the outsider's view of what members take for granted.
- **Field notes**, also **fieldnotes**, **ethnographic record**, **headnotes**, **Verbatim principle**, **Concrete principle**, **Descriptive field note**, **Reflective field note**, **reflexive note**, **analytic jotting**, **headnote**: the written record of a setting, layered as jottings or scratch notes, head notes carried in memory, and descriptive, reflective, methodological and analytic notes, governed by the verbatim, concrete and language identification principles. Costs hours per observed hour.
- **Thick description**: description dense enough that a reader can judge the meaning an act had for its participants, set against thin description that reports behaviour without it. Costs length, and cannot be produced from short exposure to a setting.
- **Access negotiation**, also **gaining entry**, **negotiating access**, **leaving the field**, **disengagement**, **rapport building**, **ethics of leaving the field**: the work of securing permission from gatekeepers, sustaining field relations and planning exit from the field. Costs concessions to the gatekeeper's interests, which then shape what can be seen and published.
- **Key informant**, also **key participant**, **informant**, **elite informant bias**, **co-optation by informants**: a member who explains the setting from inside and vouches for the researcher, source of the native's point of view. Costs a view filtered through one position, and invites elite bias when the accessible informant is the articulate one.
- **Developmental research sequence**, also **DRS**, **funnel structure of inquiry**, **Domain analysis**, **Spradley domain analysis**, **Taxonomic analysis**, **Componential analysis**, **Cultural theme analysis**, **theme analysis in ethnographic method**: Spradley's stepwise programme running from locating an informant to writing the ethnography, restated as the ethnographic research cycle, governed by ethnographic explanation to informants and delivering the cultural domain, cultural inventory and ethnographic mapping. Costs the freedom to improvise.
- **Descriptive question**, also **grand tour question**, **mini-tour question**, **Example question**, **Experience question**, **Typical grand tour question**, **Specific grand tour question**, **Guided grand tour question**, **Task-related grand tour question**, **Direct language question**, **Hypothetical-interaction question**, **Typical-sentence question**: Spradley's opening ethnographic questions, the grand tour taking typical, specific, guided and task-related forms, with mini-tour, example, experience and native-language questions in direct language, hypothetical-interaction and typical-sentence forms. Costs interview time before anything is tested.
- **Structural question**, also **Verification question**, **domain verification question**, **Cover term question**, **Included term question**, **Substitution frame question**: Spradley's questions establishing how members organize a domain, named verification, cover term, included term, substitution frame and card-sorting structural questions. Costs a rapport that tolerates repetitive questioning about terms already given.
- **Contrast question**, also **Contrast verification question**, **Directed contrast question**, **Dyadic contrast question**, **Triadic contrast question**, **Contrast set sorting question**: Spradley's questions establishing what members mean by distinguishing terms, named contrast verification, directed contrast, dyadic contrast, triadic contrast, contrast set sorting, the twenty questions game and the rating question. Costs participants' patience and a late position in the sequence.
- **Nine dimensions of a social situation**, also **Spradley's observation grid**: the checklist for describing any scene, being space, actor, activity, object, act, event, time, goal and feeling. Costs selectivity, since a full grid on every scene buries the analytic point.
- **Autoethnography**, also **performance autoethnography**, **Evocative autoethnography**, **Analytic autoethnography**, **community autoethnography**, **personal experience narrative**, **Critical autoethnography**, **co-constructed autoethnography**, **Native ethnography**, **insider ethnography**: study of a culture through the researcher's own experience of it, in the named forms of evocative, analytic, critical and interpretive autoethnography, duoethnography, collaborative autoethnography, the layered account, the co-constructed narrative and the personal narrative. Costs anonymity.
- **Critical ethnography**, also **regulatory text**: ethnography written to expose and unsettle power in the setting rather than describe it neutrally, with studying up directing attention to the powerful and ethnographic refusal declining to represent what should not be extracted. Costs continued access.
- **Institutional ethnography**, also **IE**, **Problematic**, **institutional ethnography problematic**: Smith's inquiry starting from a disjuncture in someone's everyday work and tracing the ruling relations that coordinate it, through work knowledge, boss texts and textually mediated social organization. Costs a bounded site, since the analysis follows texts outward.
- **Digital ethnography**, also **netnography**, **virtual ethnography**, **online ethnography**: fieldwork in online settings, extended by trace ethnography reconstructing action from system logs. Costs embodied cues, and raises consent problems where public posts were never written for research.
- **Focused ethnography**, also **short-term ethnography**, **micro-ethnography**, **graphic ethnography**, **Multi-sited ethnography**, **Global ethnography**, **collaborative ethnography**, **rapid assessment procedures**, **microethnography**: compressed fieldwork on a delimited question with prior knowledge of the setting, kin to rapid ethnographic assessment and rapid qualitative inquiry, and to multi-sited, global and team ethnography where scale replaces duration. Costs the discovery long immersion allows.
- **Sensory ethnography**, also **visual ethnography**, **VRE**, **video-based field research**, **sensory methods**: fieldwork attending to what a setting feels, sounds and looks like, with videography and video reflexive ethnography feeding recordings back to participants for comment. Costs consent complexity, and equipment that changes the scene it records.
- **Go-along methods**, also **walking interview**, **shadowing**, **go-along interview**, **mobile ethnography**: generating data in motion by accompanying a participant through a routine, extended by the day-in-the-life study and mobile methods. Costs recording quality and a controlled setting.
- **Tales of the field**, also **Van Maanen's tales**, **Realist tale**, **Confessional tale**, **Impressionist tale**, **Jointly told tale**, **Critical tale**, **Formal tale**: the named genres an ethnographer writes in, being the realist, confessional, impressionist, jointly told, critical, formal and literary tale, each with its own claim to ethnographic authority. The genre chosen decides what the text can admit.
- **Structured observation**, also **systematic observation**, **observation schedule**, **partial interval recording**, **narrative record**, **Focal sampling**, **focal animal sampling**, **Scan sampling**, **instantaneous scan sampling**, **all-occurrences sampling**: recording defined behaviours against an observation protocol and a sampling regime, the regimes named time sampling, momentary time sampling, event sampling, interval recording, focal, scan and behaviour sampling, with running records, specimen records and an ethogram. Costs meaning.
- **Fieldwork hazards**: the named ways prolonged immersion distorts an account, being going native or over-rapport, culture shock, reactivity or the observer effect, and the ethnographic present that writes a changing setting as timeless.
- **Named ethnographic genres**, also **Realist ethnography**, **Feminist ethnography**, **Ethnonursing research method**, **Leininger's ethnonursing**, **ethnography of speaking**, **cultural consensus model**: further traditions a reader will meet, being realist, feminist and confessional ethnography, ethnonursing research, linguistic ethnography, the ethnography of communication with Hymes's SPEAKING model, salvage ethnography, cultural consensus analysis and the discredited armchair anthropology.

### Narrative, biographical and life-history inquiry

- **Narrative inquiry**, also **narrative research**, **Three-dimensional narrative inquiry space**, **Narrative commonplaces**, **temporality sociality place**: study of experience as told stories rather than coded fragments, thought within the three-dimensional inquiry space of the commonplaces temporality, sociality and place. Costs the comparability coding gives, and binds the analyst to a few participants told at length.
- **Field text**, also **interim text**, **research text**, **re-storying**: the three states a narrative inquiry's material passes through, from records made with participants through working drafts to the published account, with restorying naming the retelling and narrative smoothing the temptation to tidy a life into a plot.
- **Life history**, also **life history method**, **life story interview**, **life story method**, **Life history analysis**, **life-story analysis**, **recorded life-story interview**, **Life history interview**: reconstruction of a whole life or a long stretch of it from a participant's own telling, the core of biographical research. Costs many hours per participant and a report that cannot anonymize a life easily.
- **Biographical interview forms**, also **biographical method**, **BNIM**, **FANI**, **SQUIN**, **Autobiographical narrative**, **Autobiographical narrative interview**: the named protocols for eliciting uninterrupted life narration, being the biographical narrative interpretive method with its single question aimed at inducing narrative, the free association narrative interview, Schutze's narrative interview and the episodic interview. Costs the interviewer's agenda.
- **Small stories research**, also **small story analysis**, **Small story research**, **small stories analysis**: attention to the brief, fragmentary tellings of everyday talk instead of the big story of a whole life, canonical narrative naming the culturally expected shape the small story departs from.
- **Narrative concepts**: the vocabulary a narrative analysis reasons with, being emplotment as the ordering of events into a plot, narrative coherence, the epiphany or turning point, and narrative truth as a story's faithfulness to a life rather than to fact.
- **Dialogical narrative analysis**, also **narrative ethnography**: Frank's treatment of stories as actors doing work between people rather than reports to be mined, extended by narrative ethnography's telling of fieldwork as story. Costs the tidy findings-and-themes results section.
- **Qualitative longitudinal research**, also **QLR**, **serial interviewing**, **longitudinal qualitative research**, **Longitudinal interviewing**, **Longitudinal qualitative analysis**, **qualitative longitudinal analysis**, **Trajectory analysis**, **Recurrent cross-sectional analysis**, **repeated cross-sectional qualitative analysis**: following the same participants across repeated waves so change is observed rather than recalled, with the repeat interview as its instrument. Costs attrition, years of funding, and an analysis that grows faster than the sample.
- **Collective memory work**, also **memory work**: Haug's group procedure in which members write and then jointly analyse memories of a common experience. Costs the individual interview's privacy, since analysis happens in front of the people whose memories are on the table.

### Discourse, conversation and language-focused traditions

- **Discourse analysis**, also **DA**: study of language in use as constitutive of the objects it describes rather than a transparent report of them. Costs the treatment of talk as evidence about an outside world, which is what most interview studies want from it.
- **Critical discourse analysis**, also **CDA**, **critical discourse studies**, **Dialectical-relational approach**, **Socio-cognitive approach**, **DHA**: discourse analysis oriented to power and ideology, in the named approaches of Fairclough's dialectical-relational analysis, van Dijk's socio-cognitive analysis and the discourse-historical approach. Costs the appearance of neutrality, and demands social theory beyond the text.
- **Three-dimensional framework**: Fairclough's simultaneous reading of a text, of the discursive practice producing it and of the social practice it belongs to, with the order of discourse, interdiscursivity, intertextuality, manifest intertextuality and recontextualization as its relational terms. Costs corpus size for depth.
- **Discursive strategies of the discourse-historical approach**, also **Nomination strategy**, **referential strategy**, **Predication strategy**, **Argumentation strategy**, **framing strategy**, **Topos**: the named strategies an analysis codes for, being nomination or referential strategies, predication, argumentation with its topoi, perspectivization, and intensification and mitigation. Costs the analyst's own reading, since the strategy list decides what the text is seen to do.
- **Discursive psychology**, also **DP**, **positioning analysis**, **narrative positioning analysis**, **positioning in discourse**: study of psychological business as it is done in talk, with the interpretative repertoire, the ideological dilemma, subject positions and positioning theory as its analytic units. Costs access to cognition, which it declines to infer from what people say.
- **Foucauldian discourse analysis**, also **FDA**, **genealogical method**, **archaeological method**: analysis of how discourses constitute subjects and objects of knowledge, worked through genealogy, the archaeology of knowledge and dispositive analysis. Costs a procedure, since these are strategies of reading rather than steps a reader can audit.
- **Conversation analysis**, also **CA**, **multimodal analysis**, **Applied conversation analysis**, **Overall structural organization**, **Multimodal conversation analysis**, **multimodal interaction analysis**, **Conversation analysis procedure**, **CA procedure**, **building a collection of instances**: study of the ordered machinery of talk in interaction from recordings of naturally occurring conduct, disciplined by unmotivated looking, the next-turn proof procedure, the unique adequacy requirement and collection building, in applied and multimodal forms. Costs interview data.
- **Turn-taking organization**, also **turn-taking**, **TCU**, **TRP**, **backchannel**, **response token**, **Turn-taking analysis**, **turn construction analysis**, **Turn-constructional unit**, **designing talk for a recipient**: the system allocating opportunities to talk, described through the turn construction unit, the transition relevance place, the transition space, turn design, progressivity, overlap, latching and recipient design.
- **Sequence organization**, also **Pre-sequence**, **Insertion sequence**, **First pair part**, **FPP**, **SPP**, **Base adjacency pair**, **SCT**, **Summons-answer sequence**, **closing sequence**, **Topic proffer**, **Sequential analysis**, **Adjacency pair analysis**, **Sequence organization analysis**, **sequential analysis of talk**: the ordering of actions across turns, described through the adjacency pair with its first and second pair parts, conditional relevance, base sequences with pre-expansion, insert expansion and post-expansion, sequence-closing thirds, summons-answer and terminal exchanges, story prefaces, continuers and second assessments.
- **Preference organization**, also **Conversational repair**, **Repair initiation**, **SRP**, **Repair analysis**, **Preference organization analysis**: the built-in bias of sequences toward some responses over others, seen in the shape of a dispreferred response, and in repair with its initiation, self-initiated self-repair, other-initiated repair, third-position repair and the preference for self-repair.
- **Membership categorization analysis**, also **MCA**, **MCD**, **Category-bound activity**, **category predicate**: analysis of the categories participants use to describe people, with the membership categorization device, category-bound activities and Sacks's standardized relational pairs. Costs sequential detail, and invites the analyst's own category knowledge into the finding.
- **Transcription convention**, also **transcription system**, **Jefferson transcription system**, **Jeffersonian transcription**, **GAT 2 transcription system**, **Gespraechsanalytisches Transkriptionssystem**, **Jeffersonian notation**, **transcription notation**, **transcription decision**: the notation deciding what a recording becomes on paper, the named systems being the Jefferson system for talk, the Mondada convention for embodied conduct and GAT 2 in German-language work. Costs a great deal of time per minute of tape.
- **Further language-focused traditions**, also **framing analysis**, **Mediated discourse analysis**, **CADS**, **institutional interaction**, **Corpus-assisted discourse study**, **collocate analysis**: adjacent named approaches, being interactional sociolinguistics with its contextualization cues, the sociolinguistic interview, genre analysis, frame analysis, mediated discourse or nexus analysis, multimodal discourse analysis, corpus-assisted discourse studies, positive discourse analysis and the study of institutional talk.

### Action research and participatory inquiry

- **Action research**, also **AR**, **plan-act-observe-reflect cycle**, **Look-think-act cycle**, **spiral of cycles**: inquiry that intervenes in a practice and studies the intervention, turning through the action-reflection cycle of plan, act, observe and reflect, the look-think-act routine and a cycle of cycles. Costs the detachment of an observer and any fixed endpoint.
- **Participatory action research**, also **PAR**, **CBPR**, **CBR**, **Youth participatory action research**, **Feminist participatory action research**, **FPAR**: action research in which those affected set the question and share the analysis, in the named forms of youth, feminist and critical participatory action research, community-based participatory research and community-based research. Costs control of the agenda and the publication schedule.
- **Cooperative inquiry**, also **co-operative inquiry**, **collaborative inquiry**, **four ways of knowing**, **Experiential knowing**, **Presentational knowing**, **Propositional knowing**: research done with people as co-researchers through cycles of action and reflection, grounded in an extended epistemology of experiential, presentational, propositional and practical knowing, and in critical subjectivity. Costs the time it takes to train co-researchers.
- **First-person inquiry**, also **second-person inquiry**, **third-person inquiry**, **living educational theory**: the three arenas of action research, on one's own practice, with a face-to-face group, and on a wider system, extended by developmental action inquiry and living theory action research. - **Action science**, also **action learning**, **Single-loop learning**, **Double-loop learning**: Argyris and Schon's study of the gap between espoused theory and theory-in-use, with single-loop, double-loop and triple-loop learning, the ladder of inference, actionable knowledge and the jointly told learning history. - **Practitioner inquiry**, also **teacher research**, **insider action research**, **practitioner research**, **teacher-as-researcher**, **Insider research**: research conducted by professionals on their own setting, in the named forms of self-study of teacher education practices, lesson study and reflective practice with its reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action. - **Conscientization**, also **conscientizacao**, **consciousness raising**, **sistematizacion de experiencias**, **Freirean culture circle**: Freire's process by which people come to read their own situation as changeable, worked through the culture circle and the generative theme, and recorded in the Latin American systematization of experiences. - **Participatory appraisal**, also **PRA**, **participatory rural appraisal**, **participatory learning and action**, **social mapping**, **rapid appraisal**, **Participatory mapping**, **matrix ranking**, **participatory ranking**, **sketch mapping**: the field tradition of visual group exercises replacing the questionnaire, its named tools community mapping, the transect walk, the seasonal calendar, pairwise ranking and participatory diagramming, with rapid rural appraisal its predecessor. - **Deliberative formats**, also **Search conference**, **Future workshop**, **participatory workshop**, **Citizens jury**, **Danish consensus conference**, **deliberative polling**, **Planungszelle**, **Twenty-first century town meeting**, **21st Century Town Meeting**: named designs for informed public judgement, being the citizens' jury, the consensus conference, the deliberative poll, deliberative dialogue, the citizens' assembly, the planning cell, the town meeting, the world cafe, open space technology and future search. - **Structured elicitation of constructs**, also **GCM**, **Trochim's concept mapping**, **Cognitive mapping**, **rep grid**, **triading**, **laddering interview**, **conceptual map**: procedures that surface a person's own dimensions of judgement, named the repertory grid technique with triadic elicitation, laddering for means-end chains, group concept mapping and cognitive or causal mapping. ### Purposeful sampling and sample adequacy

Each buys one contrast and forfeits the others.
- **Criterion and theory-driven sampling strategies**, also **criterion-based selection**, **operational construct sampling**, **theoretical construct sampling**, **Stratified purposeful sampling**, **Purposeful random sampling**, **Comparison-focused sampling**, **Group characteristics sampling**, **Criterion-i sampling**, **criterion inclusion sampling**, **Criterion-e sampling**, **criterion exclusion sampling**: the strategies picking cases against a stated rule, named criterion sampling with its inclusion and exclusion forms, theory-based sampling, confirming and disconfirming case sampling, stratified purposeful, purposeful random, comparison-focused, group characteristics and politically important case sampling. Costs flexibility.
- **Network and emergent sampling strategies**, also **Snowball sampling**, **chain sampling**, **venue-based sampling**, **Complete target population sampling**, **total population sampling**, **mixed purposeful sampling**, **hidden population sampling**: the strategies for populations without a frame, named opportunistic sampling, snowball or chain referral sampling, respondent-driven sampling, targeted sampling, time-location sampling, hard-to-reach population sampling, sequential sampling to redundancy and combination sampling. Costs control over who enters.
- **Convenience sampling**, also **accidental sampling**, **haphazard sampling**, **volunteer sampling**, **self-selection sampling**, **Expert sampling**, **Reputational case selection**, **key knowledgeable selection**: taking whoever is available or steps forward, with quota sampling filling fixed cells and expert and reputational selection relying on standing. - **Information power**, also **Malterud's information power**, **Study aim as an information power dimension**, **breadth of the study aim**, **specificity of the sample**, **theoretical support for the sample**, **strength of the interview dialogue**, **Analysis strategy as an information power dimension**, **cross-case against in-depth analysis**: the model holding that a sample needs fewer participants the more information each holds, assessed on the five dimensions of study aim, sample specificity, use of established theory, quality of dialogue and analysis strategy. - **Degrees of interview structure**, also **Structured interview**, **Semi-structured interview**, **Unstructured interview**, **non-directive interview**, **guided interview approach**, **closed quantitative interview**: the graded forms an interview takes, named the informal conversational interview, the interview guide approach, the standardized open-ended interview and the closed fixed-response interview, matching the unstructured, semi-structured and structured labels. - **Kinds of interview question**, also **Experience and behaviour question**, **behaviour question**, **Opinion and values question**, **Feeling question**, **Knowledge question**, **Sensory question**: Patton's classification of what a question asks for, being experience and behaviour, opinion and values, feeling, knowledge, sensory, and background and demographic questions. - **Interview guide**, also **interview protocol**, **topic guide**, **questioning route**, **moderator guide**, **funnel approach**: the written plan of an interview, built from main questions, follow-up questions and a funnel sequence moving from broad to specific. - **Probe**, also **probing**, **Elaboration probe**, **continuation probe**, **Clarification probe**, **Attention probe**, **Completion probe**, **Evidence probe**, **Slant probe**, **Steering probe**, **Sequence probe**, **silence probe**, **waiting probe**: a short prompt that keeps a participant talking or sharpens an answer, in the named forms of elaboration or continuation, clarification, attention, completion, evidence, slant, steering, sequence and silent probes. - **Named interview forms**, also **Merton focused interview**, **PCI**, **IttD**: distinct interviewing models a reader meets, named responsive interviewing with its conversational partner, the active interview, the problem-centred interview, creative interviewing, the interview to the double, the phenomenological interview and the focused interview. - **Interviews by standing and channel**, also **joint interview**, **couple interview**, **Telephone interview**, **Video interview**, **videoconference interview**, **Email interview**, **asynchronous written interview**, **instant messaging interview**, **chat interview**: the named variants defined by who is interviewed and how, being the elite interview, expert interview, key informant interview, dyadic interview, group interview, telephone, video, email and synchronous online text interview. Channel trades reach against rapport.
- **Stimulus-based interview techniques**, also **vignette interview**, **projective interviewing**: techniques putting material in front of the participant, named the vignette technique, projective techniques, the critical incident technique and cognitive interviewing as questionnaire pretesting. Costs the participant's unprompted framing of the topic.
- **Focus group**, also **focus group discussion**, **FGD**, **Opening question**, **Introductory question**, **Transition question**, **Key question**, **Ending question**, **all-things-considered question**, **Summary question**, **final question**: a moderated group conversation exploiting interaction between participants, sequenced through opening, introductory, transition, key, ending, summary and insurance questions. - **Focus group variants**, also **Online focus group**, **virtual focus group**, **Two-way focus group**, **Dual-moderator focus group**, **Dueling-moderator focus group**, **Respondent-moderated focus group**, **Focus group segmentation**: the named designs a group discussion may take, being the mini focus group, the online and telephone focus group, the two-way, dual-moderator, dueling-moderator and respondent-moderated group, with composition and segmentation deciding who sits together. Segmenting buys candour and multiplies groups.
- **Focus group participant dynamics**, also **dominant talker**, **Moderator effect**, **Group polarization in focus groups**, **quiet participant**, **rambling participant**, **Saturation in focus group research**, **group-level saturation**: the named ways group composition distorts what is said, being the dominant participant or talker, the self-appointed expert, the shy participant, the rambler, the moderator or facilitator effect, and group polarization toward a stated consensus.
- **Sensitive topic interviewing**: interviewing on subjects carrying distress, stigma or legal risk, resting on rapport built before the difficult question. Costs a longer protocol, a distress plan and often a limit on what may be recorded.
- **Cross-language qualitative research**, also **interpreter-mediated interview**: interviewing across a language barrier, where an interpreter or translator becomes part of the analytic chain. Costs direct access to wording, and obliges the report to state who translated what and when.

- **Generative and speculative tasks**, also **sound walk**, **walking methodology**, **story completion method**, **Speculative design**: prompts that ask participants to invent rather than report, named the story completion task, design fiction, speculative or critical design, the design charrette, the soundwalk and walking methods. - **Thematic analysis**, also **TA**, **Thematic decomposition analysis**, **Pattern-based analysis**, **pattern-based qualitative analysis**: identification of patterns of meaning across a data set, reported as themes rather than as a case-by-case account. - **Theme**, also **sub-theme**, **provisional theme**, **shared organising concept**, **theme map**, **candidate thematic map**, **Grand theme**, **overarching theme**, **Superordinate theme**: a pattern of shared meaning organized around a central organising concept, developed through subthemes, candidate themes and the thematic map. - **Inductive thematic analysis**, also **data-driven TA**, **deductive thematic analysis**, **theoretical TA**, **coding framework**: the two orientations of coding, inductive building categories from the data and deductive applying a framework brought to it. - **Mislabelled themes**, also **topic-summary theme**, **domain-summary theme**, **Bucket theme**, **thin theme**, **emergent themes claim**: the named failures a theme can be, being the topic summary or domain summary that reports a question rather than a pattern, the bucket or container theme, the underdeveloped theme, and the claim that themes emerged.
- **Data corpus**, also **coded extract**: Braun and Clarke's ladder of material, the corpus being everything collected, the data set what a particular analysis uses, the data item one interview or document, and the data extract one coded passage.
- **Quality tools for thematic analysis**, also **Braun and Clarke fifteen-point checklist**, **TA twenty-question quality tool**: the two published instruments for judging a thematic analysis, being the fifteen-point checklist for good thematic analysis and the twenty questions to guide assessment of thematic analysis research quality. - **Big Q and small q qualitative research**, also **small q TA**, **Big Q qualitative research**, **positivist qualitative research**, **method against methodology distinction**, **qualitative sensibility**, **methodological mishmash**, **mixing methods incoherently**: the distinction between qualitative work within a qualitative paradigm and qualitative technique inside a positivist frame, with qualitative positivism, theoretical flexibility, analytic sensibility and method slurring naming the ways the two get confused.

- **Qualitative content analysis**, also **QCA in the content-analytic sense**, **Conventional content analysis**, **Directed content analysis**, **directive content analysis**, **Summative content analysis**, **unit of meaning**, **level of abstraction**, **manifest content area**, **Preparation, organizing and reporting phases**, **Elo and Kyngas three phases**: category-based analysis of meaning rather than counts, in the named approaches conventional, directed and summative, working through meaning units, condensed meaning units, abstraction and content areas, and staged as preparation, organizing and reporting. ### Trustworthiness, triangulation and the audit trail

- **Trustworthiness**: Lincoln and Guba's standard for a naturalistic study, its four criteria named credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability, answering the conventional truth value, applicability, consistency and neutrality. Costs the vocabulary of validity and reliability, which reviewers outside the tradition expect.
- **Techniques for establishing credibility**, also **debriefing by a disinterested peer**: the named activities that earn the credibility criterion, being prolonged engagement, persistent observation, triangulation, peer debriefing by a disinterested colleague, negative case analysis and referential adequacy materials. Costs fieldwork months, and each must be documented.
- **Member checking**, also **member validation**, **respondent validation**, **member reflections**: returning accounts or interpretations to participants for comment. Costs analytic authority, and participants may reject a reading the data supports for reasons of self-presentation.
- **Triangulation**, also **Data triangulation**, **source triangulation**, **Investigator triangulation**, **analyst triangulation**, **Theory triangulation**, **theoretical triangulation**, **method triangulation**, **Environmental triangulation**, **setting triangulation**, **Space triangulation**, **Between-method triangulation**, **across-method triangulation**, **Within-method triangulation**, **Triangulation as convergence critique**, **naive triangulation**: comparing what independent angles on a phenomenon yield, in the named forms of data or source, investigator, theory and methodological triangulation, with environmental, space and time triangulation, and between-method against within-method. Costs the assumption of convergence.
- **Crystallization**, also **crystallisation**: the alternative to triangulation that treats multiple accounts as refracting a phenomenon rather than fixing it, expecting partial and incompatible views. Costs the reassurance convergence offers, and gives a reviewer no threshold to check.
- **Audit trail**, also **decision trail**, **Halpern's audit trail categories**, **six audit trail categories**, **Raw data record**, **raw data as audit evidence**, **methodological note**, **Materials relating to intentions and dispositions**, **reflexive material in an audit trail**: the retained record letting an outsider follow how conclusions were reached, in Halpern's six categories of raw data, data reduction and analysis products, data reconstruction and synthesis products, process notes, materials on intentions and dispositions, and instrument development information.
- **Inquiry audit**, also **external audit**, **dependability audit**, **confirmability audit**: examination of the audit trail by an outsider who judges whether process and product hang together, with stepwise replication as the parallel-team alternative. Costs an unpaid expert's weeks, which is why it is rare.
- **Reflexive journal**, also **research diary**, **field journal**, **reflexive commentary**: a dated record of the researcher's decisions, reactions and shifts of view, kept as evidence rather than as private notes. Costs candour, since a journal written for an auditor is written differently.
- **Authenticity criteria**, also **fairness criterion**: the criteria beyond method, named fairness, ontological authenticity, educative authenticity, catalytic authenticity and tactical authenticity. Costs a study that only reports, since three of the five require that participants gain understanding or capacity to act.

- **Standards for the quality of conclusions**, also **Objectivity and confirmability standard**, **confirmability standard**, **Reliability, dependability and auditability standard**, **auditability standard**, **Internal validity, credibility and authenticity standard**, **credibility standard**, **External validity, transferability and fittingness standard**, **fittingness standard**, **Utilization, application and action orientation standard**, **pragmatic validity standard**: Miles and Huberman's five, named objectivity and confirmability, reliability with dependability and auditability, internal validity with credibility and authenticity, external validity with transferability and fittingness, and utilization with application and action orientation. - **Eight big-tent criteria**, also **Tracy's eight criteria**, **rich rigour**, **evocative writing**, **multivocal representation**, **acknowledged partiality**, **Procedural ethics**, **Situational ethics**, **Exiting ethics**, **ethics as a big-tent criterion**: worthy topic, rich rigor, sincerity, credibility, resonance, significant contribution, ethical practice and meaningful coherence, with aesthetic merit, multivocality, partiality, transparency about method and the procedural, situational, relational and exiting forms of ethics as their means.
- **Yardley's four criteria**: sensitivity to context, commitment and rigour, transparency and coherence, and impact and importance, offered as flexible principles rather than a checklist. Costs specificity, since each criterion is met differently in each tradition.
- **Verification strategies**, also **Morse verification strategies**, **sample appropriateness**, **collecting and analysing data concurrently**, **Theory development as verification**, **researcher responsiveness**, **methodological congruence**: rigour built during inquiry rather than judged after it, named methodological coherence, an appropriate sample, concurrent data collection and analysis, thinking theoretically and theory development, with investigator responsiveness as the underlying capacity. Costs post hoc quality checks.
- **Primary and secondary criteria of validity**, also **Whittemore primary criteria**, **Whittemore secondary criteria**, **Primary criteria of validity in qualitative research**, **critical appraisal of one's own analysis**, **analytic integrity**, **creativity as a secondary validity criterion**, **sensitivity as a secondary validity criterion**: the primary being credibility, authenticity, criticality and integrity, the secondary being explicitness, vividness, creativity, thoroughness, congruence and sensitivity. - **Maxwell's validity typology**, also **Descriptive validity**, **Interpretive validity**, **interpretative validity**, **Theoretical validity**, **Internal generalizability**, **generalisation within the case**, **generalisation beyond the case**, **investigator bias**, **researcher effect on the setting**: the kinds of account a qualitative claim can get wrong, named descriptive, interpretive, theoretical and evaluative validity, with internal and external generalizability, and researcher bias and reactivity as the two standing threats.
- **Maxwell's validity checklist**, also **Discrepant evidence search**, **long-term participation**, **richly detailed data**, **simple numerical claims in qualitative reports**, **Intervention as validity test**, **Comparison as validity test**, **comparative check**: the named tests against those threats, being intensive long-term involvement, rich data, respondent validation, searching for discrepant evidence and negative cases, triangulation, quasi-statistics, comparison, and deliberate intervention as a validity test. - **Criteria for a grounded theory**, also **fit of a grounded theory**, **Workability**, **work of a grounded theory**, **originality of a grounded theory**, **usefulness of a grounded theory**: two published sets, Glaser's grab with fit, work, relevance and modifiability, and Charmaz's credibility, originality, resonance and usefulness. - **Five criteria for creative analytic ethnography**, also **Richardson's five criteria**, **contribution to understanding social life**, **expresses a reality**, **credibility of the lived account**: substantive contribution, aesthetic merit, reflexivity, impact and expression of a reality. - **Evolving guidelines for publication of qualitative research**, also **Elliott, Fischer and Rennie guidelines**, **Coherence as a publication guideline**, **analytic coherence**, **task specification guideline**: owning one's perspective, situating the sample, grounding in examples, providing credibility checks, coherence, accomplishing general against specific research tasks, and resonating with readers. - **Quality in Qualitative Evaluation framework**, also **Cabinet Office quality framework**, **contributory in advancing wider knowledge**: an appraisal framework built on four guiding principles, named contributory in advancing knowledge, defensible in design, rigorous in conduct and credible in claim. Costs fit with academic reporting, since it was written for commissioned evaluation.
- **Validity as craftsmanship**, also **validation as quality of craftsmanship**, **Kvale's three craftsmanship activities**: Kvale's relocation of validity into the researcher's ongoing checking, questioning and theorising rather than a final procedure. - **Alternative validity terms**, also **Transactional validity**, **Transformational validity**, **Communicative validity**, **Pragmatic validity**, **pragmatic validation**, **Ecological validity of interpretation**, **naturalistic fidelity**, **Empathic validity**, **Substantive validation**, **phenomenal fidelity**: the further validities argued for in interpretive work, named transactional, transformational, communicative, pragmatic, empathic and ecological validity, substantive and methodological validation, interpretive sufficiency, verisimilitude and fidelity to the phenomenon.
- **The criteria debate**, also **criteriology**, **parallel perspective on rigour**, **rejection of criteria**, **goodness in qualitative inquiry**, **Rigor or rigor mortis**, **overproceduralised rigour critique**: the dispute over whether interpretive work should be judged by stated criteria at all, its named positions parallel criteria, criterial thinking, goodness criteria, the anti-criterial position, and the warning of rigor turning into rigor mortis.

- **Two cultures of research**, also **Deterministic causal claim**, **deterministic causation**, **Probabilistic causal claim**, **probabilistic causation**, **case universe**, **Variable-oriented research**, **variable-based research**, **Effects-of-causes approach**, **Causes-of-effects approach**, **Rule of inclusion**, **Rule of exclusion**, **non-case**, **population of relevant cases**, **Individual case causation**, **case-level causation**, **Population-level causation**, **average-effect reasoning**, **measurement asymmetry**: Goertz and Mahoney's contrast of effects-of-causes with causes-of-effects reasoning, and of variable-oriented with case-oriented and diversity-oriented research, with the possibility principle and its rules of inclusion and exclusion deciding which negative cases belong in the universe of possible cases.

- **Fallacies of historical time and narration**, also **hindsight in historical judgment**, **present-mindedness**, **retrospective illusion of fatality**, **Teleological explanation**, **teleology in history**, **Whig interpretation of history**, **tunnel vision in history**, **Didactic fallacy**, **Fallacy of anachronism**, **Nunc pro tunc fallacy**, **now for then**, **Fallacy of false periodization**, **Telescopic fallacy**, **Interminable fallacy**, **Chronic fallacy**, **Static fallacy**, **Fallacy of presumptive continuity**, **Fallacy of presumptive change**: faults of historical time and telling, being anachronism, nunc pro tunc, presentism, hindsight, chronological snobbery, the historian's fallacy, retrospective determinism, false periodization, the chronic, static, telescopic, interminable and didactic fallacies, presumptive continuity, presumptive change, teleology, Whig history and tunnel history.

- **Fallacies of typing past actors**, also **Fallacy of identity**, **Pathetic fallacy**, **Fallacy of archetypes**, **Fallacy of the universal man**, **Fallacy of essences**, **essentialism in historical explanation**, **Apathetic fallacy**, **Idealist fallacy**, **Fallacy of the one-dimensional man**, **Fallacy of the mass man**, **Fallacy of the man-mass**: faults in typing past actors and their ideas, being the apathetic, pathetic and idealist fallacies, the one-dimensional man, the mass man, the man-mass, the psychologists' fallacy, the universal man, and the fallacies of identity, essences and archetypes.

- **Design textbooks for qualitative, case and mixed studies**, also **Creswell and Poth**, **Choosing Among Five Approaches**, **Creswell and Plano Clark**, **Teddlie and Tashakkori**: the volumes a design follows, being Qualitative Inquiry and Research Design, Case Study Research and Applications, The Art of Case Study Research, Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research and Foundations of Mixed Methods Research. ## F8. Inference and analysis

### The analysis plan and the estimand

- **Estimand**: the precise quantity a study sets out to estimate, fixed by four attributes, the treatment condition of interest, the population, the variable, and the population-level summary. Estimand and estimator alignment is the requirement that the analysis match it.
- **Intercurrent event**: an event after treatment starts that affects the outcome, handled by one of five named strategies, treatment policy, hypothetical, composite variable, while on treatment and principal stratum. Each answers a different question, so the choice fixes what is estimated.
- **Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials**, also **ICH E9**, **ICH E9(R1)**, **estimand addendum**: the regulatory statistical guideline for trials, with its addendum adding the estimand framework and requiring a sensitivity analysis for every estimand. Binds a trial to choices made before data arrive.
- **Analysis set definition**, also **analysis population definition**: the rule fixing whose data enters an analysis, the named sets being intention-to-treat, modified intention-to-treat, full analysis set, per-protocol, as-treated, completer, evaluable-patient and safety. Post-randomization exclusion breaks randomization, the price of the narrower sets.
- **Intention-to-treat principle**, also **ITT**, **ITT analysis**: analyse every randomized participant in the assigned group whatever they received, preserving the randomization that makes the comparison unbiased. Costs a diluted estimate under non-adherence, and it needs outcome data on people who left.
- **Statistical analysis plan**, also **SAP**: the document fixing analysis before data are seen, with mock tables or table shells, a dry-run analysis, blind data review and database lock as its machinery. Costs flexibility a real dataset may later demand.
- **Endpoint hierarchy**, also **outcome hierarchy**, **key secondary endpoint**: the ordering of primary, secondary, exploratory and tertiary endpoints that fixes which claims a trial may make, enforced by fixed-sequence testing, gatekeeping and alpha allocation. Costs the promotion of a finding the ordering demoted.
- **Composite endpoint**, also **hierarchical composite endpoint**, **win ratio**: a single outcome built from several events, letting a trial reach power no component would give, with the win ratio ordering components by severity. Costs interpretability when components differ in importance.
- **SAMPL guidelines**, also **Statistical Analyses and Methods in the Published Literature**: the reporting standard for statistical methods and results in a manuscript, alongside the CHAMP statement for appraising a medical paper's statistics and the Guidelines for the Content of Statistical Analysis Plans in Clinical Trials. Each costs journal space.
- **STRATOS initiative**, also **STRengthening Analytical Thinking for Observational Studies**: the collaboration issuing level-graded guidance on analysing observational data, with topic groups on missing data, measurement error, variable selection, functional form and high-dimensional data. Costs a search across many papers rather than one document.

### Researcher degrees of freedom and undisclosed flexibility

- **Researcher degrees of freedom**, also **analytic flexibility**, **analytic degrees of freedom**: the choices in cleaning, exclusion, measurement and modelling that a defensible analysis leaves open, each able to move a result, so that a report of one path from many overstates what was found.
- **Degrees of Freedom checklist**, also **Wicherts checklist of researcher degrees of freedom**: the item-by-item inventory of flexibility across hypothesizing, design, data collection, analysis and reporting, offered as a preregistration and review aid. Costs effort in advance, and its length invites box-ticking.
- **Selective exclusion**, also **post hoc exclusion criterion**, **undisclosed outlier removal**: dropping participants or observations under a rule chosen after seeing how it moves the result, whether a new criterion, a shifted threshold or silent deletion of data points.
- **Selective reporting of analyses**, also **outcome cherry-picking**, **condition dropping**, **covariate fishing**, **undisclosed multiverse**, **robustness reporting selectivity**: reporting only the analyses that worked, across dependent variables, conditions, covariates, subgroups, time points and specifications, so a p value computed as though the analysis stood alone is uncalibrated.
- **Data dredging**, also **fishing expedition**, **data snooping**, **specification search**, **testing hypotheses suggested by the data**: searching a dataset for a reportable result rather than testing a stated hypothesis, including model tinkering until significance, which makes any stated error rate a fiction.
- **Undisclosed flexibility**, also **failure to report all analyses performed**: flexibility exercised and never declared, covering scale scoring and item deletion chosen after results, composite construction, transformation choice, category collapsing, splitting a continuous variable and retrospective covariate creation.
- **Choice of statistical test after seeing results**, also **switching between parametric and nonparametric tests**: picking the test, the tail or the rounding after seeing which choice crosses the threshold, so the nominal error rate no longer describes the procedure that produced the number.
- **Analysis-plan deviation**, also **deviation from the SAP**, **undisclosed analysis-plan change**, **outcome switching**, **endpoint switching**: departure from the prespecified plan, which buys nothing once undeclared, with outcome switching the case of a primary endpoint changed between protocol and publication.

### Multiverse, specification curve and analytic robustness

- **Multiverse analysis**, also **multiverse grid**, **data multiverse**, **processing multiverse**, **model multiverse**, **explorable multiverse analysis**: fitting every defensible combination of processing and modelling choices and reporting the whole distribution of results, including a multiverse of exclusion criteria. Costs a result that no longer points one way.
- **Specification curve analysis**, also **SCA**, **specification curve**: plotting every reasonable specification's estimate in rank order over a set of theoretically justified specifications, then testing the curve jointly by permutation and reporting the median effect and the share of dominant signs. Costs a defensible boundary on reasonableness.
- **Vibration of effects**, also **VoE**, **relative hazard ratio**, **relative odds ratio**: the spread of an estimate across model specifications, quantified as the ratio of the extreme estimates and drawn as a vibration plot, with the Janus effect the case where the sign itself reverses.
- **Many-analysts study**, also **multi-analyst approach**, **crowdsourced data analysis**, **parallel independent analysis**, **red team analysis of an analysis**: handing one dataset and one question to independent teams to measure how far the answer depends on the analyst, with independent reanalysis the smaller form. Costs coordination and yields a spread rather than an answer.
- **Analytical variability**, also **analyst-induced variation**, **software-dependent analytic variation**: between-analyst variance in results from the same data and question, arising from idiosyncratic analytic choice and from implementation differences between software packages, which makes one analyst's number an unrepresented draw.
- **Estimation method choice**, also **choice of estimator and its implementation**: the decision among estimators fitting the same model, such as maximum likelihood against restricted maximum likelihood or a Bayesian fit, each with different small-sample behaviour. Costs a result resting on a choice rarely reported.
- **Sensitivity analysis**, also **robustness check**, **robustness analysis**, **alternative-specification table**, **prespecified robustness protocol**: refitting under a changed assumption to see whether the conclusion holds, reported as a robustness table. Costs its whole evidential value when only the favourable checks reach the page.
- **Negative control analysis**, also **positive control analysis**, **falsification test**, **placebo test**, **placebo outcome test**: testing a relationship theory says must be absent, or must be present, to expose bias the main analysis cannot show. Costs a control genuinely unaffected, and failure indicts without saying by how much.
- **Leave-one-out analysis**, also **drop-one analysis**, **leave-one-covariate-out analysis**, **LOCO**, **leave-one-site-out analysis**: refitting with one observation, covariate or site removed at a time to find conclusions resting on a single element. Costs many fits and offers no threshold for how much movement is too much.

### Data preparation, cleaning and linkage

- **Data cleaning**, also **data cleansing**, **data screening**: the pass over raw data that finds and resolves errors before analysis, using range, consistency, cross-field and plausibility checks written as validation or edit rules, with Fellegi-Holt edit and imputation the formal survey version. Costs judgement calls that move results.
- **Blind data cleaning**, also **cleaning before unblinding**, **data masking during analysis**, **analyst masking**: cleaning and deciding with treatment labels or the outcome hidden, so choices cannot be steered, with blind data review the formal pre-lock version. Costs the errors that only the labels would reveal.
- **Data entry error**, also **transcription error**, **variable coding error**, **miscoding**: an error introduced between source and dataset, in the named forms of reverse-coded item mishandling, silent coercion of a data type, date parsing failure, spreadsheet-induced corruption and a sentinel missing-value code read as real.
- **Merge error**, also **join error**, **many-to-many merge error**, **fan-out**, **row duplication on merge**: corruption introduced when datasets are joined, where an unintended many-to-many key duplicates rows and inflates the sample while a failed match silently drops it.
- **Implausible value**, also **out-of-range value**, **impossible value**: a recorded number the measurement cannot produce, with mixed units in one variable, end-digit preference and rounding heaping the patterned forms that no single-value range check will catch.
- **Record linkage**, also **data linkage**, **probabilistic record linkage**, **fuzzy matching**: joining records for the same unit across sources with no shared identifier, scored on partially agreeing fields. Costs linkage error in both directions, the false match and the missed match, biasing every downstream estimate.
- **Codebook**, also **data dictionary**, **data provenance record**, **data lineage**: the written definition of every variable, code and derivation, with provenance tracing each value to its source and the derived variable definition fixing how the analysis-ready dataset was built. Costs upkeep, and a stale codebook misleads.

### Outliers, influence and robust alternatives

- **Outlier**, also **univariate outlier**, **multivariate outlier**, **contextual outlier**, **conditional outlier**: an observation far from the rest, split into the error outlier that should go and the interesting outlier carrying real information, and contextual where it is extreme only given the other variables.
- **Outlier identification**, also **outlier detection**: flagging extremes by a fixed rule, the named rules being the standard deviation or z-score rule, three-sigma, Tukey's inner and outer fences, interquartile range, boxplot, median absolute deviation and Mahalanobis distance screening. Every threshold is convention.
- **Grubbs' test**, also **maximum normed residual test**: a formal test of whether the most extreme observation shares the others' distribution, with Dixon's Q test, Rosner's generalized extreme studentized deviate test, Chauvenet's criterion and Peirce's criterion as alternatives. All assume a normality the outlier undermines.
- **Influence diagnostics**: measures of how far one observation moves a fit, the named ones being Cook's distance, DFBETA, DFFITS, the hat value or leverage, COVRATIO and the internally and externally studentized residuals. None of them states how much influence is too much.
- **Leverage point**, also **high-leverage observation**, **influential observation**: an observation extreme in the predictors, able to move a fit far without leaving a large residual, so that masking hides one outlier behind another and swamping flags clean points beside a real one.
