Costs error control, since no long-run rate attaches to the report.
- **Error statistics**, also **error-statistical philosophy**, **severity of a test**, **severe testing**, **severity principle**, **argument from coincidence**, **error probe**, **frequentist principle of evidence**, **FEV**, **Statistical inference as severe testing**, **bad evidence no test**, **BENT**: the frequentist philosophy asking what a procedure could have detected, not what it reported. Costs applicability, since severity must be computed case by case.
- **Jeffreys-Lindley paradox**, also **Lindley's paradox**, **Bartlett's paradox**, **Berger-Sellke bound**, **irreconcilability of p values and evidence**, **frequentist-Bayesian reconciliation**: the divergence in which a p value rejects while a Bayes factor favours the null, sharpening as the sample grows, and the related result that vague priors drive the Bayes factor toward the null.
- **Statistical significance**, also **bright line**, **bright-line thinking**, **point-oh-five convention**, **the .05 level**, **the ninety-five percent convention**, **publication threshold**, **local against global significance**, **practical significance**, **substantive significance**, **clinical significance**, **economic significance**: a verdict passed by comparing a p value to a convention, which says nothing about whether the effect matters in the units anyone cares about.
- **Redefine statistical significance**, also **the .005 proposal**, **suggestive evidence**, **Retire statistical significance**, **Abandon statistical significance**, **Justify your alpha**, **decision-theoretic alpha**, **alpha as a function of sample size**, **five sigma**, **three sigma**, **genome-wide significance threshold**, **two-trials rule**, **threshold-free reporting**, **graded evidence language**: the proposals to move, justify or abolish the threshold. Each trades false positives against false negatives, so the relative seriousness of the two errors must be argued.
- **ASA Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values**, also **Wasserstein-Lazar statement**, **Moving to a World Beyond p < 0.05**, **ATOM**, **ASA Task Force Statement on Statistical Significance and Replicability**, **The Earth Is Round (p < .05)**, **journal ban on p-values**: the professional statements and the founding critique behind them, urging that uncertainty be accepted and that no threshold decide a claim. Costs the guidance a rule provided.

### Misreading a p value, an interval and a power calculation

- **Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: a guide to misinterpretations**, also **the twenty-five misinterpretations**, **the Greenland guide**: the enumerated catalogue of false readings of tests, intervals and power, usable as a checklist against a manuscript. Costs nothing to apply, and its length is itself the argument that the apparatus is misread by default.
- **Fallacy of the transposed conditional**, also **transposed conditional**, **confusion of the inverse**, **inverse probability fallacy**, **P value fallacy**, **chance alone fallacy**, **Bayesian wishful thinking**, **posterior illusion**, **unconditional interpretation of a p value**: reading the probability of the data given the hypothesis as the probability of the hypothesis given the data, or as the probability that chance produced the association.
- **Fallacy of accepting the null hypothesis**, also **acceptance of the null**, **absence of evidence fallacy**, **evidence of absence error**, **nonsignificance as no effect**, **nonsignificance as a small effect**, **large p as support for the null**, **fallacy of rejection**, **nullism**, **no evidence of effect against evidence of no effect**: treating failure to reject as proof of no effect, and its mirror, treating rejection as disproof of the tested hypothesis.
- **Significance as substantive importance**, also **significance-importance conflation**, **significance as a property of the phenomenon**, **effect size fallacy**, **large sample fallacy**, **P value dependence on sample size**, **sizeless science**, **sizeless stare**, **oomph**, **cult of statistical significance**, **variance explained fallacy**: reading a threshold verdict as a statement of magnitude, when a large sample makes any nonzero effect significant and significance is a property of the study.
- **Difference in significance fallacy**, also **significant-versus-nonsignificant comparison error**, **agreement fallacy**, **conflicting results fallacy**, **vote counting by significance**, **replication fallacy**, **dance of the p values**, **dance of the means**, **cliff effect**, **marginal significance**, **trending toward significance**: comparing verdicts instead of estimates, across studies or across subgroups, when only a direct test of the difference speaks to it.
- **Confidence level as the probability the interval contains the parameter**, also **interval probability fallacy**, **exclusion fallacy**, **overlapping confidence intervals fallacy**, **precision fallacy**, **confidence interval prediction fallacy**, **robust misinterpretation of confidence intervals**, **Hoekstra six-statement test**, **credibility against confidence conflation**: reading a confidence interval as a probability statement, as a range of refuted values outside it, or as a credible interval.
- **Abuse of power**, also **post hoc power fallacy**, **observed power**, **retrospective power**, **post hoc power**, **power approach paradox**, **low power result as consistent with the alternative**, **five percent error rate fallacy**, **beta as the probability of a false negative**: computing power from the observed effect after the test, which adds nothing beyond the p value and makes a nonsignificant result look stronger the higher it comes out.
- **Dichotomania**, also **dichotomous thinking**, **reification**, **null ritual**, **mindless statistics**, **statistical rituals**, **surrogate science**, **illusion of certainty**, **cargo-cult statistics**, **crud factor**, **Meehl's paradox**, **belief in the law of small numbers**, **sample size fallacy**, **interocular traumatic test**, **P value censoring**, **two-sided default fallacy**, **naked p value**, **asterisk convention**: the habits of mind sustaining all of the above, forcing graded evidence into two bins and the model into reality.

### Diagnosing the evidence in a body of work, and reading a null

- **Positive predictive value of a research finding**, also **PPV of a claim**, **prestudy odds**, **prestudy probability**, **poststudy probability**, **Ioannidis corollaries**, **Why most published research findings are false**, **false-positive report probability**, **FPRP**, **false positive risk**, **false discovery risk of a single claim**: the chance a claimed finding is true, which falls with low power, many tested relationships and flexibility, and which no p value reports.
- **S value**, also **surprisal**, **Shannon information transform of p**, **binary surprisal**, **surprisal reasoning**, **Bayes factor bound on the p value**, **likelihood ratio bound**, **Goodman's Bayes factor**, **P value calibration**, **calibrated p value**: recasting a p value as bits of information against a hypothesis, or as the strongest Bayes factor it could support. Costs familiarity, and it still says nothing about which hypothesis is true.
- **P curve**, also **p-curve analysis**, **P uniform**, **p-uniform star**, **Z curve**, **z-curve analysis**, **Test of excess significance**, **TES**, **Ioannidis-Trikalinos test**, **Test of insufficient variance**, **TIVA**, **R index**, **replicability index**, **Caliper test**, **P value bunching**, **evidential value of a literature**: reading the distribution of reported test statistics for signs of selection or fabrication. Costs a set of studies large and homogeneous enough to have a distribution.
- **Statistical consistency check**, also **reported-statistic recomputation**, **GRIM test**, **granularity-related inconsistency of means**, **GRIMMER test**, **SPRITE**, **Fragility index**, **reverse fragility index**, **fragility quotient**, **unit fragility**: recomputing a published number from what the paper states, to see whether the reported mean or variance is attainable and how few outcome flips would undo significance. Costs the ability to distinguish error from misconduct.
- **Failed replication**, also **non-replication**, **negative result**, **null result**, **null finding**, **informative null**, **uninformative null**, **inconclusive result**, **indeterminate result**, **underpowered null**, **decline effect in inferential terms**, **Proteus phenomenon in inferential terms**: a result that did not reproduce or did not resolve, where an underpowered study yields a null carrying no information at all.
- **Replication success criterion**, also **significance-based replication criterion**, **estimate-consistency replication criterion**, **direction-and-significance criterion**, **three-outcome classification**, **meta-analytic combination of original and replication**, **replication Bayes factor**, **sceptical Bayes factor**, **sceptical p-value**, **analysis of credibility**, **AnCred**, **reverse-Bayes analysis**, **second-generation p-value**: the rule declaring a replication successful. Costs comparability, since the rules disagree on the same pair of studies.
- **Claim calibration**, also **overclaiming**, **underclaiming**, **strength-of-claim matching to evidence**, **causal language from a noncausal test**, **generalization beyond the tested range**, **post hoc explanation of a null**, **salvaging a null by subgroup search**, **evidential wording ladder**, **registered null result**, **power reporting for a null result**, **reporting a null with a Bayes factor**: matching the wording of a conclusion to what the design and the estimate support. Costs rhetorical force.


## F9. Computational and simulated evidence

### Leakage in a training-and-test pipeline

- **Data leakage**, also **leakage**: information from outside the training data reaching the model, so a held-out score no longer estimates performance on new data, defined by Kapoor and Narayanan as a spurious relationship between predictors and target introduced by the pipeline.
- **Reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science**, also **ML reproducibility crisis**: the pattern of published machine-learning findings that fail on clean re-evaluation, traced across seventeen fields to leakage rather than to fraud or to ordinary sampling error.
- **Textbook leakage taxonomy**, also **eight types of leakage**: Kapoor and Narayanan's three-part frame with eight subtypes, separating a broken train-test boundary, illegitimate features, and a test set not drawn from the distribution of scientific interest.
- **Lack of clean separation of training and test set**, also **L1**, **train-test overlap**: the first leakage class, whose named subtypes are no test set at all, preprocessing on the train-test union, feature selection on full data, and duplicate records across splits.
- **Preprocessing on the training and test set**, also **L1.2**, **preprocessing leakage**: fitting a transformation on data that includes the held-out rows, in the named forms of imputation before splitting, scaling or normalisation before splitting, oversampling before splitting, and target encoding computed on the full data.
- **Duplicates in datasets**, also **L1.4**, **duplicate records across splits**: identical or near-identical rows on both sides of a split, covering near-duplicate contamination, augmented copies split across train and test, synthetic oversampled duplicates, and overlapping windows in sequential data.
- **Model uses illegitimate features**, also **L2**, **target leakage**, **label leakage**: the second leakage class, where a predictor encodes the outcome, covering the outcome proxy feature, the leaky variable, feature-engineering leakage and reverse causation in feature construction.
- **Test set not drawn from the distribution of scientific interest**, also **L3**: the third leakage class, covering temporal leakage, non-independence between training and test samples, and sampling bias in the test distribution, each leaving the split intact while voiding the claim.
- **Temporal leakage**, also **look-ahead leakage**, **lookahead bias**: use of information unavailable at the moment of prediction, whether a future-dated feature, a random split across a time series, or a recommender scored against interactions that had not yet happened.
- **Group leakage**, also **subject leakage**, **patient-level leakage**: one unit contributing rows to both sides of a split, so the model recognises the unit rather than the pattern, with relatedness leakage, within-subject leakage and repeated-measures leakage as its recurring instances.
- **Spatial autocorrelation induced optimism**, also **spatial leakage**: neighbouring observations sharing information across a random split, with population structure in genomic prediction and chemical-series or scaffold similarity in molecular prediction as the analogous cases in other data types.
- **Tuning on the test set**, also **test-set tuning**, **threshold leakage**: fixing hyperparameters, a decision threshold or a prompt against the data reserved for the final estimate, which converts an estimate into a selection maximum.
- **Test-set peeking**, also **leakage through repeated test-set consultation**, **peeking**: repeated consultation of held-out data across a sequence of decisions, each look leaking a little, with early-stopping leakage and development-set overuse as its everyday forms.
- **Double dipping**, also **circular analysis**: selecting features, subjects, confound adjustments or a threshold on the full sample and then testing on that same sample, so the test inherits the selection it was meant to judge.
- **Batch effect confounding a classifier**, also **batch-effect leakage**, **site effect**, **scanner effect**: a technical grouping that predicts the label, so a classifier separates acquisition batches or centres rather than biology and reports accuracy that no new site reproduces.
- **Model info sheet**, also **model evaluation info sheet**: Kapoor and Narayanan's template recording, for each split, what was fit on which rows and which features existed at prediction time. Costs author effort and catches only leakage the author can already articulate.

### Contamination in pretrained and foundation models

- **Benchmark contamination**, also **evaluation-set contamination**, **data contamination**, **corpus contamination**: a benchmark's items present in a model's pretraining corpus, so a reported score measures recall of seen text rather than the capability the benchmark was built to probe.
- **Input contamination**, also **input-only contamination**: test inputs present in the corpus without their labels, graded against input-and-label or full contamination where the answers appeared too, and against indirect or second-order contamination where the benchmark was seen through derivative text.
- **Memorisation**, also **verbatim memorisation**: reproduction of training text from a prompt, graded by counterfactual memorisation and by k-eidetic memorisation, with canary exposure measuring how far an inserted marker has been absorbed into the model.
- **Canary string**, also **canary**, **BIG-bench canary GUID**: a unique marker placed in a benchmark so its appearance in a corpus or in model output proves ingestion. Costs nothing to insert and fails whenever a redistributor strips it.
- **Contamination detection**: the family of probes for whether a benchmark was seen, the named members being guided prompting, min-k percent probability, the perplexity gap, shuffled-option ordering, membership inference and training-data extraction. Each infers exposure from behaviour, so a negative result clears nothing.
- **Time-split contamination check**, also **cutoff-based contamination test**: comparison of scores on items published before and after a model's training cutoff. Costs a disclosed cutoff, and confounds item difficulty and topic drift with date.
- **Dynamic benchmark**, also **living benchmark**, **rolling benchmark**, **benchmark refresh**, **held-out-by-date benchmark**: an evaluation set replaced or extended on a schedule so items postdate every candidate model. Costs comparability across versions and a standing commitment to write new items.
- **Private test set**, also **hidden test set**, **sequestered test set**, **sequestered evaluation**: labels withheld and scoring performed by the organiser, so participants cannot consult them. Costs external auditability of the grading and blocks error analysis by the people best placed to do it.
- **Decontamination**, also **corpus decontamination**, **n-gram decontamination**: removal of benchmark-matching text from a training corpus, by substring or n-gram overlap filtering, by embedding-similarity semantic deduplication, or by training-data deduplication. Costs corpus volume and leaves paraphrase and translation untouched.
- **Contamination-free evaluation claim**, also **decontamination claim**: an assertion that a benchmark was absent from training, whose warrant is the completeness of a filter applied to a corpus that is usually undisclosed.
- **Task contamination**, also **in-context task leakage**: exposure to a task's format rather than its items, so a zero-shot claim describes a model that has already read the instructions and worked examples somewhere in its corpus.
- **Evaluation-through-the-training-loop**, also **validation-set overuse in pretraining**: use of a benchmark to steer architecture, data mixture or checkpoint selection during pretraining, which makes it part of the training signal while it still reports as held out.
- **Solution leakage from the internet**, also **web-sourced answer leakage**, **prompt leakage of evaluation criteria**, **rubric leakage**: an agent or model reaching the reference answer or the grading criteria at evaluation time, so the score reflects retrieval rather than the capability under test.

### Error, optimism and model assessment

- **Model selection against model assessment**, also **selection versus assessment distinction**, **algorithm selection against model selection**: Hastie's separation of choosing among candidates from estimating the chosen candidate's error, the reason a training, validation and test partition exists. Costs data spent on a split that neither fits nor tunes.
- **Training error**, also **apparent error**, **resubstitution error**, **apparent performance**: the loss measured on the same data the model was fitted to, biased downward by however much the fit followed noise.
- **Test error**, also **generalisation error**, **extra-sample error**: expected loss on data drawn independently of the training set, distinguished from in-sample error, from expected prediction error averaged over training sets, and from the conditional test error at one fixed training set.
- **Optimism of the training error rate**, also **optimism**: the gap between in-sample error and training error, whose expectation is the average optimism and whose magnitude grows with the effective number of parameters a fit consumed.
- **Bias-variance decomposition**: the separation of expected prediction error into squared bias, variance and irreducible error, the arithmetic behind the bias-variance tradeoff or dilemma and behind overfitting and underfitting as its two ends.
- **Effective number of parameters**, also **effective degrees of freedom**, **degrees of freedom of a smoother**: the trace-based count of the freedom a fit actually used, which lets a penalised model, a smoother and an unpenalised model be placed on one scale.
- **Information criterion**, also **Mallows Cp**, **Akaike information criterion**, **AIC**, **AICc**, **corrected Akaike information criterion**, **Bayesian information criterion**, **BIC**, **Schwarz criterion**, **minimum description length**, **MDL**: penalised in-sample estimates of test error that avoid a held-out split. Cost an honest parameter count and an assumed model class, neither of which survives a tuned pipeline.
- **Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension**, also **VC dimension**: the largest sample a hypothesis class can shatter, the capacity term in distribution-free generalisation bounds.
- **Structural risk minimisation**, also **SRM**: selecting a model by minimising empirical risk plus a capacity penalty derived from the Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension. Costs bounds far looser than observed error, so it orders candidates better than it predicts them.
- **Curse of dimensionality**, also **wide-data problem**, **p greater than n regime**: as predictor count grows, sample density collapses and neighbourhoods stop being local, so local methods need sample sizes exponential in dimension.
- **Pessimistic bias**: understatement of achievable performance caused by estimating from a model trained on less data than the deployed one will use, which is the standing cost of a holdout.
- **Optimistic bias**, also **optimistically biased estimate**: overstatement of performance caused by any consultation of the evaluation data during fitting, feature selection, tuning or threshold choice.
- **Double descent**: the non-monotone relation between capacity and test error, which peaks at the interpolation threshold and falls again beyond it, with benign overfitting and grokking as the adjacent findings that zero training error need not mean failure.
- **Learning curve**, also **validation curve**, **hyperparameter response curve**: performance plotted against training-set size or against a hyperparameter, read to judge whether bias or variance dominates. Costs repeated refits, and misleads wherever double descent or a badly chosen metric shapes the curve.
- **Bayes error rate**, also **irreducible error**: the loss no predictor can beat given the available features, the floor against which a benchmark's remaining headroom is measured.

### Resampling protocols

- **Holdout method**, also **holdout validation**, **split-sample validation**, **random split validation**: one random partition into training and test, scored once. Costs a high-variance estimate on small samples, a training set smaller than the deployed model's, and a split ratio with no principled setting.
- **Three-way holdout method**, also **training, validation and test partition**, **three-way split**, **independent test set for the final estimate**: separate partitions for fitting, for selection and for the final estimate, with refitting on the combined data afterwards. Costs more data than any other protocol.
- **Repeated holdout validation**, also **Monte Carlo cross-validation**, **repeated random subsampling**: many independent random splits, averaged. Buys a picture of split-induced variance and costs overlapping test sets, so the average is not an average of independent estimates.
- **K-fold cross-validation**, also **k-fold CV**: each observation serving once as test and k minus one times as training. Costs k refits, a bias that grows as folds shrink the training set, and fold dependence that invalidates ordinary paired tests.
- **Leave-one-out cross-validation**, also **LOOCV**, **LOO**, **leave-p-out cross-validation**, **LPOCV**, **leave-many-out cross-validation**: folds of a single observation, or of p. Nearly unbiased for training-set size and high in variance, at a cost of one refit per observation.
- **Stratified k-fold cross-validation**, also **stratified sampling for splits**, **stratification**: folds built to preserve the outcome distribution. Buys stability under class imbalance and small samples, and costs the pure randomness that some permutation and parametric tests assume.
- **Repeated k-fold cross-validation**, also **repeated CV**: the whole partition redrawn several times and averaged, which separates split variance from fitting variance. Costs a multiple of the refits and leaves the estimates correlated all the same.
- **Nested cross-validation**, also **double cross-validation**, **inner-outer loop protocol**: tuning in an inner loop and estimating in an outer loop, so selection never touches the data behind the estimate. Costs the product of both loops, and its omission is the commonest single-loop selection fault.
- **Pipeline-internal cross-validation**, also **the right way to do cross-validation**, **cross-validating the whole pipeline**: refitting imputation, scaling, encoding and feature selection inside every fold. Costs repeated preprocessing, and Hastie names the alternative of screening on all data first as the wrong way.
- **Bootstrap estimate of prediction error**, also **leave-one-out bootstrap**, **out-of-bag error estimate**, **OOB error**, **point six three two estimator**, **point six three two plus estimator**: error from resamples drawn with replacement, scored on the observations left out. Costs a known upward bias the corrected estimators exist to remove.
- **One-standard-error rule**, also **one-SE rule**: choosing the most parsimonious model within one standard error of the best cross-validated score. Buys stability against fold noise and gives up real predictive performance whenever the extra complexity was genuine.
- **Test-set size and precision of the estimate**, also **evaluation sample size**, **split ratio choice**, **train-test proportion**: the relation between held-out count and the width of the interval around a score. Every point of precision is bought with training data, and no fixed ratio suits every sample size.

### Split design for structured, shifted and deployed data

- **Independent and identically distributed split**, also **iid split**, **random split**: the default partition, which treats rows as exchangeable and is the correct protocol only when no grouping, ordering, spatial structure or duplication links them.
- **Grouped k-fold cross-validation**, also **group k-fold**, **leave-one-group-out cross-validation**, **LOGO**, **leave-one-subject-out cross-validation**, **leave-one-site-out cross-validation**, **leave-one-cluster-out cross-validation**: splits keeping every record of a unit, subject, site or cluster on one side. Costs effective sample size, and cannot repair a grouping nobody recorded.
- **Blocked cross-validation**, also **block CV**, **h-block cross-validation**, **hv-block cross-validation**, **spatial cross-validation**, **environmental block cross-validation**, **buffered leave-one-out cross-validation**: folds separated by a gap in space or time so autocorrelated neighbours cannot straddle a boundary. Costs the data inside the buffer and a block size that must be argued for.
- **Time-series cross-validation**, also **rolling-origin evaluation**, **rolling-origin recalibration evaluation**, **fixed-origin evaluation**, **expanding-window validation**, **sliding-window validation**, **walk-forward validation**: repeated fits at advancing origins, always predicting forward. Costs many refits, and the earliest origins are fitted on very little history.
- **Chronological split**, also **temporal split**, **forward-chaining split**, **global timeline split**: a single cut in time with everything before it for training. Costs one arbitrary boundary and a test period whose regime may have moved, which is the honesty a random split lacks.
- **Purged k-fold cross-validation**, also **purging**, **embargo period in cross-validation**, **embargoing**, **combinatorial purged cross-validation**, **CPCV**: removal of training observations whose label windows overlap the test period, plus a waiting gap after it. Costs training data and requires every label's formation window to be known.
- **Backtesting**: evaluation of a trading or forecasting rule on recorded history, distinct from software regression testing. Exposed to backtest overfitting when many rules were tried, which the deflated Sharpe ratio corrects by discounting the best of a known number of trials.
- **Prequential evaluation**, also **test-then-train evaluation**: scoring each arriving example before learning from it, which needs no split and suits streams. Costs comparability with batch protocols and weights early examples heavily in the running score.
- **Scaffold split**, also **structure-based split**, **time-split validation in drug discovery**: partitioning molecules by chemical scaffold or by assay date rather than at random, so nearly identical analogues cannot span the boundary. Costs a harder and lower benchmark score that is nonetheless the honest one.
- **External validation**, also **independent validation**, **temporal external validation**, **geographic validation**: assessment on data untouched by development and separated in time, place or source, as against internal validation, which resamples the development data. Costs a second dataset, and its absence is the commonest gap in prediction-model evidence.
- **Internal-external cross-validation**, also **IECV**, **leave-one-study-out validation**: rotating whole studies or centres out of a pooled dataset so every round is an external validation and no data is wasted. Costs enough clusters to rotate, and reports heterogeneity a single validation would hide.
- **Out-of-distribution evaluation**, also **OOD evaluation**, **domain generalisation evaluation**, **cross-domain split**, **adversarial split**, **compositional generalisation split**, **template split**, **cross-lingual transfer evaluation**: splits built to break an assumption rather than to sample from it. Each encodes a designer's guess about which shift will matter.
- **Prospective validation**, also **silent-mode evaluation**, **silent trial**, **shadow evaluation**, **shadow deployment**: running a model on live inputs while withholding its outputs from any decision. Buys evidence under real data flow and costs calendar time and instrumentation before any benefit accrues.
- **Off-policy evaluation**, also **counterfactual policy evaluation**, **inverse propensity scoring estimator for off-policy evaluation**, **IPS estimator**, **self-normalised inverse propensity scoring**, **SNIPS**, **clipped inverse propensity scoring**, **direct method for off-policy evaluation**, **doubly robust off-policy estimator**, **fitted Q evaluation**, **FQE**, **high-confidence off-policy evaluation**, **effective sample size of importance weights**: estimating a new policy's value from logs another policy produced. Costs recorded propensities, and importance weights collapse the effective sample size.

### Comparing learners statistically

- **Statistical comparison of classifiers over multiple data sets**, also **multi-dataset comparison**: Demsar's protocol, ranking each method within each dataset and testing the ranks. Costs the intuition of an average accuracy, which he rejects because scores on unlike datasets are not commensurable.
- **Friedman test for classifier comparison**, also **Iman-Davenport correction**, **average rank of a classifier**, **mean rank**, **Friedman aligned ranks test**, **Quade test**: the omnibus rank tests over many datasets. Cost sensitivity to which datasets were chosen, and conclude only that some method differs from some other.
- **Nemenyi post-hoc test**, also **critical difference**, **CD**, **critical difference diagram**, **CD plot**, **Bonferroni-Dunn test**: all-pairs comparison of mean ranks against one threshold, drawn as connected bars. All-pairs costs power, which comparison against a single control classifier recovers.
- **Holm step-down procedure for classifier comparison**, also **Hochberg procedure for classifier comparison**, **Finner procedure**, **Li procedure**, **Hommel procedure**, **Shaffer static procedure**, **Bergmann-Hommel procedure**: the sequentially rejective corrections for many method comparisons, reported as adjusted p values. Buy power over a single-step threshold at the cost of assumptions about hypothesis structure.
- **Wilcoxon signed-ranks test for classifier comparison**, also **sign test over data sets**, **win-loss-tie tally**, **win-tie-loss record**: paired nonparametric comparison across datasets. Costs power against a parametric test and buys freedom from the commensurability the paired t-test over data sets assumes.
- **McNemar's test for classifier comparison**: Dietterich's recommended test on the discordant predictions of two fitted classifiers over one test set. Costs any account of training-set variability, so it compares two models and not two learning algorithms.
- **Five-by-two cross-validated paired t test**, also **5x2cv paired t test**, **combined five-by-two cross-validated F test**, **5x2cv F test**: Dietterich's tests over five repetitions of a twofold split. Buy approximately correct type one error where the resampled paired t test is badly anti-conservative, at ten training runs per method.
- **Corrected resampled t test**, also **Nadeau-Bengio corrected t test**: a paired t statistic whose variance term is inflated to account for overlap between training sets. Costs an assumed correction factor and stays an approximation rather than an exact test.
- **Overlapping training sets violate independence**, also **dependent-fold problem**, **fold dependence**: resampling protocols reuse data across folds, so per-fold scores are correlated and any procedure treating them as independent, including a binomial test on cross-validated accuracy, runs an inflated type one error.
- **Question of comparing algorithms against comparing classifiers**, also **algorithm-level versus model-level comparison**: Dietterich's distinction between a claim about a learning procedure and a claim about one fitted model, which decides whether training-set and seed variance belong inside the test.
- **Permutation test for classifier significance**, also **label-permutation significance test**, **Y-randomisation**, **Y-scrambling**, **response permutation control**, **permutation of features within class test**: refitting on shuffled labels to build a null distribution for the observed score. Costs many refits and answers only whether any signal is present.
- **Almost-stochastic-dominance comparison**, also **ASO test**, **stochastic order comparison of score distributions**: comparison of whole score distributions rather than their means. Buys a claim that survives skew and multimodality, and costs sample size and a readily interpretable effect measure.
- **Region of practical equivalence**, also **ROPE**, **Bayesian correlated t-test for classifier comparison**, **Bayesian signed-rank test for classifier comparison**, **Bayesian hierarchical model for multi-dataset comparison**: the Bayesian apparatus reporting how probably one method is better, worse or practically equivalent. Costs a stated equivalence margin and a prior.
- **Paired bootstrap resampling test**, also **bootstrap significance test for system comparison**, **approximate randomisation test for system comparison**, **permutation test for system scores**: resampling or permuting paired per-item scores of two systems. Costs item-level outputs, and neither procedure speaks to training-set or seed variability.
- **Standard error of an eval score**, also **clustered standard error for eval questions**, **paired-and-clustered standard error**: Miller's recipe for uncertainty on a language-model evaluation, clustering questions that share a passage or template and pairing question-level differences between models. Costs per-question scores and a declared cluster structure.
- **Power analysis for an evaluation**, also **eval question-count planning**: sizing a benchmark so that a difference worth acting on would be detected. Costs items and pilot data, and answer resampling or next-token-probability scoring can buy the same precision more cheaply.

### Variance, seeds and honest reporting of a comparison

- **Sources of variance in a benchmark**, also **variance budget**: Bouthillier's enumeration of what moves a benchmark score, being data sampling, data splits, weight initialisation, data ordering, dropout and stochastic regularisation, data augmentation, hyperparameter optimisation, label noise and library nondeterminism.
- **Seed hacking**, also **seed lottery**, **cherry-picked seed**, **best-run reporting**, **max-over-seeds reporting**: reporting the best result across random seeds, with seed fixing, the reporting of one seed as if representative, as its quieter twin.
- **Randomising multiple sources of variation**, also **multi-source randomisation**, **multiple-run reporting**: varying seeds, splits and initialisations together and reporting mean and spread. Buys an estimate of expected performance, and costs compute that the deliberately biased cheaper estimator exists to save.
- **Paired comparison across shared seeds**, also **seed-paired comparison**, **probability of improvement**: comparing methods under matched randomness and reporting how often one wins. Buys power from the pairing and costs the ability to speak about conditions outside the shared set.
- **Compute budget as a comparison variable**, also **budget-matched comparison**, **cost-adjusted comparison**, **compute-matched comparison**, **parameter-matched comparison**, **data-matched comparison**, **hyperparameter-tuning fairness**: equalising trials, FLOPs, parameters, tokens or tuning effort across compared methods. Costs the headline number and exposes tuning-budget asymmetry as the source of many reported gains.
- **Interquartile mean of normalised scores**, also **IQM**, **performance profile**, **run-score profile**, **optimality gap**, **stratified bootstrap confidence interval for aggregate scores**: the aggregate reporting apparatus for few-run reinforcement-learning results. Buys robustness to a single lucky run at the cost of a familiar arithmetic mean.
- **Statistical precipice**, also **edge of the statistical precipice**: the condition of a field ranking methods from three to five runs each, where point-estimate-only reporting cannot separate a method's effect from environment and seed variance.
- **Number of runs justification**, also **run-count power analysis**: stating in advance how many runs the intended comparison requires. Costs planning and compute, and is what turns a reported spread into evidence rather than decoration.
- **Model selection multiplicity**, also **selection-induced optimism**, **winner's curse in model selection**, **empirical winner's curse**: inflation of the best observed score when many candidates were scored on one validation set, so the winner carries the maximum of the noise along with the signal.
- **Reproducibility of training under nondeterminism**, also **nondeterministic training**, **hardware and library nondeterminism**, **bitwise reproducibility of a training run**, **deterministic training mode**: a run that cannot be repeated exactly because of reduction order, library version and unseeded operations. Deterministic mode buys repeatability and costs throughput.
- **Show your work reporting**, also **reporting of search budget and score distribution**, **expected validation performance curve**, **number-of-trials disclosure**: publishing how many hyperparameter trials were run and how validation scores were distributed, so a result can be read against its budget. Costs the appearance of a clean single number.
- **Reporting of compute**, also **compute accounting**, **inference-cost reporting**, **latency and throughput reporting**, **carbon and energy reporting for an experiment**, **experiment-impact statement**, **green artificial-intelligence reporting**: disclosure of what an experiment and a served model consume. Costs instrumentation, and the efficiency misnomer warns that one cost indicator misstates the total.

### Holdout reuse, leaderboards and adaptivity

- **Adaptive data analysis**, also **adaptive analysis**, **adaptive analyst model**: analysis whose later questions depend on earlier answers from the same data, so classical guarantees lapse because no hypothesis was fixed in advance. Freedman's paradox is its classical instance.
- **Holdout reuse**, also **test-set reuse**: repeated querying of one held-out set across a chain of adaptive decisions, where the damage grows with the number of queries rather than with the quality of any one of them.
- **Reusable holdout**, also **Thresholdout**, **SparseValidate**: Dwork's mechanisms answering holdout queries with added noise under a budget, so a bounded number of adaptive questions retains a guarantee. Cost accuracy in every answer and a budget that must be enforced rather than promised.
- **Ladder mechanism for leaderboards**, also **the Ladder**: a leaderboard algorithm that reveals a score only when it improves on the best by more than a threshold. Buys a bound on leaderboard overfitting and costs resolution, since small genuine gains go unreported.
- **Leaderboard overfitting**, also **leaderboard climbing**, **adaptive overfitting**, **community-level overfitting to a benchmark**, **standard-split exhaustion**: the accumulated fit of many teams' many submissions to one evaluation set, for which no single team's protocol is at fault.
- **Differential privacy as a generalisation guarantee**, also **privacy-implies-generalisation**, **max-information**, **description-length bound on adaptivity**: results bounding how much a released answer can encode about the sample it came from. Buy guarantees holding against any analyst, and cost noise or a compression limit on what may be released.
- **Holdout budget**, also **query budget on the test set**, **submission-limit policy**, **rate-limited leaderboard**: an explicit cap on consultations of the evaluation data. Costs iteration speed, and is what makes an adaptivity bound enforceable rather than aspirational.
- **Public and private leaderboard split**, also **public-private split**, **leaderboard shakeup**: scoring on a visible subset while ranking on a hidden one, the reordering at reveal being the shakeup. Costs evaluation data divided in two, and rewards teams that resist tuning to the visible half.
- **Competition-based evaluation**, also **shared task**, **challenge evaluation**: a common dataset, metric and deadline with scores computed centrally. Buys comparability that no self-reported table achieves, and costs a metric fixed before anyone knows what it will reward.
- **Benchmark replication study**, also **new-test-set replication**, **new test set construction by pipeline replication**, **dataset reconstruction**: rebuilding an evaluation set by rerunning the original collection pipeline and rescoring existing models. Costs a faithfully documented pipeline and, in Recht's case, a large fresh annotation effort.
- **Adaptivity gap**, also **distribution gap**: the decomposition of an accuracy drop on a fresh test set into overuse of the old one, a shift between the two sets and ordinary statistical error, with rank preservation across test sets as the observed pattern.
- **Standard split**, also **canonical split**, **fixed benchmark split**: one fixed partition shared across a community so numbers are comparable. Costs slow collective overfitting, and Gorman and Bedrick showed system rankings reverse under repeated random splits.
- **Recommendation to report multiple random splits**, also **multi-split reporting**, **random-split evaluation**, **repeated-split significance testing**: rerunning a comparison across many partitions and testing across them. Costs comparability with published standard-split numbers and several times the compute.
- **Leaderboard illusion**: the distortion of arena rankings by undisclosed pre-release testing of private variants, selective disclosure of the best variant's score, unequal sampling rates between providers, and silent removal of listed models.

### Baselines, ablation and empirical rigor

- **Ablation study**, also **ablation**, **component ablation**, **feature ablation**, **layer ablation**, **data ablation**, **loss-term ablation**, **lesion study**, **knockout experiment on a model**, **additive study**, **reverse ablation**: removal or addition of one part at a time to attribute a gain. Costs a run per variant, and the one-factor-at-a-time critique warns that interacting parts are misread this way.
- **Strong-baseline requirement**, also **baseline adequacy**, **baseline parity**, **matched-effort baseline**, **apples-to-apples comparison**, **controlled comparison**: tuning the comparator with the effort spent on the proposal. Costs the margin an insufficiently tuned baseline manufactures, which is the margin many published gains consist of.
- **Trivial baseline**, also **naive baseline**, **majority-class baseline**, **random baseline**, **chance baseline**, **nearest-neighbour baseline**, **linear-model baseline**, **bag-of-words baseline**, **persistence baseline**, **naive forecast**, **seasonal naive baseline**, **random-search baseline for hyperparameter methods**: the cheapest comparators a result must beat. Cost almost nothing and settle more claims than elaborate comparators do.
- **Hypothesis-only baseline**, also **partial-input baseline**, **shuffled-input control**, **untrained-model baseline**, **random-feature baseline**, **random-encoder control**, **feature-noise sensitivity check**: comparators that withhold part of the input or all of the training. Buy a direct measure of how far a benchmark yields without the reasoning it claims to require.
- **Oracle upper bound**, also **oracle performance**, **skyline**, **human baseline**, **human performance reference**, **human ceiling on a benchmark**: the best achievable or best observed reference at the top of a scale. Costs a measurement whose own protocol is reported far less carefully than the model's.
- **Benchmark saturation**, also **saturated benchmark**, **ceiling effect on a benchmark**, **floor effect on a benchmark**, **headroom on a benchmark**, **benchmark shelf life**, **benchmark obsolescence**: the state of an evaluation set whose remaining margin has fallen below its own label noise, so further gains carry no information.
- **Reproducibility gap between reported and reproduced results**, also **reported-versus-reproduced gap**, **reimplementation gap**, **reproduction gap**: the difference between a published number and an independent rerun's, produced by undisclosed settings, unequal tuning effort and environment as often as by error.
- **Reproduction as a contribution**, also **replication paper**, **reporting negative results**, **null-result reporting in machine learning**: publication of work that confirms, fails to confirm, or finds nothing. Costs novelty credit, which the standing reviewer incentive against negative results keeps expensive.
- **Failure to identify the sources of empirical gains**, also **unattributed empirical gain**, **empirical claim without an ablation**, **explanatory experiment against confirmatory experiment**: Lipton and Steinhardt's charge that an improvement is reported without establishing which change produced it, with retrospective rationalisation of the architecture as the usual substitute.
- **Mathiness**: mathematics deployed to impress rather than to clarify, where the notation neither constrains the claim being made nor connects to the experiments reported beneath it.
- **Suggestive definition**, also **suggestive naming**, **overloaded terminology**, **term overloading**, **suitcase word**, **anthropomorphic language about models**, **misuse of language in machine learning writing**: naming practices that let a narrow technical result be read as a broad capability, so the language carries argument the evidence does not.
- **Failure to distinguish explanation from speculation**, also **speculation presented as fact**, **unmarked speculation**, **intuition section that hardens into claim**: conjecture presented in the register of finding, with no marker separating what was shown from what is supposed.
- **State-of-the-art chasing**, also **SOTA chasing**, **leaderboard chasing**, **pace-over-rigor tradeoff**, **Red artificial intelligence**, **Red AI**: a publication culture rewarding a new best number over an explained one, sustained by the incentive to publish a win and by undisclosed hyperparameter sensitivity.
- **Error analysis**, also **qualitative error inspection**, **instance-level analysis of results**, **per-item error analysis**, **sanity check**, **robustness check on an empirical claim**: inspection of individual failures instead of an aggregate. Costs analyst time and is the cheapest route to a benchmark's artefacts.
- **Source works of the machine-learning evaluation critique**, also **Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship**, **Winner's Curse? On Pace, Progress, and Empirical Rigor**, **We Need to Talk about Standard Splits**, **Machine Learning that Matters**, **Are We Really Making Much Progress?**, **Deep Reinforcement Learning that Matters**, **A Metric Learning Reality Check**, **Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in Machine-Learning-Based Science**, **The Elements of Statistical Learning**, **ESL**: the papers and text that named these faults and supplied the resampling apparatus, listed so a reader meeting a title reaches the concept.

### Benchmark validity and metric validity

- **Benchmark as a measurement instrument**, also **evaluation-as-measurement framing**, **measurement modelling of an unobservable construct**, **downstream-task correlation of a benchmark**: treating an evaluation set as an instrument for a construct rather than as a task list, so its validity can be examined and its correlation with deployed performance measured. Costs a stated construct before any item is written.
- **Construct validity of a benchmark**, also **construct validity of a metric**, **operationalisation gap**, **construct-to-task gap**, **target construct definition for a benchmark**, **content validity of an evaluation set**, **criterion validity of a benchmark**, **convergent validity of a metric**, **discriminant validity of a metric**, **consequential validity of an evaluation**, **face validity of a measurement model**, **hypothesis validity**, **ecological validity of an evaluation**, **internal validity of a benchmark**, **external validity of a benchmark**: whether an evaluation measures the capability it is named for, in the psychometric senses Jacobs and Wallach import.
- **Reliability of a benchmark**, also **evaluation reliability**, **test-retest reliability of an evaluation**, **rerun stability**: whether readministering the same evaluation to the same system returns the same score, which decoding randomness, prompt formatting and judge variation each disturb.
- **General-purpose benchmark**, also **everything in the whole wide world benchmark**, **generality claim from a limited benchmark**, **limited task validity**: Raji and Liao's name for an evaluation presented as measuring general capability, whose narrow task coverage cannot support the claim drawn from it.
- **Coverage of the task distribution**, also **task-space coverage**, **representativeness of the evaluation set**, **sampling bias in benchmark construction**, **non-representative evaluation set**, **difficulty distribution of a benchmark**, **task selection bias in a benchmark suite**: how far the items span what the claim covers. Costs a stated task distribution, without which coverage cannot be judged at all.
- **Annotation artefact**, also **dataset artefact**, **annotation bias**, **spurious cue in a benchmark**, **dataset bias**, **solvable-by-shortcut item**: a regularity in how items were written that lets a system score well without the competence the items were meant to require.
- **Label noise in a benchmark's test set**, also **test-set label error**, **test-set label error audit**, **label-quality audit**: wrong reference labels in evaluation data, which cap achievable accuracy and can reverse a ranking once the contested margin falls below the error rate.
- **Benchmark documentation requirement**, also **benchmark card**, **benchmark scope statement**, **intended-use statement for a benchmark**, **benchmark deprecation policy**, **benchmark data collection protocol**, **item-writing protocol**: a record of what an evaluation measures, how its items were made and when it should be retired. Costs maintainer effort long after publication.
- **Adversarial data collection**, also **human-and-model-in-the-loop collection**, **dynamic adversarial data collection**: item writing in which authors see model predictions and are rewarded for defeating them. Buys items current models fail, and costs a benchmark whose difficulty is defined by the model used to build it.
- **Metric-task mismatch**, also **metric mismatch**, **task-specific metric validity**, **fitness-for-purpose of a metric**, **metric choice justification**, **metric selection rationale**, **metric justification**: the requirement that the chosen measure match what the decision needs. Costs an argument that convention usually supplies instead.
- **Goodhart's law**, also **proxy-metric drift**, **surrogate objective mismatch**: a measure ceases to measure once it becomes a target, in the named mechanisms of regressional, extremal, causal and adversarial Goodhart.
- **Metric gaming**, also **benchmark gaming**, **specification gaming**, **reward hacking**, **reward gaming**, **reward misspecification**, **reward tampering**, **metric overfitting**: optimisation that satisfies the stated measure while defeating the purpose the measure stood for.
- **Benchmark lottery**, also **single-number summary of a benchmark suite**, **composite benchmark score**, **score normalisation across tasks**, **human-normalised score**, **rank aggregation across benchmarks**, **choice of aggregation statistic**: the sensitivity of a ranking to which tasks, normalisation and averaging statistic a suite happens to use.
- **Item response theory analysis of a benchmark**, also **IRT-based benchmark analysis**, **item difficulty of a benchmark item**, **item discrimination of a benchmark item**, **ability estimate for a model**, **test information function for a benchmark**, **computerised adaptive testing of models**, **benchmark item pruning**, **tiny-benchmark selection**: psychometric modelling of items and systems together. Buys a shorter evaluation of known precision at the cost of a fitted model between answers and score.
- **Elo rating for model comparison**, also **Bradley-Terry model for pairwise preference**, **pairwise win rate**, **head-to-head win rate**, **arena-style evaluation**, **crowdsourced pairwise arena**: ranking derived from pairwise outcomes. Buys a scale needing no absolute reference and costs sensitivity to who voted, on which prompts, and in what order models were listed.

### Discrimination, thresholds and classification metrics

- **Confusion matrix**, also **contingency table of predictions**: the table of counts by predicted and true class, from which every threshold-dependent metric is derived. A metric reported without it, the opaque single-number report, cannot be re-thresholded or recomputed by a reader.
- **Receiver operating characteristic curve**, also **ROC curve**, **ROC analysis**, **empirical ROC curve**, **nonparametric ROC**, **binormal ROC model**, **ROC convex hull**, **ROCCH**: sensitivity plotted against one minus specificity across all thresholds. Buys a threshold-free view of ranking and says nothing about calibration or about the threshold actually used.
- **Area under the ROC curve**, also **AUC**, **AUROC**, **c-statistic**, **concordance statistic**, **partial area under the curve**, **pAUC**, **standardised partial AUC**, **McClish transformation**, **two-alternative forced-choice interpretation of AUC**, **threshold-free metric**, **ranking metric**: the probability that a random positive outranks a random negative. Costs an implicit weighting of misclassification costs across thresholds.
- **The AUC critique**, also **incoherence of the AUC**, **implicit cost distribution of a metric**, **cost-weighting assumption**, **class-imbalance insensitivity of the ROC curve**: Hand's argument that the area applies a different implied cost distribution to each classifier compared, so the ordering it yields carries no consistent decision meaning.
- **H measure**, also **Hand's H measure**, **cost curve**, **Drummond and Holte cost curve**, **skew-sensitive evaluation**, **isometric plot of a metric**, **cost matrix**, **cost-sensitive evaluation**, **expected cost of a classifier**: the apparatus that fixes a cost or skew distribution before scoring. Costs an explicit statement of relative harms that most applications will not commit to.
- **Sensitivity**, also **true positive rate**, **recall**, **specificity**, **true negative rate**, **false positive rate**, **one minus specificity**, **fall-out**, **false negative rate**, **miss rate**: the rates conditioned on true class, which is why they do not move with prevalence.
- **Positive predictive value**, also **PPV**, **precision**, **negative predictive value**, **NPV**, **prevalence dependence of predictive values**, **base-rate dependence**: the rates conditioned on the prediction, which therefore change with prevalence even when the classifier does not.
- **Positive likelihood ratio**, also **LR positive**, **negative likelihood ratio**, **LR negative**, **diagnostic odds ratio**, **DOR**: prevalence-free summaries of evidential weight, which convert pre-test odds into post-test odds by multiplication.
- **Optimal cut-point selection**, also **threshold selection**, **cut-off optimisation**, **Youden's index**, **Youden's J statistic**, **closest-to-the-top-left-corner criterion**, **Euclidean-distance cutpoint rule**, **concordance probability method for cutpoints**: rules turning a score into a decision. Cost data-driven cut-point optimism whenever the same sample chooses and then evaluates the threshold.
- **Precision-recall curve**, also **PR curve**, **area under the precision-recall curve**, **AUPRC**, **average precision**, **precision-recall-gain curve**, **Saito-Rehmsmeier argument**: the tradeoff curve conditioned on predicted positives, preferred under heavy imbalance. Moves with prevalence, so unlike the ROC it is not comparable across populations.
- **Classification accuracy**, also **accuracy**, **correct classification rate**, **error rate**, **misclassification rate**, **accuracy paradox**, **balanced accuracy**, **balanced error rate**, **BER**: the proportion correct, with balanced variants averaging per-class rates. Costs nothing and reports nothing under imbalance, where scoring on rebalanced data compounds the problem.
- **F-measure**, also **F1 score**, **F-score**, **F-beta measure**, **weighted F measure**, **precision-recall tradeoff**, **critique of the F-measure**: the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Buys one number and costs an unstated verdict on how the two error types compare, which is the substance of the standing critique.
- **Matthews correlation coefficient**, also **MCC**, **phi coefficient**, **Cohen's kappa as a classifier metric**, **bookmaker informedness**, **informedness**, **markedness**, **geometric mean of sensitivity and specificity**, **G-mean**, **Jaccard index as an evaluation metric**, **intersection over union**, **IoU**: chance-corrected and skew-aware single-number summaries. Buy robustness to imbalance and cost meaning at any particular operating point.
- **Macro-averaged metric**, also **macro average**, **micro-averaged metric**, **micro average**, **weighted-average metric**, **support-weighted average**, **per-class metric reporting**, **class-wise breakdown**, **top-k accuracy**, **exact-match accuracy**, **multi-label evaluation metric**, **prevalence-adjusted metric**: the choices in collapsing per-class scores into one, which decide whether rare classes count. Costs a decision that a single headline number conceals.
- **Discrimination against calibration**, also **separation-versus-accuracy-of-risk distinction**: the distinction between ranking cases correctly and getting absolute risks right, since a model may rank perfectly while every probability it reports is wrong.
- **Harrell's concordance index**, also **c-index**, **Uno's concordance statistic**, **time-dependent ROC curve**, **cumulative-dynamic ROC**, **Royston-Sauerbrei D statistic**, **net reclassification improvement**, **NRI**, **integrated discrimination improvement**, **IDI**: discrimination and added-value measures for censored outcomes. Cost censoring assumptions, and the NRI is criticised for moving under a useless marker.
- **Multi-reader multi-case analysis**, also **MRMC**, **Dorfman-Berbaum-Metz method**, **DBM method**, **Obuchowski-Rockette method**, **free-response ROC**, **FROC**, **alternative free-response ROC**, **AFROC**, **JAFROC**, **localisation ROC**, **LROC**, **DeLong test for correlated AUCs**, **bootstrap comparison of areas under the curve**: reader-study designs and paired tests for curves measured on the same cases. Cost many readers and a fitted variance model.

### Metrics for generation, ranking, regression and clustering

- **Reference-overlap metric for generated text**, also **BLEU**, **bilingual evaluation understudy**, **ROUGE**, **recall-oriented understudy for gisting evaluation**, **ROUGE-L**, **METEOR**, **chrF**, **character n-gram F-score**, **CIDEr**, **SPICE**: the family scoring output against human references, BLEU by n-gram precision with a brevity penalty, ROUGE by recall and longest common subsequence, METEOR by alignment, chrF by character n-grams, CIDEr by rarity-weighted consensus, SPICE by scene-graph propositions.
- **Edit-distance metric for generated text**, also **translation edit rate**, **TER**, **translation error rate**, **human-targeted translation edit rate**, **HTER**, **word error rate**, **WER**, **character error rate**, **CER**: the family counting insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to reach a reference, normalised by its length, the human-targeted variant counting edits a real post-editor made.
- **Learned metric for generated text**, also **BERTScore**, **BLEURT**, **COMET**, **crosslingual optimised metric for evaluation of translation**, **MoverScore**, **YiSi**, **MAUVE**, **reference-free metric**, **quality estimation as a metric**: metrics scoring similarity with a trained model, by embedding alignment, by regression on human ratings, or by comparing whole text distributions. Cost a scorer whose own validity must be established.
- **Perplexity**, also **bits per byte**, **bits per character**, **Self-BLEU**, **Distinct-n**: the intrinsic measures of a language model and of its output variety, perplexity being exponentiated average negative log likelihood and comparable only across models sharing a tokenisation.
- **Multidimensional Quality Metrics**, also **MQM**, **scalar quality metric**, **SQM**, **adequacy and fluency rating**, **relative ranking judgement**, **post-editing effort**: human error-annotation and rating schemes for translation quality. Buy an error typology with severity weights and cost trained annotators working at professional rates.
- **Meta-evaluation of an automatic metric**, also **metric validation study**, **correlation with human judgement**, **metric-human correlation**, **segment-level against system-level metric correlation**, **pairwise ranking accuracy of a metric**, **metric sensitivity to small quality differences**, **automatic metric validity**, **Kendall tau correlation of system rankings**: validation of a metric against human judgement. Costs a human evaluation, and system-level correlation flatters metrics that fail segment by segment.
- **Discounted cumulative gain**, also **DCG**, **normalised discounted cumulative gain**, **alpha-nDCG**, **expected reciprocal rank**, **ERR**, **rank-biased precision**, **RBP**, **mean reciprocal rank**, **precision at k**, **recall at k**, **R-precision**, **hit rate at k**, **success at k**, **rank-biased overlap**, **RBO**, **catalogue coverage**: graded and cut-off ranking measures, each carrying its own assumption about how far a user reads down a list.
- **Cranfield paradigm**, also **test-collection evaluation**, **pooling of retrieval results**, **depth-k pooling**, **relevance judgement**, **qrel**, **graded relevance assessment**, **topic set size design**, **inferred average precision**, **infAP**, **statistical average precision**, **statAP**, **geometric mean average precision**, **GMAP**, **bpref measure**, **condensed-list evaluation**: the reusable collection of documents, topics and judgements, with estimators built for shallow pools. Costs assessor effort and carries pool bias against runs that retrieved unjudged documents.
- **Offline evaluation**, also **retrospective log-based evaluation**, **online-offline gap**, **sampled-metric evaluation**, **critique of sampled metrics**, **popularity bias in offline evaluation**, **missing-not-at-random feedback**, **position bias in click data**, **inverse propensity weighted offline evaluation**, **leave-one-out evaluation in recommendation**, **per-user split**, **cold-start evaluation protocol**, **weak against strong generalisation in recommendation**: scoring a ranker on logged interactions. ### Verification and validation, the terms of the argument

- **Verification**, also **verification of codes**, **verification of calculations**, **code verification**, **solution verification**, **calculation verification**, **Completed verification**: the determination that a computation solves its equations correctly, split by Roache into codes and calculations. Not the held-out-data sense of evaluation, and silent about whether the equations describe the world. Costs a test suite with known answers.
- **Validation**: the determination that a model represents the reality of interest closely enough for its intended use, judged against measurement. Not the machine-learning validation set, whose counterpart here is calibration data. Costs an experiment designed for comparison rather than for discovery.
- **Model qualification**, also **qualification**, **SCS terminology for model credibility**, **Schlesinger report**: the third term of the original triad, the determination that a conceptual model adequately represents the reality of interest before any code exists. Buys an accountable decision and costs an approval process longer than the modelling.
- **Reality of interest**, also **Referent**, **Comparator**, **System response quantity**, **SRQ**, **Quantity of interest**, **QoI**, **Conceptual model**, **Mathematical model**, **Computational model**, **discrete model**, **Simulation**, **computational simulation**, **Problem entity**, **Communicative model**, **Programmed model**, **Experimental model**: the chain of objects a validation argument runs over, from the thing modelled through the conceptual and mathematical statements to executed code and the quantities actually compared.

Extrapolation beyond it is the usual case and the unearned one, answering to out-of-distribution evaluation in learned models.
- **Model credibility**, also **credibility**, **Fidelity**, **model fidelity**, **Predictive capability**, **Sufficiency of validation evidence**, **Usefulness criterion for a model**, **fitness for purpose of a model**, **All models are wrong**, **Box's aphorism**, **Complexity-realism tradeoff**, **Medawar zone of model complexity**, **Model parsimony against realism**: the judgement that a model may be relied on for a decision, established by no single test and treated throughout the tradition as a degree rather than a verdict.
- **Tuning**, also **fudging**, **parameter tweaking**, **Calibration mistaken for validation**, **Tuning against calibration distinction**, **Overfitting a simulation to observations**, **overcalibration**, **Right answer for the wrong reason**, **compensating errors**, **error compensation**, **Excessive detail**, **over-elaboration of a model**: adjustment of parameters until agreement improves, and the fault of presenting that agreement as validation. - **Probability box**, also **p-box**, **Interval analysis**, **interval arithmetic**, **Probability bounds analysis**, **PBA**, **Dempster-Shafer theory**, **evidence theory**, **theory of belief functions**, **Belief function**, **Plausibility function**, **Basic probability assignment**, **mass function**, **Possibility theory**, **Fuzzy representation of uncertainty**, **Imprecise probability**, **Credal set**, **Robust Bayesian analysis**, **Info-gap decision theory**: representations that refuse to name a single distribution. - **Deep uncertainty**, also **Knightian uncertainty**, **true uncertainty**, **Robust decision making**, **RDM**, **Many-objective robust decision making**, **MORDM**, **Exploratory modelling and analysis**, **EMA**, **Scenario discovery**, **Patient rule induction method**, **PRIM**, **Dynamic adaptive policy pathways**, **DAPP**, **Minimax regret criterion**, **regret analysis**, **Worst-case analysis**, **bounding analysis**, **envelope analysis**: decision methods for conditions where no probability can be agreed. - **Quantification of margins and uncertainties**, also **QMU**, **Design margin**, **margin-to-uncertainty ratio**, **Best estimate plus uncertainty**, **BEPU**, **Code scaling, applicability and uncertainty**, **CSAU**, **Wilks formula**, **95/95 criterion**, **SAPIUM**, **PREMIUM benchmark**, **BEMUSE**, **Uncertainty Methodology Study**, **UMAE**, **Accuracy extrapolation**, **CIAU**, **Internal assessment of uncertainty**, **GRS method**, **CIRCE method**, **Probabilistic risk assessment**, **PRA**, **Deterministic safety analysis**, **Conservatism in a bounding calculation**, **Uncertainty importance analysis**, **Scaling state-of-the-art report**: the safety-analysis apparatus that replaces conservative bounding with a best estimate plus a quantified band. - **Sobol indices**, also **Sobol' sensitivity indices**, **variance-based indices**, **Variance-based sensitivity analysis**, **ANOVA decomposition of variance**, **First-order sensitivity index**, **main effect index**, **Total-effect index**, **total-order index**, **Second-order interaction index**, **Closed sensitivity index**, **Interaction effect**, **non-additivity**, **Additive model**, **Saltelli estimator**, **Jansen estimator**, **Pick-freeze estimator**, **Fourier amplitude sensitivity test**, **FAST**, **Extended FAST**, **EFAST**, **Random balance design**, **RBD-FAST**, **High-dimensional model representation**, **HDMR**, **Shapley effects**, **Group sensitivity index**, **Given-data estimation of sensitivity indices**, **Effective dimension of a model**: the variance decomposition and its estimators. - **Moment-independent sensitivity measure**, also **density-based sensitivity measure**, **Delta moment-independent measure**, **Borgonovo delta index**, **PAWN index**, **Variogram analysis of response surfaces**, **VARS**, **Integrated variogram across a range of scales**, **IVARS**, **Distributed evaluation of local sensitivity analysis**, **DELSA**, **Standardised regression coefficient**, **SRC**, **Standardised rank regression coefficient**, **SRRC**, **Partial correlation coefficient**, **PCC**, **Partial rank correlation coefficient**, **PRCC**, **Correlation ratio**, **Coefficient of model determination as a sensitivity check**, **Scatterplot-based sensitivity analysis**, **Cobweb plot**, **Emulator-based sensitivity analysis**, **Correlated input sensitivity analysis**, **Time-varying sensitivity analysis**, **Sensitivity analysis of the model structure**, **Response surface topology**: measures using the whole output distribution or a regression surrogate rather than variance alone. - **Factor prioritisation setting**, also **Factor fixing setting**, **Variance cutting setting**, **Factor mapping setting**, **Monte Carlo filtering**, **Regional sensitivity analysis**, **RSA**, **generalised sensitivity analysis**, **Smirnov test in Monte Carlo filtering**, **Generalized likelihood uncertainty estimation**, **GLUE**, **Behavioural and non-behavioural parameter sets**, **Dotty plot**, **Sensitivity index convergence check**, **Bootstrap confidence interval on a sensitivity index**, **Factor ranking stability**, **Multi-method sensitivity comparison**, **Benchmarking of sensitivity analysis methods**, **Objective-function dependence of sensitivity**, **Computational budget for sensitivity analysis**, **Sensitivity analysis of a diagnostic against a predictive purpose**, **Sensitivity analysis under interacting inputs**, **Sensitivity analysis of high-dimensional models**, **Sensitivity analysis reporting standard**: naming what a sensitivity analysis is for before choosing a method, since the setting decides which measure answers the question. - **Sensitivity auditing**, also **Garbage-in garbage-out science**, **GIGO science**, **Quantitative storytelling**, **Instrumental use of a model**, **rhetorical use of a model**, **Model-based advocacy**, **Uncertainty inflation and deflation**, **Overparameterisation as a sensitivity fault**, **Ethics of quantification**, **Socially robust knowledge**, **Assumption hunting**, **rule of assumption hunting**: extension of sensitivity analysis to a model's framing, assumptions and rhetorical use, asking what was left out and whom the framing serves. Costs an audit of the question rather than of the code.

### Calibration, emulation and inverse problems

- **Bayesian calibration of computer models**, also **Kennedy-O'Hagan framework**, **KOH framework**, **Model discrepancy term**, **model inadequacy function**, **structural discrepancy**, **Calibration parameter**, **Control input**, **Code uncertainty**, **Modular Bayes calibration**, **modularisation**, **cut distribution**, **Full Bayes calibration**, **Two-stage calibration**, **plug-in calibration**, **Model calibration**, **Automatic calibration**, **Manual calibration**, **Multi-objective calibration**, **Pareto calibration**, **Bayesian total error analysis**, **BATEA**, **Transitional Markov chain Monte Carlo**, **TMCMC**, **Bayesian melding**, **Bayesian model averaging**, **BMA**, **Model updating**: inferring parameters and a discrepancy function jointly from observations. - **Identifiability of calibration parameters**, also **Confounding of discrepancy and calibration**, **discrepancy-parameter confounding**, **Equifinality**, **Structural identifiability**, **Practical identifiability**, **numerical identifiability**, **Profile likelihood identifiability analysis**, **Ill-posed inverse problem**, **ill-posedness**, **Observability of a parameter**, **Sloppy model**, **model sloppiness**, **stiff and sloppy parameter directions**, **Dynamic identifiability analysis**, **DYNIA**, **Structural stability of a model**: the condition in which many parameter sets fit equally well, so a calibrated value carries no information about the system it names.
- **Emulator**, also **statistical surrogate of a simulator**, **Gaussian process emulation**, **GP emulator**, **Kriging**, **Gaussian process regression**, **Bayes linear analysis**, **Linked Gaussian process emulation**, **Deep Gaussian process emulation**, **Treed Gaussian process**, **TGP**, **Multilevel emulation of a stochastic simulator**, **Multi-fidelity modelling**, **Co-kriging**, **Reduced-order model**, **ROM**, **Proper orthogonal decomposition**, **POD**, **Emulator diagnostics**, **Leave-one-out validation of an emulator**, **Mahalanobis distance emulator diagnostic**, **Nugget effect**, **Correlation function specification**, **Bayesian prediction interval for a simulator**, **Digital twin**: a fast statistical stand-in for an expensive simulator. - **Computer experiment**, also **in silico experiment**, **numerical experiment**, **Design and analysis of computer experiments**, **DACE**, **Deterministic simulator**, **Stochastic simulator**, **Space-filling design**, **Maximin distance design**, **Minimax distance design**, **Maximum entropy design**, **Integrated mean squared prediction error criterion**, **Uniform design**, **Good lattice points design**, **Orthogonal array design**, **Sliced Latin hypercube design**, **Nested space-filling design**, **Sequential design of computer experiments**, **adaptive sampling**, **Screening in computer experiments**, **Ranking and selection procedure**, **Two-stage selection procedure**, **Dudewicz-Dalal procedure**, **Multiple comparisons with a control in simulation**, **Factorial simulation experiment**, **Response surface methodology in simulation**, **Simulation metamodel**: designing runs of a code where replication buys nothing and coverage of the input space is everything. - **History matching**, also **Implausibility measure**, **Not-ruled-out-yet space**, **NROY space**, **Refocussing**, **waves of history matching**, **Pukelsheim three-sigma rule**, **Limits of acceptability approach**, **GLUE limits of acceptability**, **Informal likelihood measure**, **pseudo-likelihood**, **Hard and soft information in calibration**, **Signature-based calibration**, **Bayesian error analysis with reordering**, **BEAR**, **Split-sample calibration and validation**, **Differential split-sample test**, **Proxy-basin test**, **Proxy-basin differential split-sample test**, **Klemes hierarchical validation scheme**: ruling out regions of input space instead of fitting one best point, with the four-level scheme testing transfer across time and place. - **Simulation-based inference**, also **likelihood-free inference**, **Approximate Bayesian computation**, **ABC**, **Simulated method of moments**, **SMM**, **Indirect inference**, **Synthetic likelihood**, **Sequential Monte Carlo**, **particle filter**, **Data assimilation**, **Ensemble Kalman filter**, **EnKF**, **Variational data assimilation**, **3D-Var**, **4D-Var**, **Nudging**, **Newtonian relaxation**, **Observing system simulation experiment**, **OSSE**, **twin experiment**, **Posterior predictive check**, **Prior predictive check**, **Bayesian p-value**: inference where the likelihood cannot be written but the model can be run. Costs very many simulations and a summary statistic whose sufficiency is unproven.

### Pedigree, typology and the quality of a policy-relevant number

- **Walker uncertainty matrix**, also **Walker-Harremoes uncertainty matrix**, **Uncertainty typology for model-based assessment**, **Van der Sluijs uncertainty typology**, **Location of uncertainty**, **Level of uncertainty**, **Nature of uncertainty**, **Statistical uncertainty**, **Recognised ignorance**, **Total ignorance**, **Indeterminacy**, **Ambiguity in model framing**, **framing uncertainty**, **Value-laden assumption**, **Context uncertainty**, **Model outcome uncertainty**, **Uncertainty cascade**: the three-axis classification of an uncertainty by where it sits in the modelling chain, how much is known about it, and whether it is variability or want of knowledge. - **NUSAP**, also **Numeral Unit Spread Assessment Pedigree**, **Numeral**, **Unit**, **Spread**, **Assessment**, **Pedigree**, **pedigree of a number**, **Pedigree matrix**, **pedigree scoring matrix**, **Pedigree criteria**, **Theoretical understanding**, **Pedigree matrix for model structure**, **Strength of the knowledge base**, **Diagnostic diagram**, **Kite diagram**, **Model quality checklist for assessment**: Funtowicz and Ravetz's notation qualifying a policy-relevant number by its spread, its assessment and a scored pedigree covering proxy, empirical basis, methodological rigour and validation.
